paragraphs.text: It is good to watch the contests of the best of men, the athletes of virtue, and to draw benefit from them through the eyes. When praiseworthy things are seen, they seem worth acquiring and become objects of love, and they urge the spectators on to acquire them. Yet no small benefit also comes from accounts of such achievements, brought by those who know them to the ears of those who do not. Some say that sight is more trustworthy than hearing; but hearing is persuaded too, judging what is said by the truthfulness of those who say it. Just as the tongue and palate are trusted to judge sweetness, bitterness and other such qualities, and they cast their vote accordingly, so hearing has been entrusted with judging words, and knows how to tell those that bring some benefit from those that do harm. Now if the memory of beneficial stories remained secure, and the ravages of forgetfulness did not settle on it like a mist and make it fade, it would surely be superfluous and pointless to write such things down, since the benefit they bring would pass very easily even to those who come later. But time ravages bodies by bringing old age and death, and it ravages noble deeds by producing forgetfulness and dulling memory. So no one could fairly blame us for undertaking to write about the way of life of men who loved God. Just as those entrusted with healing bodies prepare medicines to fight disease and help the sick, so the careful labor of such writing becomes a kind of remedy against harm, an enemy of forgetfulness and an ally of memory. Would it not be absurd for poets and historians to record valor in war, for tragedians to put on open display calamities better left hidden, and to leave behind a written memorial of these things, while others spend their words on comedy and laughter, and yet for us to stand by while men are handed over to oblivion who, in a mortal body subject to passion, displayed freedom from passion and imitated the bodiless nature? What penalty would we not justly pay if we looked on while the memory of these admirable contests faded? For if they themselves, imitating the supreme philosophy of the saints of old, engraved the memory of those saints not in bronze and letters but, by taking the impress of all their virtue, made themselves into living images and monuments of them, what pardon could we fairly expect if we did not honor this celebrated life even with letters? And this when those who compete at the Olympic Games, and indeed the charioteers who are proclaimed victors in the races, receive this very honor. And not only these: lovers of spectacles also paint on panels men [?], effeminates, and creatures of whom one cannot tell whether they are men or women, striving to make their memory last as long as possible.

Yet the memory of such people brings harm to souls, not benefit. Nevertheless those who love these figures, or those, honor them with painting, even though they do damage. And since death plunders our nature, which is mortal, they mix colors, set the likenesses of these people on panels, and contrive that their memory should last far longer than their lives. We, however, are writing about a life that teaches philosophy and imitates the way of life in heaven. We do not paint the features of bodies or display their outlines to those who do not know them; rather we sketch the forms of invisible souls, and display unseen wars and hidden struggles. For such is the armor with which the general and champion of their phalanx, Paul, has clothed them. 'Take up,' he says, 'the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to withstand on the evil day, and having done everything, to stand.' And again: 'Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.' Having clothed them in this armor, he led them into the contests.

For such too is the nature of the enemy: bodiless, invisible, approaching unseen, plotting in secret, lying in ambush and attacking suddenly. This same general taught this when he said, 'Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.' Yet though the company of these saints had such adversaries, or rather though each of them was surrounded by so many and such enemies (for the enemies did not attack them all together, but assailed now this one, now that one), they won so brilliant a victory that their adversaries fled, while they pursued them in force and raised a trophy with no one standing in their way. It was not their nature that gave them victory, for that is mortal and full of countless passions, but their will, which drew down divine grace. For they became ardent lovers of the divine beauty and chose gladly to do and suffer anything for the one they loved. So they nobly bore the uprising of the passions and stoutly beat off the blizzards of the devil's arrows; and, to speak in the Apostle's words, by pummeling the body and bringing it into subjection, they calmed the inflammations of anger and forced the frenzy of the desires to keep quiet. Having thus lulled the passions to sleep by fasting and sleeping on the ground, and put a stop to their leaping, they compelled the body to make a truce with the soul. So they brought this inborn war to an end; and having arbitrated peace between the two, they drove out the whole host of their opponents. For the enemies had no thoughts within to betray the place to them, and, deprived of the cooperation of human members, they were unable to wage war. The devil uses our own members as arrows against us. If the eyes are not ensnared, the ears not bewitched, the touch not tickled, and the mind does not accept evil counsels, the zeal of the plotters is in vain. A city built on a height, encircled by strong walls and surrounded on every side by deep ravines, could not be taken by any enemy unless someone inside betrayed it and secretly opened some postern gates. In the same way it is impossible for the demons who wage war from outside to overcome a soul encircled by divine grace, unless the slackness of some thought opens a postern among our senses and admits the enemy through it. Those whom we are praising were clearly taught this by the divine Scripture, and they heard God saying through the prophet, 'Death has come up through the windows.' So they shut their senses with the divine laws as with bars and bolts, and entrusted the keys to the mind. Neither tongue nor lips were opened unless the mind commanded it, nor did the pupil of the eye venture to peep out from behind the eyelids without permission. Hearing, which cannot wall off its entrance with eyelids or lips, thrust away foolish words and admitted only those in which the mind took delight.

So they trained their sense of smell not to long for fragrances, since these by nature make one soft and slack. So they drove out the surfeit of the belly and taught it to take only such things as met need, not pleasure, and only as much as could prevent death from hunger. So they overthrew the sweet tyranny of sleep, freed their eyelids from slavery to it, and trained them to rule instead of serve, accepting the service sleep provides not whenever it came upon them but whenever they themselves summoned it, for the brief relief of nature. Having thus taken care to guard the walls and the gates, and having established harmony among the thoughts within, they laughed at the adversaries attacking from outside. The enemies could not break in by force, because of the security provided by divine grace, and they found no traitor willing to let them in. And though the enemies have an invisible nature, they could not master a visible body subject to the necessities of nature. For its charioteer, musician and helmsman, holding the reins with great skill, persuaded the horses to run in good order; he tuned the strings of the senses to produce a perfectly harmonious sound in rhythm; and moving the rudder with expertise, he broke the force both of the waves' assault and of the winds' onslaught.

These men journeyed through life by way of countless labors and tamed the body with sweat and hardship. They did not know the experience of laughter, but spent their whole lives in weeping and tears. They thought fasting a Sybaritic luxury, toilsome vigil the sweetest sleep, the hardness of the ground a soft bed, and time spent in prayers and psalmody a boundless and insatiable pleasure. Who could fail to admire, as is fitting, these men who gathered every kind of virtue? Or rather, who could praise them as they deserve? I too know well that no words could match their virtue; nevertheless the attempt must be made. It would not be right that, because they became perfect lovers of true philosophy, they should receive not even lesser praise. We shall not, however, write one common eulogy for them all, for different gifts were given to them by God. The blessed Paul taught this when he said, 'To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the same Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.' And showing the source of all these, he added, 'All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as he wills.' Since, then, they received different gifts, it is fitting that we give an account of each one separately. We shall not go through all that they did, for a whole lifetime would not suffice for such a work; rather we shall relate a few of the things each one lived or did, and having shown through these few the character of the whole life, we shall move on to another. Nor shall we try to record the way of life of all the saints who have been distinguished everywhere, for we do not know all those who have shone everywhere, nor could they all be written about by one person.
I shall write, then, only of the lives of those who appeared like luminaries in the East and whose rays have reached the ends of the inhabited world.

The account will proceed as a plain narrative, not following the rules of encomium, but simply relating a few things. I ask those who will read this History of the Lovers of God, or Ascetic Way of Life (let anyone call the work as he pleases), not to disbelieve what is said if they hear of things beyond their own strength, nor to measure the virtue of these men by themselves. Rather let them know clearly that God is accustomed to measure out the gifts of the Holy Spirit according to the dispositions of the devout, and to give greater gifts to the more perfect. Let this be said to those who are not very thoroughly initiated into divine things. For those initiated into the sanctuaries of the Spirit know the generosity of the Spirit, and the kinds of wonders he works among people through people, drawing unbelievers to the knowledge of God by the magnificence of his miracles. Whoever disbelieves what we are about to relate clearly does not believe that the things done through Moses, Joshua, Elijah and Elisha really happened, and regards as a myth the miracles worked through the holy apostles too. But if he testifies to the truth of those, let him believe that these too are free from falsehood. For the grace that was at work in those men is the same that has worked through these. Grace is ever-flowing; it chooses the worthy and, as through fountains, pours forth through them the streams of its benefaction. Of the things I shall relate, I was an eyewitness of some; what I did not see I heard from those who saw these men, lovers of virtue who were counted worthy to see them and receive their teaching. In writing down the teaching of the gospel, too, it is not only Matthew and John who are trustworthy, the first and great evangelists, who were eyewitnesses of the Lord's miracles, but also Luke and Mark, whom those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning and ministers of the word instructed precisely, not only in what the Lord suffered and did, but also in what he continually taught.

Though the blessed Luke was not an eyewitness, at the beginning of his work he says that he is giving an account of matters that have been fully established. And we, though we hear that he was not an eyewitness of these very events but received this teaching from others, pay no less attention to him and to Mark than to Matthew and John. For each of them is a trustworthy narrator, having been taught by those who saw. Accordingly we too shall relate some things as eyewitnesses, and others trusting eyewitnesses who told us of them, men who imitated the life of these saints. I have spent more words on this because I wish to persuade you that what I shall relate is true. I shall begin my narrative, then, from this point.

Moses, the divine lawgiver, who laid bare the bottom of the sea, flooded the waterless desert with water, and worked all his other wonders, wrote down the way of life of the saints of old, not by using the wisdom he had learned from the Egyptians, but by receiving the radiance of grace from above. From what other source could he have learned the virtue of Abel, the love of God of Enoch, the righteousness of Noah, the devout priesthood of Melchizedek, and Abraham's calling, his faith, his endurance, his attentive hospitality, the celebrated sacrifice of his son, and the list of his other achievements—in short, the contests, victories and proclamations of those inspired men—unless he had received the rays of the spiritual and divine Spirit? I too need that same help at present, as I attempt to write the lives of the saints who shone a little before us and in our own day, and wish to set before those who desire to imitate them a kind of legislation. We must therefore call upon their prayers and begin the narrative.

Nisibis is a city on the border between the Roman and Persian empires. In former times it paid tribute to the Romans and was subject to their rule. Setting out from this city, the great James embraced the solitary and quiet life. He took to the peaks of the highest mountains and lived there. In spring, summer and autumn he used the thickets, with the sky for a roof; in the winter season a cave received him and gave him a little shelter. For food he did not eat what is sown and grown with labour, but what springs up of its own accord.

He gathered the fruits that grow wild on the trees, and the edible herbs and greens, and from these he gave his body what was enough to keep it alive, doing without the use of fire. He had no need of wool either, for the coarsest goat hair served in its place. From this he made himself both a tunic and a simple cloak. While he wore down his body in this way, he constantly offered spiritual food to his soul. He cleansed the eye of his mind and made it a clear mirror of the divine Spirit, and, in the words of the divine Apostle, "with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, he was transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Lord, the Spirit." From this his boldness before God grew day by day, and whatever he asked of God, so far as it was right to ask it, he received at once. From this too he foresaw things to come, as a prophet does, and by the grace of the Holy Spirit he received the power to work miracles. I will tell a few of these, and so show those who do not know it a ray of his apostolic radiance.

At that time people's madness for idols was at its height. Lifeless wooden images claimed the worship that belongs to God, and most people neglected the service of God. Those who would not share in that drunkenness were held in contempt. Being sober, they judged things accurately: they laughed at the weakness of the idols and worshipped the Creator of all things.

At that time he went into Persia to see the plants of true religion and to give them the care they needed. As he was passing a spring, some girls were standing at their washing and treading clothes clean with their feet. They felt no shame at the strangeness of his garb. Casting modesty aside, they stared at the man of God with brazen faces and shameless eyes, neither covering their heads nor letting down their tucked-up clothes. The man of God was displeased at this. He wished to show the power of God at the right moment, so that by a miracle he might set them free from their impiety. He cursed the spring, and at once its stream vanished. He cursed the girls too, and punished their shameless youth with premature gray hair. The deed followed the word: the black of their hair was changed, and they looked like young trees in spring clothed in autumn leaves.

So they became aware of their punishment, for the waters of the spring had fled, and as they looked at one another's heads they saw that sudden change. They ran to the city to report what had happened. The people ran out, found the great James, and begged him to relax his anger and lift the punishment. Without the slightest delay he offered his supplication to the Lord and ordered the waters to gush forth again. At once they reappeared from their own storehouses, channelled back at the righteous man's nod. Having obtained this, the people also begged that their daughters' locks be given back their former colour. They say he granted this too, but asked for the girls who had received that correction. When they did not come, he let the punishment stand, as a lesson in chaste behaviour, an occasion for decorum, and a lasting and clear reminder of divine power. Such was the miracle of this new Moses, worked not by a blow of a rod but drawing its power from the sign of the cross. For my part, besides the miracle I greatly admire his gentleness as well. He did not hand those shameless girls over to bloodthirsty bears, as the great Elisha did; instead he used a harmless correction involving only slight disfigurement, and taught them both piety and decorum. I say this not to accuse the prophet of harshness—may I never be so mad!—but to show that, though James had that same power, he did what befitted the gentleness of Christ and the New Covenant. On another occasion he saw a Persian judge give an unjust verdict. He cursed a very large stone that lay nearby, commanding it to shatter and scatter, and so to expose the injustice of that verdict. At once the stone split into countless fragments, and those present were terrified. The judge, filled with dread, revoked his former verdict and gave another, just one. Here too James imitated his own Lord. Wishing to show that he endured his passion willingly, and that he could easily have punished the wicked had he wished, the Lord brought no punishment on them, but showed his own power by withering a lifeless fig tree with a word. Imitating this same love for humankind, James did not punish the unjust judge but taught him justice by striking the stone.

Distinguished by these deeds, loved by all and on everyone's lips, he was called to the ministry of the episcopate and given charge of his native city. He exchanged that life in the mountains for a life in the city, though not by his own choice, yet he changed neither his food nor his clothing. His places changed, but his way of life admitted no change. His labours, rather, increased and became many times greater than before. To his fasting, his sleeping on the ground and his wearing of sackcloth were added constant cares for those in need: I mean attention to widows, protection of orphans, rebuking of wrongdoers, and just help for the wronged.

But why list for those who already know them all the duties that surround anyone who takes on this charge? He embraced such labours with exceptional zeal, since he both loved and feared the Lord of the sheep exceptionally. And the greater the wealth of virtue he gathered, the more abundantly he enjoyed the grace of the all-holy Spirit. Once, as he was setting out for some village or city—I cannot say the place exactly—some poor men came up to him. They had laid out one of their companions as if he were dead and begged him for something toward his burial. He granted their request. And he offered a prayer to God as for a dead man, asking him to forgive the sins committed in his life and to count him worthy of the company of the righteous. As these words were spoken, the soul of the man who had been feigning death flew away, and the grave-clothes were supplied for the body. When the holy man had gone on a little way, the men who had staged this drama told the one lying there to get up. But when they saw that he did not hear, that the pretence had become reality and the mask had turned into the face, they caught up with the great James. Lamenting and rolling at his feet, they said that poverty was the cause of the drama they had dared to stage, and begged him to forgive them their offence and to give back to the dead man the soul that had been taken away. Imitating the Lord's love for humankind, he accepted their plea and worked the miracle, restoring by prayer to the man lying there the life that prayer had taken from him. To me this seems like the miracle of the great Peter, who sent Ananias and Sapphira to their death for stealing and lying.

For in the same way James took away the life of a man who had stolen the truth and used a lie. But Peter knew of the theft, since the grace of the Spirit revealed it to him, and inflicted the penalty; James did not know what lay behind the drama, but offered his prayer and so stopped the course of the pretender's life. And the divine Apostle did not undo the calamity of those who died, for the beginnings of the saving proclamation needed fear; but James, filled with apostolic grace, both punished at the right moment and quickly lifted the punishment, for he knew that the offenders would profit by this. But we must move on to his other deeds and recount them briefly too.

Arius, father and author of the blasphemy against the Only-begotten and the all-holy Spirit, had set his tongue in motion against its own Maker and filled Egypt with uproar and confusion. Constantine, the greatest of emperors, was the Zerubbabel of our flock: in his time he brought back from exile the whole captivity of the faithful and raised up on high the divine temples that had been thrown to the ground. When this emperor assembled all the presidents of the churches at Nicaea at that time, the great James came with the rest to fight for the true doctrines, like a champion and a front-line fighter for the whole army.

For Nisibis was then under Roman rule. In that great council many things were said well and rightly, and many otherwise. There were a few who held contrary views but did not dare to lay bare their impiety; instead they disguised it with certain baits, which not everyone could recognize but which were quite plain to those accurately initiated into the truth. The confession of faith was dictated that prevails and is proclaimed throughout the whole world to this day. All signed it, confessing with hand and pen that this was how they believed and thought. Most did so gladly; but seven advocates of Arius's blasphemy, though they agreed with tongue and hand, held a conviction that contradicted their tongue. So the prophecy says: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me"; and so Jeremiah's voice cries out plainly: "You are near their mouth, and far from their inmost parts." In agreement with these the blessed David also said of such men: "With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed"; and again: "Their words were softer than oil, yet they are darts." These men urged the great Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, to take pity on Arius, who had been condemned by that whole army. Alexander knew their hidden treachery and suspected Arius's wickedness, and so he did not grant their request. Some others, who had lived in simplicity, then delivered many praises of compassion, saying that the God of all rejoices in it. But the great Alexander called this unjust compassion toward one man inhumanity, since it would bring ruin to many, and he said it would become an occasion of harm to all the flocks. Then the divine James advised everyone to undergo the hardship of fasting and to entreat God together for seven days to bring about what would benefit the churches.

All accepted the divine man's proposal, for they knew that he shone with apostolic gifts. Fasting was joined with prayer, and the Pilot of the churches decreed what was for their good. When the Lord's day came, on which most expected the wicked man to be received, and the time of the divine liturgy had arrived, and all were waiting to see the enemy of God shown mercy, then a truly divine and astonishing miracle took place. In a loathsome and foul-smelling place, that accursed man, while voiding the waste of his gluttonous food, voided along with it the very vessels that hold it. His bowels were thus dissolved and passed out with the excrement, and the wretch fell down on the spot and suffered that most shameful death. He paid the penalty for his foul-smelling blasphemy in a foul-smelling place, and received his slaughter through the tongue of the great James.

Divine Scripture admires Phinehas the priest, and rightly, because he slew Zimri, who was bringing destruction on the people. That is why the blessed David said in his psalm: "Phinehas stood up and made atonement, and the plague ceased; and it was counted to him as righteousness, from generation to generation for ever." Yet Phinehas used a weapon of war to carry out that just and celebrated slaughter, whereas for James his tongue was enough in place of spear and sword, and he slew the ungodly man, "so that he might not see the glory of the Lord." This alone is enough to expose the folly of the heirs of Arius's impiety. For so great a man was a herald and advocate of the doctrines we hold in honour, and he so utterly loathed their impiety that he struck down its very father, using his tongue as a weapon. When the sacred assembly broke up and each returned to his own home, James too went back, like a victorious champion exulting in the trophies of true religion. As time went on, that great and wonderful emperor departed this life with the crowns of piety, and his sons inherited the rule of the world. Then the king of the Persians, whose name was Shapur, despising the sons as not having their father's power, marched against Nisibis with a very large force of cavalry and a very large army of infantry; he also had a great many elephants. He divided his army as for a siege and surrounded the city on every side. He set up siege engines and built towers; he drove in stakes and fenced the spaces between them with branches woven like basketwork, ordered his soldiers to heap up earth, and raised towers against the city's towers. Then he sent archers up onto them and ordered them to shoot their arrows at those standing on the wall, while he ordered others to undermine the wall from below. But since all these efforts came to nothing, undone by the prayer of the holy man, he finally used his multitude of hands to dam the river that flowed past the city. When he had collected as much of the river's water as possible behind the dam, he released it all at once against the wall, using it as a most violent siege engine. The wall could not withstand the onslaught of the water; shaken by its force, the whole of that section collapsed completely.

The besiegers raised a great shout, thinking the city would now be easy to take, for they did not know of the great wall that protected its inhabitants. Still, they postponed their assault, seeing that the water had made the city impassable.

So they withdrew to a distance, as if their labour were over, and rested themselves and tended their horses. The people of the city turned to more earnest supplication, with the great James as their intercessor. All those of age rebuilt the wall in haste, caring neither for beauty nor for neat construction but putting everything together as it came—stones, bricks, and whatever anyone brought. In a single night the work advanced and reached a height sufficient to stop the charge of horses and to prevent men from climbing over without ladders. Then they all begged the man of God to appear on the wall and to shoot the enemy down with curses.

He agreed and went up. When he saw their countless thousands, he begged God to send a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes upon them. He spoke, and God sent them, obeying him as he had obeyed Moses. The men were wounded by these divine arrows, while the horses and elephants broke their tethers and ran off, scattering in every direction, unable to bear those stings. The impious king saw that all his siege engines had been of no use and that his assault with the river had proved fruitless, since the wall that had fallen had been rebuilt. He saw his whole army worn out by its labours, suffering in the open air, and driven by a plague sent from God. He also saw the divine man walking on the wall and, supposing that he was the emperor directing the work—for he appeared to be clad in purple and a diadem—he grew angry with those who had deceived him, who had persuaded him to make war and had told him the emperor was not there. He passed sentence of death on them, broke up his army, and returned to his own palace as fast as he could. Such wonders God worked for this new Hezekiah too, wonders not less than those of old but, it seems to me, even greater. For that the city was not taken even when its wall had fallen—what greater miracle could there be? I also greatly admire this: that even when he used curses, he did not ask for thunderbolts and lightning to be sent, as the great Elijah did when two captains of fifty came to him, each with his fifty men. For he had heard the Lord say plainly to James and John, who tried to do this very thing: "You do not know what spirit you are of." That is why he did not ask that the earth open up for them, nor pray that their army be given over to fire, but that they be wounded by those tiny creatures, so that, recognizing the power of God, they might at last come to learn true religion. Such was the boldness this divine man had before God; such was the grace he enjoyed from above. Continuing in these ways and growing day by day in divine things, he laid down this life in the greatest glory and set out on his journey from here. When time had passed and this city had been handed over to the Persian kingdom by the emperor then reigning, all its inhabitants left it and carried their champion's body with them. They grieved and lamented their removal, yet sang of the power of their victorious champion. For had he been alive, they would never have fallen under barbarian rule. Having told these things about this divine man, I will pass on to another account, begging to share in his blessing.

Julian, whom the local people honoured with the surname Saba—in Greek the name means "old man"—built his ascetic hut in the region once called the land of the Parthians and now called Osroene. On the west this region stretches to the very bank of the river, whose name is the Euphrates; on the east it marks the boundary of Roman rule, for there Assyria begins, the western limit of the Persian kingdom, which later generations named Adiabene. In this province there are many large and populous cities, and a great deal of land that is inhabited, but also a great deal that is uninhabited and desert. This divine man went to the farthest part of this desert and found a cave, not made by hands nor well and properly dug, but able to give a little shelter to those wishing to take refuge in it. He gladly settled in the place, thinking it more splendid than palaces gleaming with gold and silver.
There he lived, taking food once a week.

His food was bread made of millet, and coarse bran bread at that; his relish was salt; his sweetest drink was the water of a natural spring, and even this was not measured by how much would satisfy him but limited to what the food he had eaten required. His luxury, his delicacy and his feast of every kind was the psalmody of David and unceasing converse with God. He enjoyed these insatiably and never wished to have his fill; he was always being filled, and always crying out: "How sweet are your words to my throat! Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth." He had heard the blessed David say again: "The judgments of the Lord are true, all of them righteous, more to be desired than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." He had heard him say again: "Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart"; and again: "Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice"; and: "Gladden my heart, that I may fear your name"; and: "Taste and see that the Lord is good"; and: "My soul thirsted for God, the mighty and living"; and: "My soul has clung to you." And he took into himself the love of the one who had said these things. It was for this very reason that the great David taught them in song, so that he might make many people sharers with him and fellow lovers of God. Nor was he disappointed in his hope: he wounded this inspired man too, and countless others, with divine love. For this man received so great a flame of love that he was drunk with longing, saw nothing of earthly things, and dreamed of his Beloved alone by night and pictured him by day.

Many learned of this supreme philosophy of his, some living nearby and others far away, for his fame ran everywhere as if on wings. They hastened to him, begging to share in his wrestling school and to spend the rest of their lives under him as their trainer and coach. For it is not only birds that hunt birds, singing and calling those of their own kind to them and entangling them in the snares laid around; men too hunt their fellows, some to their ruin, others to their salvation. Gathering together in this way, they soon became ten, then twice and three times as many, and then they made up the number of a hundred. Even when they had grown so many, that cave held them, for they had learned from the old man to condemn care for the body. Like their trainer, they too ate millet bread seasoned with salt. Some time later they also gathered wild greens, filled jars with them, and mixed in as much brine as was needed, and so those who needed some relief had a relish. But damp dwellings are hostile to this vegetable, for they naturally make it go mouldy and rot.

So when this happened to this relish (for the cave took in a great deal of damp from every side), the members of the company begged the old man to allow them to build a small hut, big enough for the jars of this relish.

At first he would not accept the request; but at length he was persuaded, for he had been taught by the great Paul not to seek his own interests but to associate with the lowly. He gave them the measurements of the hut, which were short and small, and went off far from the cave to offer his customary supplications to God.

For it was his custom to walk through the desert, often fifty stades and sometimes twice that, separating himself from all human company and turning inward, so as to converse with God alone and to behold, as in a mirror, that divine and ineffable beauty. Taking advantage of this absence, those who had been counted worthy of his care built the hut to suit their needs, but larger than they had been told.

He returned after ten days, like a Moses coming down from the mountain and from that inexpressible vision, and when he saw that the building had been made larger than he wished, he said: "I fear, my friends, that by enlarging our dwellings on earth we may make our dwellings in heaven smaller. Yet these are temporary and useful to us for only a short while, while those are eternal and can have no end." He said this to train the company in what is more perfect. Nevertheless he put up with it, heeding the apostle's words: "I do not seek my own advantage, but that of the many, that they may be saved." He also trained them to offer their hymnody to God in common inside, and after daybreak to go out into the desert two by two; one would bend his knees and offer the Master the worship due to him, while the other stood and sang fifteen of David's psalms; then they would exchange tasks, the one standing up to sing and the other bowing to the ground in worship. This they continued to do from early morning until late evening. A little before sunset they rested briefly and returned to the cave, some from one direction and some from another, and all together made their offering to the Master.
The old man himself used to take one of the more distinguished brothers as his partner in this service.

The one who most often went with him was a Persian by race, tall and admirable in appearance, but possessing a soul more wonderful than his appearance. His name was James. After the old man's death he shone in every virtue and was distinguished and admired not only by those there but also in the schools of philosophy in Syria, where he died, having lived, as they say, a hundred and four years. When he shared the great old man's journey into the desert, he followed at a distance, for the teacher would not let him come near, lest this give them occasion for conversation and conversation steal the mind away from contemplating God. As he followed, he saw lying on the path a huge serpent.

When he saw it, he did not dare go forward, and though fear often made him want to turn aside, he took heart again. Then he bent down, picked up a pebble and threw it, and saw that the serpent stayed in the same position and could not move at all. Realizing that it was dead, he concluded that the beast's death was the old man's doing. He finished the journey and completed the service of hymnody, and when the time for rest came and the old man sat down and told him to rest his body a little too, at first he sat in silence. But when the old man began some conversation, James, with a smile, begged him to make plain to him what he did not know. When he gave him leave to ask, James said: "On the way I saw a huge serpent lying there. At first I was afraid, thinking it was alive, but when I saw that it was dead, I took courage and went on. So tell me, Father, who killed it? For you were leading the way, and no one else has gone along that path." The old man said: "Stop prying into such things, which can bring no benefit to those who concern themselves with them." But the admirable James pressed him no less, eager to learn the truth. The old man, after trying for a long time to keep it hidden, could no longer bear to vex his devoted disciple, and said: "I will tell you, since you are eager to learn. But I charge you not to let anyone else share what I am about to say while I am alive. For such things ought to be kept hidden, since they often stir up boastfulness and pride. When I depart from here and am free of such passions, I do not forbid you to speak and to tell of the power of divine grace. Know, then," said the great Julian, "that as I was walking along the path that beast came at me and opened its mouth, eager to swallow me.

"But I called on the name of God and pointed the trophy of the cross at it with my finger, and I shook off all fear; and I saw the beast fall to the ground at once, and after singing praise to our common Savior I went on my way." Having finished the story in this way, he rose and set off on the road back to the cave.

On another occasion a young man of noble birth, brought up in luxury, but possessed of a zeal greater than his strength, begged the old man to let him share his journey into the desert, not the ordinary one that all of them took every day, but the longest, which often meant an absence of seven days and often even ten.

This was the much-celebrated Asterius. The inspired old man tried to dissuade the young man, telling him how waterless the desert was, but the young man kept pressing his entreaties to be granted this favor. Overcome by his pleas, the old man gave in. At first the young man followed eagerly; but when the first, second and third days had passed, scorched by the sun's rays (for it was summer, and at the height of summer the heat is, of course, fiercer), he was tormented by thirst. At first he was ashamed to admit his distress, remembering what his teacher had warned him beforehand; but when he was overcome and seized with faintness, he begged the old man to have pity on him. The old man reminded him of his warnings and told him to go back. When the young man said that he did not know the way back to the cave, and that even if he did he could not make the return journey, since thirst had used up his strength, the godly man took pity on the youth's suffering and made allowance for the weakness of his body. Bending his knees, he besought the Master, watered the ground with warm tears, and sought a way of deliverance for the young man. And he who does the will of those who fear him and hears their prayer turned the stream of tears that touched the dust into a spring of water; and when the young man had drunk his fill of it, he told him to go back at once. The spring has remained to this day, bearing witness to the Mosaic prayer of the inspired old man.

For just as Moses long ago struck that barren rock with his rod and flooded it with streams of river-water, to satisfy those many thousands who were thirsty, so this godly man, by watering that driest of sands with his tears, drew forth flowing springs, not to relieve the thirst of many tens of thousands but of one young man. His soul being enlightened by divine grace, he foresaw very clearly the perfection the young man would one day attain. For many years later Asterius, called by divine grace to train many others in the same virtue, set up his ascetic wrestling school in the district of Gindarus, a very large village under the jurisdiction of Antioch. He drew to himself many other athletes of philosophy, and among them the great Acacius, I mean the renowned and much-celebrated one, who was distinguished in the monastic life and sent forth brilliant rays of virtue when he was made a bishop and was appointed to shepherd Beroea. Entrusted with leadership of the flock for fifty-eight years, he did not abandon the form of the ascetic life, but blended ascetic virtue with the virtue of public life; taking the strictness of the one and the prudent management of the other, he united what had been separate. Of this virtue the hunter and trainer was that same Asterius, who remained so ardent a lover of the great old man that he made the journey to him often twice a year, and often three times.

When he came, he used to bring dried figs for the company, loading them onto three or four beasts of burden. Setting aside two medimni, enough to last the old man the whole year, he put this load on his own shoulders, making himself his teacher's beast of burden. And carrying this load he walked not ten or twenty stades but a journey of seven days. Once, when the old man saw him carrying the load of figs on his shoulders, he was displeased and said that he would not take this food; for it was not right for Asterius to endure so much toil while he himself feasted on the other's sweat. But Asterius swore that he would not take the load off his shoulders unless the old man agreed to partake of the food he had brought. "I will do as you bid," said the old man; "only put the sack down as quickly as you can." In this too he imitated the first of the apostles, who, when the Lord wished to wash his feet, at first refused, flatly insisting that this would not happen; but when he heard that he would be cut off from fellowship with the Master unless he allowed it, he begged him to wash his hands and his head as well as his feet. So too the great John, when told to baptize the Savior, first confessed his own servitude and pointed to the Master, but afterwards did what he was told, not out of presumption but in obedience to the Master. So too this godly man found it hard to enjoy food for which another had toiled; but when he saw his attendant's most ardent zeal, he put the other's service before his own preference.

Perhaps some fault-finder, someone who has learned only to mock what is good, might say that this story is not worth recording. But I have added it to the man's other wonders not only because I wish to show the reverence great men had for him, but also because I consider it profitable to make known the sweetness and modesty of his character.

For though he was so great and of such virtue, he did not think himself worthy even of ordinary honor. He would push it away as in no way befitting him, yet he would put up with it again, since it benefited those who offered it.

Fleeing this honor (for he had become known to all and, through his fame, drew to himself those who love what is good), he finally set out for Mount Sinai with a few of his closest companions, not passing through any city or village, but making the trackless desert passable. On their shoulders they carried the food they needed, that is, bread and salt, together with a wooden cup and a sponge tied to a cord, so that if they ever found water too deep to reach, they could draw it up with the sponge, squeeze it out into the cup, and drink. So, after completing a journey of many days, they reached the mountain they longed for, worshiped their Master, and spent a long time there, regarding the solitude of the place and the stillness of soul as the greatest delight. Under that rock where Moses, chief of the prophets, hid and was counted worthy to see God, as far as it was possible to see him, Julian built a church and consecrated a holy altar, which has survived to this day; and then he returned to his own wrestling school.

He learned of the threats of the emperor who shared his name but was impious: having threatened the godly with utter destruction, he had set out on his campaign against the Persians, and those who shared his views were eagerly awaiting that accursed return. Then Julian offered earnest prayer to God and prolonged it for ten days, until he heard a voice saying that the foul and stinking swine had been slain. Yet even when he had received this answer to his prayer, he did not bring his prayer to an end at once, but changed his petition into hymnody, sending up a hymn of thanksgiving to the Savior of his own people, the forbearing yet mighty enemy of those who are not his. For he had shown long patience with the impious man; but since that patience only trained the wretch in greater fury, he brought punishment on him in due time. When he had completed his prayer and turned to his companions, it was plain that he was in good spirits, for his face shone with gladness.

His companions were amazed at this novel sight, for he who always looked stern was now seen smiling, and they asked the reason. "Now, my friends," he said, "is the time for joy and gladness. For the wicked one has ceased, as Isaiah says, and has paid the penalty his outrages deserved. He who played the tyrant against God, who made and saved him, has received a just death at the hand of one of his subjects. That is why I rejoice, seeing the churches he made war on exulting, and seeing that the wretch obtained no help from the demons he honored." Such was the foreknowledge he was granted concerning the death of that impious man. Later Valens, who took up the reins of Roman rule after him, abandoned the truth of the gospel teachings and embraced the deceit of Arius's error, and then a greater storm arose against the Church: its helmsmen were driven out everywhere, and pirates and enemies were brought in to replace them. And so as not to recount that whole tragedy now, I will pass over the rest and mention only one thing, which clearly showed the grace of the divine Spirit that blossomed in this old man.

The great Meletius, to whom the God of the universe had entrusted the shepherding of Antioch, had been driven out of that city. All who belonged to the sacred clergy had also been driven out of the holy churches, together with the like-minded people who upheld the one substance of the divine Trinity. Sometimes they would gather on the lower slopes of the mountain and hold their sacred assemblies there; at other times they made the bank of the river their place of prayer; at other times again the military drill ground that lies before the northern gate. For their enemies would not allow the godly to settle in any one place. The nurslings of falsehood spread a rumor and sowed the report through that city that the great Julian, I mean this old man, had embraced communion with the doctrines they professed.

This especially grieved the godly, who feared that the rumor might deceive the simpler and more naive and entangle them in the nets of the heretics. But those inspired and blessed men Flavian and Diodore, who had been counted worthy of the priesthood and were leaders of the holy people, together with Aphrahat, whose life I shall, God willing, relate to you separately, persuaded the great Acacius, whom we have already mentioned, to take as his companion on the road his own teacher, the disciple of this holy old man, that excellent Asterius, and to hasten to the common glory of the Church, the support of the gospel teaching, and persuade him to leave his life in the desert and come to the help of so many thousands who were perishing through deceit, and to quench the flame of Arius with the dew of his coming. The godly Acacius hastened, taking the great Asterius as he had been told, and came to that greatest luminary of the Church. After greeting him, he said: "Tell me, Father, for what reason do you endure all this toil so gladly?" He replied: "The service of God is more precious to me than body and soul and life and all my existence, and I try as far as I can to offer him worship that is pure of defilement, and to please him in all things." "I will show you a way," said Acacius, "by which you will serve him more than you do now. And I shall say this not relying on my own reasoning alone, but having learned it from his own teaching.

"For once he asked Peter whether he loved him more than the others did, and learned what he knew even before Peter spoke—'You know, Lord, that I love you,' Peter said—and he showed him by what action he might serve him more: 'If you love me,' he said, 'shepherd my sheep and feed my lambs.' This, Father, is what you too must do. For the flocks are in danger of being destroyed by wolves, and the one you love so much loves them very much; and it is characteristic of lovers to do what delights those they love. Besides, there is no small danger, and the loss of all those many great labors, if you allow yourself to abandon in silence the truth that is being so fiercely attacked, while those devoted to it are caught, and your name becomes the bait for those being hunted. For the champions of Arius's abomination boldly claim that you share in their impiety." As soon as the old man heard this, he said farewell to his stillness for the time being and, undaunted by the unfamiliar turmoil of city life, hurried to Antioch.

After he had covered two or three stages through the desert, evening overtook him and he came to a village. A wealthy woman, learning that this holy company had arrived, ran to reap the blessing of his presence, and throwing herself at his feet she begged him to make her house his lodging. The old man agreed, even though for more than forty years he had kept himself apart from the sight of women. While that admirable woman, who emulated Sarah's hospitality, was busy serving those holy men, her seven-year-old child, the only child she had, fell into the well, for it was evening and dark. As you would expect, there was an uproar over it. When the mother realized what had happened, she told everyone to keep quiet, put a cover over the well, and went on with her serving. When the table had been set before the godly men, the godly old man asked for the woman's child to be called in to share in the blessing. The admirable woman said that the child was unwell, but he insisted that it be brought. When the mother revealed what had happened, the old man left the table and ran to the well. He ordered the cover to be taken off and lights to be brought, and he saw the child sitting on the surface of the water, splashing it with his hand as children do, and treating what was thought to be his death as a game and a plaything. They tied a man with ropes and let him down, and drew the child up; at once the child ran to the old man's feet, saying that he had seen him in the water holding him up and keeping him from going under. This was the reward the admirable woman received from the blessed old man for her hospitality. To pass over the other things that happened on the way: they reached Antioch, and everyone came running together from every side, longing to see the man of God, and each hoping to receive some cure for his ailment.

He lodged in the caves at the foot of the mountain, where they say the divine apostle, blessed Paul, also lodged and hid. But at once, so that everyone might learn that he was a man, he was seized by a very violent attack of fever. The great Acacius, seeing the crowd that had gathered, was distressed at the illness that had come upon him, for he thought that those who had come would be shaken if they learned of the sickness, since they were men who expected to find healing through his hand. "Do not lose heart," the old man said. "If health is necessary, God will grant this too at once." Immediately after these words he turned to supplication, and, as was his custom, bringing his knees and forehead down to the ground, he begged to recover his health, if any benefit would come from it to those who had gathered. He had not yet finished his prayer when a heavy sweat suddenly broke out and quenched the flame of the fever.

After freeing many from all kinds of diseases there, he went to the assembly of the orthodox. As he was passing the gates of the palace, a beggar who moved on his buttocks instead of his feet, dragging himself along the ground, stretched out his hand and touched the old man's rough cloak. By his faith he drove out the affliction, and leaping up he showed off the running he had been capable of before his infirmity, doing the same as the lame man whom Peter and John raised up. When this happened, the whole population of the city streamed together, and the military training ground was filled with people running to see. The slanderers and craftsmen of falsehood were put to shame, while the nurslings of true religion were full of good cheer and joy. From there those in need of healing kept drawing the luminary of true religion into their homes.

A man who had been entrusted with very high office, and had been charged with holding the helm of the East, sent and begged him to come and free him from the illness that had come upon him. Without delay he came, and after praying to the common Master he dispelled the affliction with a word, and urged the man to give thanks to God.
Having accomplished these and similar deeds, he decided at last to return to his ascetic hut.
Making his way through Cyrrhus, a city two stages distant from Antioch, he lodged at the shrine of the victorious martyr Dionysius.

The leaders of the orthodox there came together and begged him to help them, since they were expecting obvious ruin. For they said that Asterius, who had been raised in the false reasoning of the sophists and had worked his way into the church of the heretics and been made a bishop, was a formidable advocate of falsehood and used his cunning against the truth. "We are afraid," they said, "that he will cloak his falsehood with eloquence as with bait, spread the tangles of his arguments like nets, and catch many of those who have lived in simplicity. For this is why he has been summoned by our opponents." The old man said, "Take courage, and pray to God with us, adding fasting and self-denial to your prayer." So they besought God, and one day before the festival on which the advocate of falsehood and enemy of the truth was to give his discourses, he received a blow sent by God; after being ill for a single day he was removed from the roll of the living, hearing, no doubt, that voice: "Fool, this very night your soul is demanded of you; and the evils you prepared, the nets and the snares, will be for you and not for another." He suffered the same as Balaam, who was also summoned against the people of God, and who, having given Balak unholy counsel against them, paid the penalty, meeting his slaughter at the hand of an Israelite. So this man too, since he devised a crafty scheme against the people of God, was deprived of his life through the people of God.

This deliverance Cyrrhus enjoyed through his prayer. These stories were handed down to me by that divine head, the great Acacius, who knew everything about him accurately. Departing from there, he rejoined his disciples, and after spending no little time with them he passed most eagerly into the life that knows neither age nor grief, having practised freedom from passion in his mortal nature, and awaiting the immortality of the body. Here I bring my account of this story to a close and will move on to another, beseeching the saints mentioned in this story to win for me by their intercession the favour from above.

How could we admire the great Marcianus as he deserves? Plainly only by ranking him with Elijah and John and those like them, who went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom this world was not worthy, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. Long ago his homeland was Cyrus, which I mentioned earlier as well, and after that the desert; and now, having left both, he has heaven. The first gave him birth, the second nurtured him and made him victorious, and the third received him as one crowned. He despised the distinction of his family, for he was descended from patricians, and the splendour of the palace, where he was flourishing. He had received from the Creator of nature great stature and beauty of body, and he had a soul adorned with keenness of mind. Yet he transferred his love to God and the things of God, bade farewell to everyone, and made his way to the very heart of the desert. There he built a small hut, not even large enough for his body, surrounded it with another small enclosure wall, and shut himself in for good. He was cut off from all human company, but he conversed with the Lord of the universe and listened to that sweet voice. When he read the divine oracles, he believed he was enjoying the divine voice; and when he prayed and offered his supplications, it was he himself who was speaking with the Lord. And though he always enjoyed such delight, he did not wish to have his fill of it. For he had heard the divine Spirit singing through the great David: "He who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night shall be like the tree planted by the streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall." Longing for these fruits, he embraced this sweetest of toils. Psalmody took over from prayer and prayer from psalmody, and the reading of the divine oracles in turn took over from both. His only food was bread, and this he took by weight. The weight was so small that it would not meet the needs of a child just weaned from the breast: they say that a pound of bread was divided into four and spread over four days, one portion allotted to each day. For he had resolved to eat once each day, in the evening, but never to eat his fill: to be always hungry and always thirsty, and to give the body only what was enough to keep it alive. He used to say that someone who eats only every few days performs the Lord's service more feebly on the days without food, and on the day when he eats again he naturally takes more and loads his stomach, and the stomach, weighed down, makes the soul more sluggish in keeping vigil. So he said it was better to take nourishment every day but never to submit to being full, for true fasting is constant want. These were the rules this divine man kept throughout his life. Though he had a very large body, being the tallest and handsomest of all the men of his time, he sustained it on very little food.

After some time had passed, he took in two companions: Eusebius, who became the heir of that holy hut, and Agapetus, who transplanted this angelic way of life to the territory of Apamea. There is a very large and populous village there called Nikertai, and in it he built two very large schools of philosophy: one named after himself, the other after the admirable Simeon, who shone in this philosophy for fifty years. In these, down to the present day, more than four hundred men live, athletes of virtue and lovers of piety, who buy heaven with their labors. The lawgivers of this way of life were Agapetus and Simeon, who had received its laws from the great Marcianus. From these, countless other dwellings of ascetics have been planted, adorned by these same laws, and they are not easy to count. Yet the one who planted them all was that inspired man; for whoever supplied the finest seed may rightly be called the cause of the good things that grew from it.

At first, as I said, he occupied that voluntary prison alone. Then, when he received these two, he did not have them live with him, for the little cell was not even big enough for him alone. It was very small, and caused him much hardship whether he stood or lay down. Standing, he could not straighten up, since the roof bent his head and neck; lying down, he could not stretch out his feet, since the house was not as long as his body. So he allowed them to build another, and told them to live in it and to sing hymns, pray and read the divine oracles on their own. And since more people needed to share in this benefit, he directed that another dwelling be built some distance away, and told those who wished to live there. Eusebius was put in charge of them, passing on the teaching of the great Marcianus. That divine Agapetus, once he had been trained as he should be, exercised, and thoroughly schooled in this athletic discipline, returned, as I said, and sowed the seeds he had received from that divine soul. He became so celebrated and admired that he was deemed worthy of the high-priestly presidency: he was entrusted with pastoral care and given charge of his own homeland.

The admirable Eusebius, presiding over the flock that had gathered, also took on the care of his teacher, and he alone was permitted to visit him at the proper time and ask whether he wanted anything. Once, wishing to see what he did at night, he ventured to approach the window (it was a small one). Peeping in, he saw a light not from a lamp nor made by hands, but given by God and of grace from on high, flashing from his teacher's head and showing up the lettering of the divine oracles.

For he happened to be holding a book and searching for the inviolable treasure of the divine will. When the admirable Eusebius saw this, he was filled with fear and full of awe; he learned of the grace poured out on the divine servant, and came to know God's kindness toward his servants.

On another occasion, while the great Marcianus was praying in the forecourt, a serpent crawled up the wall facing east and peered over the top of it, its jaws gaping and its glare grim, signaling its evil intent. Eusebius, standing some way off, was terrified by that dreadful sight; supposing that his teacher had not noticed, he pointed it out with a shout and begged him to flee. But Marcianus rebuked him and told him to cast out his cowardice, for this too, he said, is a deadly passion. Then he traced the sign of the cross with his finger, breathed on it from his mouth, and so showed the ancient enmity. And the serpent, as though set alight by the breath of his mouth as by a fire, and burnt up as it were, was consumed like stubble and fell apart into many pieces. Consider, then, whether he did not imitate the Master like a loyal servant. For the Master, when the sea once raged against the disciples' boat and he saw them in anguish, did not calm the storm on the sea until he had put an end to the disciples' lack of faith by rebuking them. Taught by this, the admirable Marcianus first removed his disciple's cowardice, and only then handed the beast over to punishment.

Such were the wisdom, the wonder-working and the boldness toward God of the great Marcianus. Yet, though he had been granted such grace and was able to work great wonders, he was eager to hide his power, wary of the schemes of the thief who strips away virtue.
For by sowing the passion of vainglory, that thief tries to plunder the fruits gathered by toil.

But though he was eager to hide the grace he had been given, he worked wonders against his will, since the radiance of his achievements shone out and laid bare the hidden power. Once, for example, the following happened. A man of noble family, who had often held military commands, set out from Beroea in Syria, because his daughter had for a long time been frenzied, troubled by an evil demon and raving. He came to the desert, being acquainted with the great Marcianus and expecting, because of their former acquaintance, to meet him and plead with him. Disappointed in his hope and failing to see the divine servant, he begged an old man, who at that time had been entrusted with serving the holy man, to take a small flask full of oil and set it by the door of the little cell. The old man refused the task many times, but was entreated many times again, and at last gave in to the plea. The great Marcianus heard the noise and asked who it was and what he had come for. The old man hid the true reason, and pretended he had come to learn whether Marcianus had any orders; and with that answer he was sent away.

Toward dawn the girl's father again begged that the flask be returned to him. The old man went, afraid but nonetheless as quietly as he could, and stretching out his hand he took the flask and tried to escape notice. But Marcianus again asked what he had come for. When he gave the same excuse he had given the evening before, the holy man was displeased, since the old man's visit was out of the ordinary, and told him to tell the truth.

Frightened and trembling, and unable to hide anything from one filled with divine grace, the old man told him who had come, recounted the tragedy of the affliction, and showed him the flask. Marcianus was indignant, as was natural, not wishing to display his virtue; but he threatened that if the old man ever dared do such a thing again, he would be deprived of his company and removed from his service (and for those who knew its value, this was the greatest penalty). Then he sent him off, telling him to return the flask to the one who had given it. And while he was giving these orders, the demon, four days' journey from the one driving it out, was crying aloud his power; and Marcianus was acting the judge in Beroea, using certain executioners against the demon, driving out that accursed being and setting the girl free of its working. The girl's father learned this precisely. For as he was returning home and was a few stades from the city, a servant met him, sent to the country by his mistress. On seeing his master, he brought him the good news of the wonder that had taken place, saying that the miracle had happened four days before. So, counting the days and carefully examining the time, he learned that it was the very moment when the old man had carried out the flask.

For my part, I reflect on what this great man would not have done if he had wished to work wonders. For if, while striving to hide the grace he had received, he gave off such radiance, what marvel would he not have performed had he wanted to? In the same way, he did not reveal his spiritual wisdom to everyone either, and this although in his last years he allowed those who wished to come in to him after the feast of the saving Passion and the Lord's Resurrection; naturally, everyone was eager to see him at that time. And once the foremost of the bishops came to him together: the great Flavian, entrusted with shepherding the people of Antioch; the divine Acacius, whom I mentioned earlier; Eusebius of Chalcis; and Isidore, then entrusted with governing Cyrrhus, all of them distinguished for virtue. With them was also Theodotus, who held the reins of Hierapolis, resplendent in asceticism and gentleness. Present too were some men in office and high rank who kept the spark of faith alive. While they all sat in silence, waiting for his sacred voice, he too sat silent for a long time, keeping his tongue idle but his hearing active.

Then one of those seated there, who was close to him through care for his soul and was distinguished by rank as well, said: “Father, everyone, including the divine Fathers, thirsts for your teaching and is waiting for your sweetest streams. So share the benefit with all who are here, and do not hold back the springs of your kindness.” He groaned deeply and said: “The God of the universe speaks every day both through creation and through the divine Scriptures; he urges what is right, recommends what is useful, frightens us with threats and encourages us with promises, and yet we reap no profit. How then could Marcianus be of use by speaking, when along with everyone else he turns away so great a benefit and does not wish to gain profit from it?” After this the Fathers raised many points in conversation, which I have thought it superfluous to include in the narrative. Then they rose and prayed, and though they wanted to lay on him the ordination of the priesthood, they shrank again from the attempt. Each urged the other to do it, but all alike declined, and they went back home.
But I wish to add yet another story to these, which is a token of his divine understanding.

A certain Avitus was the first to set up an ascetic hut in the other desert, which lies further north and a little to the east, toward the point where the north wind meets the east wind. He was older than the great Marcianus both in years and in toil, a man of philosophy, raised on a hard life. When he learned of the virtue of Marcianus, which was being talked about everywhere, he considered that such a sight would be more profitable than a little stillness, and hurried off, eager to see the man he longed for.
When the great Marcianus learned of his arrival, he opened the door and received him, and he directed the admirable Eusebius to cook some pulse, and vegetables too if he had any.

When they had had their fill of conversation with each other and had come to know each other's virtue, they performed the office of the ninth hour together. Then Eusebius came bringing a table and setting out bread. The great Marcianus said to the inspired Avitus: “Come, dearest of all to me, let us share this table too.” He replied: “I do not think I have ever taken food before evening; often I even go two or three days at a stretch without eating.” The great Marcianus said: “Then for my sake let the custom be changed today; for my body is weak, and I cannot wait until evening.” When even by saying this he could not persuade the admirable Avitus, he is said to have groaned and said: “I am very disheartened and stung in my soul, because you have endured so much toil to see a man devoted to toil and philosophy, and, disappointed in your hope, you have seen instead of a philosopher a tavern-keeper and a profligate.” The most divine Avitus was pained at this and said that he would sooner eat meat than hear such things. The great Marcianus then said: “We too, my friend, follow the same life as you and embrace the same way of living: we prefer toil to rest and choose fasting over food, and we take food only when night comes on. But we know that the thing called love is more precious than fasting. For the one is the work of divine law, the other is in our own power, and it is fitting to regard the divine laws as far more precious than our own labors.” After talking with each other in this way, taking a little food and singing hymns to God, and spending three days together, they parted, continuing to see each other in spirit. Who, then, would not admire the wisdom of this man? Guided by it, he knew the time for fasting and the time for philosophy and brotherly love; he knew too the difference between the parts of virtue, which should give way to which, and to which, as occasion demands, the prize should be awarded.

I have another story too, a token of his perfection in divine things. His sister came to him from their homeland with her son, a grown man and one of the leading men of Cyrrhus, bringing him an abundant supply of necessities. He would not consent to see his sister, but he received his nephew, for it was the time set for meetings.

When they begged him to accept what they had brought, he asked: “How many monasteries did you pass on the way? To which of them did you give some of these very things?” When his nephew said that they had given to none, he said: “Go away with what you have brought. We need none of it, and even if we did need it, we would not accept it. For it was out of concern for natural kinship, not for divine service, that you wished to show us kindness with these things. Had you not honored family relationship alone, you would not have shared what you brought with us only.” With these words he sent his nephew away along with his sister, without allowing even a little of what they offered to be accepted. So far was he beyond nature, so fully had he passed over into the citizenship of heaven. What clearer proof could anyone give than this that he was worthy of God, according to the voice of God himself? For he says: “Whoever does not leave father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children, is not worthy of me.” And if the one who does not leave them is unworthy, then the one who leaves them, and with such exact perfection, was clearly most worthy. Besides this, I admire the precision of his divine doctrines. He loathed the madness of Arius, which at that time was being fanned into flame by imperial power, and he abhorred the insanity of Apollinaris.
He also fought nobly against those who held the views of Sabellius and merged the three hypostases into one.

He utterly shunned the so-called Euchites as well, who under the guise of monks suffer from the disease of the Manichees. So warm was his zeal for the doctrines of the Church that he even took up a just fight against an admirable and divine man.

There was in that desert a certain Abraham, an old man, grey of hair but greyer still in wisdom, resplendent in every virtue and always welling up with tears of compunction. At first, led on by a certain simplicity, he persisted in keeping Easter at the earlier date, being ignorant, no doubt, of what the Fathers at Nicaea had decreed on the matter, and choosing to remain bound to an ancient custom. Many others too at that time suffered from this ignorance. But the great Marcianus, having often addressed many arguments to him, tried to bring the old man Abraham (for that is what the local people called him) over into agreement with the Church.

When he saw that he would not be persuaded, he openly broke off communion with him. But after some time that inspired man cast off this blemish, embraced agreement about the divine feast, and could truthfully sing: “Blessed are the unblemished in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” This too was an achievement of the great Marcianus's teaching.
Many people in many places built chapels of prayer for him: in Cyrrhus his nephew Alypius, and in Chalcis a certain Zenobiana, illustrious in birth, distinguished in virtue and abounding in wealth.
Not a few others did the same, vying with one another to carry off that victorious athlete.

When the man of God learned of this, he called on the admirable Eusebius, binding him with oaths full of every kind of dread, to lay his body in that very place, and to let no one know the grave except two of his closest companions, until many years had passed. And that admirable man fulfilled this oath. For when the end of the victor came, and a choir of angels carried that holy and divine soul to the dwellings in heaven, he did not announce his death until he had dug the grave with the two closest companions, laid the body in it, and leveled the surface of the ground.

And though fifty years or more have passed, and countless people have come flocking and searched for the body, the grave has remained unknown. But since each of the chapels mentioned has received relics, some of apostles and some of martyrs, the heirs of his tent and his teaching at last took courage, and two years ago they made a stone coffin and transferred into it the remains of the precious body, one of them pointing out the grave; for he alone of the three was still alive.

The admirable Eusebius, who became an imitator of his virtue, went on wearing down his body with even greater labors. For he wore a hundred and twenty pounds of iron, and he also put on himself the most divine Agapetus's fifty more, and added as well the great Marcianus's eighty.

For his dwelling he had a dry cistern, and he continued living in this way for three years. I have digressed into these accounts because I want to show how many other men of great achievements the great Marcianus was responsible for. The admirable Basil also profited from his philosophy, who many years later built a monastic dwelling near Seleucobelus (a city of Syria), and shone in many forms of virtue, but especially in the God-beloved possession of love and the divine achievement of hospitality. Who could easily count how many workers he too presented to God, who, to speak in the apostle's words, had no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth? To pass over the others for the present, who deserve praise but would lengthen the narrative, I will mention just one of them. He had a disciple named Sabinus, who wore out his body with countless labors. He took neither bread nor any relish; his food was flour soaked in water. He used to mix a whole month's food at once, so that it went moldy and gave off a powerful stench. He wanted this kind of food to blunt his body's appetites, and by the stench of his food to wither pleasure. Though he lived like this on his own, whenever one of his acquaintances came, he would simply partake of everything set before them. He received such grace from God that a woman of high standing, proud of her birth and wealth, hurried to him from Antioch and begged him to help her daughter, who was being assailed by a demon.
“For in a dream,” she said, “I saw someone urging me to hurry here and to obtain my daughter's healing through the prayers of the one in charge of the monastery.”

The one who gave answers to visitors told her that it was not the custom for the superior to speak with women. But as the woman persisted, weeping, lamenting and bitterly imploring, the head of the monastery came out.
