The woman, however, said that this was not he, but that someone else had been shown to her, ruddy-faced and with some spots on his cheeks. When they realized who was being sought (he was third in the monastery, not first), they persuaded him and brought him to the woman. At once she recognized his face, and the evil demon cried out and left the girl. Such were the achievements of the disciples of the great Marcianus; such were the plants that excellent gardener planted everywhere.
Bringing this narrative, too, to an end, I entreat and pray that through the intercession of all these I may obtain divine help.

What fruits the fruitless desert has offered to God, ripe and mellow, dear to the one who planted them, and lovely and much desired by people of good sense, we have shown in the accounts already written. But so that no one may suppose that virtue is confined to a place, and that the desert alone is fit to bear such a yield, come, let us now move on in our account to the inhabited world, and show that it is no obstacle at all to acquiring philosophy.

There is a high mountain lying to the east of Antioch and to the west of Beroea. It rises above the mountains around it, its topmost peak has the shape of a cone, and it takes its name from its height, for the people who live around it call it Koryphe, "the Summit." Long ago, on its very peak, there was a precinct of demons that the neighbouring people held in great honour. To the south a plain spreads out below it like a bay, enclosed on either side by ridges that are not very high. These ridges run down as far as the highway used by horsemen, and on each side they take in the tracks that cut through them from south to north. In this plain villages both small and large have been settled against the mountains on either side. Beside the very skirts of the high mountain there is a very large and populous village, which in the local language they call Teleda. Above the foothills there is a glen that is not very steep. It slopes gently down toward that plain and faces the south wind. In it a certain Ammianus built a school of philosophy. He was a man who shone with many other kinds of virtue but surpassed others above all in the modesty of his mind. Here is the proof. He was quite capable of teaching not only his own followers but twice as many, yet he often ran to the great Eusebius and begged him to become his partner, and to be trainer and teacher of the wrestling school he had set up.

Eusebius lived twenty-five stades away, shut up in a very small dwelling that did not even have windows. He had been guided to this virtue by Marianus, his uncle and a faithful servant of God. It is enough to say this much, since the Master honoured even the great Moses with this title. Once this Marianus had tasted divine love, he did not want to enjoy its good things alone. He made many others his fellow lovers, and he also hunted down the great Eusebius and his brother, who was his brother in way of life as well. He thought it unreasonable to catch people who were nothing to him for virtue and leave his own nephews uncaught. He shut them both up in a small hut and trained them in the angelic way of life.
But the brother fell ill, and the illness cut short his race. Death followed the illness: he lived only a few days after leaving that place and then reached the end of his life.

The great Eusebius stayed there for the whole of his uncle's life. He spoke with no one and never saw the light, but remained shut in continually. Even after his uncle's death he held fast to this life, until the wonderful Ammianus won him over with many entreaties and persuaded him. "Tell me, my excellent friend," he said to him, "whom do you think you are pleasing by following this laborious and squalid life?" Eusebius naturally answered, "God, the lawgiver and teacher of virtue." "Then since you love him," said Ammianus, "I will show you a way by which you will both kindle your love further and serve the one you love. For to turn all one's care toward oneself would not, I think, escape the charge of self-love.

The divine law commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, and to bring many into a share of one's wealth is the proper achievement of love. The inspired Paul called love the fulfilment of the law, and again Scripture cries out: 'The law and the prophets are summed up in this one saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself.' In the holy Gospels the Lord, when Peter had confessed that he loved him more than the others did, charged him to tend his sheep. And reproaching those who have not done this, he cries out through the prophet: 'O shepherds, do shepherds feed themselves? Do they not pasture the sheep?' For this reason he ordered even the great Elijah, who was following this way of life, to go about among the ungodly.
And the second Elijah, the renowned John, who had embraced the desert, he sent to the banks of the Jordan, charging him to baptize and preach there.

"So since you too are an ardent lover of God, who made you and saved you, make many others lovers of him along with you. This is very dear to our common Master. That is why he called Ezekiel a watchman and charged him to bear witness to sinners, and why he ordered Jonah to run to Nineveh and, when Jonah was unwilling, sent him there as a prisoner." With these words and others like them he won over the godly man. He dug through that voluntary prison, led him out and took him away, and handed over to him the care of his followers. I do not know which I should admire more, the modesty of the one or the obedience of the other. Ammianus fled from leadership and preferred to be one of those under it, wary of the danger of being in charge. The great Eusebius shrank from living among many people, yet he gave way. Caught in the nets of love, he accepted the care of the flock and led the company, and he did not need many words to teach. Merely being seen was enough for him to make even the most sluggish keen to run the race of virtue.

Those who saw him say that his face was always grave and filled those who looked at him with considerable awe. He himself took food only every third or fourth day, but he told those who lived with him to eat every other day. He charged them to converse with God continually and to let no moment go without a share in this work. They were to perform the appointed services together. In the parts of the day between these, each was to entreat the Master by himself and ask for salvation, whether under the shade of a tree, or beside some rock, or wherever he could find some quiet, and whether standing or lying on the ground. He so trained each member of his own body in virtue that it did only what reason allowed. To make this clear to everyone, I shall tell one story about him.

He and the wonderful Ammianus were once sitting on a rock. Ammianus was reading the narrative of the divine Gospels, and Eusebius was explaining the meaning of the more obscure passages. Some farmers were breaking up the ground in the plain below, and the great Eusebius was drawn into watching them. When the inspired Ammianus had read the Gospel passage and was waiting for its interpretation, the great Eusebius asked him to read it again. Ammianus said, "You were enjoying the plowmen, so of course you did not hear." At that Eusebius laid down a law for his eyes: never again to look at that plain, nor to feast on the beauty of the sky and the dance of the stars. He used a very narrow path leading to the house of prayer, whose width they say was a span, and from then on he would not walk outside it. They say he lived more than forty years after this under that law. And so that some compulsion might hold him to this along with his own will, he bound his waist with an iron belt and put a very heavy collar around his neck. Then he joined the belt to the neck collar with another piece of iron, so that, bent over in this way, he would be forced to stoop toward the ground continually. Such were the penalties he exacted from himself for watching those farmers. Many others who had observed him and knew his life accurately told me these things, and this very story was related by the great elder Acacius, whom we mentioned earlier in other accounts. Acacius said that once, seeing him bent over, he asked him what benefit he gained by not letting himself look up to heaven, nor gaze at the plain below, nor walk outside the narrow path. Eusebius replied that he devised these things against the schemes of the wicked demon. "So that he does not wage war over great things," he said, "trying to steal my temperance and justice, arming my anger, kindling my desire, making me swell and puff up with pride, and plotting everything else against my soul, I try to shift the war to these small matters. Here even if he wins he does no great harm, and if he is beaten he becomes all the more ridiculous, since he could not prevail even in small things. Since I know that this war is less dangerous, I shift the form of battle to it. Whoever is struck in these matters suffers no great loss: what harm is there in seeing the plain or raising one's eye to heaven? Here he can neither kill nor wound me, for these arrows are not deadly, since they lack those iron points." The great Acacius said that when he heard this he was struck by his wisdom and marvelled at his courage and experience in war. For this reason he offered this story too, as admirable and worth remembering, to those eager to learn such things.
His fame spread everywhere and drew all lovers of virtue to him.

Among those who came were the rams of the excellent flock of the most godly elder Julian, whose story we told earlier. When that inspired man reached the end of his life and passed to the life above, James the Persian and Agrippa, the leaders of that flock, ran to the great Eusebius, thinking it better to be well led than to lead. I have already mentioned James earlier and shown his virtue in that chapter, and now I will present clear proof of his supreme philosophy as well.

When the godly Eusebius was departing this life, he charged James to preside over the flock. James declined the charge, and when he could not persuade those who were pressing that care on him, he went off to another flock, choosing to be pastured rather than to pasture. He lived for a very long time and ended this life there. So Agrippa succeeded to that leadership. He was a man rich in many other good qualities, but above all in purity of soul. Through it he received the vision of divine beauty, and set ablaze by the torch of that love, he drenched his cheeks with continual tears. When he too had shepherded that choice and divine flock rightly for a long time and then departed this life, the godly David, whom I too had the joy of seeing, took over the leadership. He was a man who had truly put to death his members on earth, as the divine Apostle says. He profited so much from the teaching of the great Eusebius that he spent forty-five years in that school and lived that whole time without temper or anger. Not even after he became leader did anyone ever see him overcome by this passion, although countless things, as you would expect, provoked him. A hundred and fifty men were shepherded under his hand. Some were supreme in virtue and imitated the citizenship of heaven. Others had only just grown their wings and were being taught to rise above the earth and fly over it. Many were being trained in divine things, and some of them, as you would expect, did go astray, for it is not easy for a newcomer to get everything right. Yet that godly man remained unmoved, like someone without a body, and nothing gave him occasion for anger.
I learned this not only from hearsay but from experience.
Once, wanting to see that flock, I went there, and others who had embraced the same life as I shared the journey with me.

We spent the whole round of a week with this godly man, and we saw a face that never changed. It did not brighten at one moment and cloud over with gloom at the next. His eye likewise was not stern at one time and cheerful at another; his eyes always kept the same composure. These signs are enough to prove the calm of his soul. But some may suppose that he looked like this only because nothing provoked him. So I must tell of something of the kind that happened in our presence. The godly man was sitting with us, opening discussions about philosophy and inquiring into the summit of the Gospel way of life. While this conversation was going on, a certain Olympius came to us. He was a Roman by birth, himself admirable in character and honoured with the priesthood, and he held second place in that leadership. He began shouting against the godly David. He called his gentleness a ruin for everyone, said that his mildness was doing harm to all, and called that supreme philosophy folly rather than gentleness. But David, as if his soul were made of adamant, took in the words without being stung by what is meant to sting. He did not change his expression or abandon the discussion in hand. In a gentle voice, with words that showed the clear sky of his soul, he sent the elder away, urging him to see to whatever he wished. "As you see," he said, "I am talking with those who have come to visit us, and I think this attention is necessary." How could anyone better display mildness of soul? He had been entrusted with that office, and yet he received such drunken abuse from his second-in-command, and that in front of strangers who heard the insults, without suffering any storm or turmoil of anger. What higher degree of courage and endurance does that leave? The divine Apostle, considering the weakness of human nature, measures his legislation to nature: "Be angry," he says, "and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger." He knows that the movements of anger belong to nature rather than to the will, so he does not undertake to legislate what is very hard and perhaps even impossible. Instead he sets the day as the limit for the stirring of nature and the storm of anger. He commands us to throttle anger with reason and rein it in with the bridle, and he does not allow it to go beyond those bounds. But this godly man contended beyond the established rules and leapt past the marks. He did not let his anger stir until evening; he did not let it stir at all. Such was the benefit he too drew from his life with the great Eusebius.

I have seen many others too who became lovers and zealous followers of this philosophy at that hut, some in the prime of bodily strength, others in deep old age. Men who had lived more than ninety years refused to give up the laborious life and shone with the sweat of youth. They entreated God all night and all day, performed those holy services, and ate that plain food only every other day. I will pass over the others, not because they deserve silence, for they deserve acclaim and every kind of praise, but so as not to make this account too long. There was in that godly place a man they call Abbas. He sprang from the root of Ishmael, but unlike his ancestor he was not banished from the house of Abraham. Instead he shared the paternal inheritance with Isaac, or rather he seized the kingdom of heaven itself. He took up this ascetic way of life at once, under a man then living in the desert who was an excellent trainer in such things; his name was Marosas. Later Marosas too gave up leading others and came with Abbas to this flock. He lived for no short time, and after contending brilliantly and becoming famous he departed this life. Abbas has already spent thirty-eight years there, and he longs for labour like someone who has only just begun. To this day he has never covered his feet with sandals. He keeps to the shade in the cold and welcomes the sun in the blazing heat, receiving its flame as if it were a breath of the west wind. In all this time he has not allowed himself to drink water. He does not eat the foods that those who practise not drinking usually take, for they generally eat moister foods. He takes the same food as the others, but he eats little, and only what gives little strength, and so he considers the need for water superfluous. With his waist girded in heavy iron, he rarely sits down. For most of the night and day he stands or kneels, offering the Master the service of prayer, and he has entirely renounced lying down. To this day no one has ever seen him lying down. Although he has been appointed head of the company and given its leadership, he bears all this toil gladly and sets himself as a model of philosophy for all those under him. Such were the victorious athletes that the godly Eusebius, trainer and coach of these contests, presented to God. He made very many others like them and sent them out as teachers to other wrestling schools, and they filled that whole holy mountain with these divine meadows and fragrant flowers. To the east of the ascetic hut that was first set up, and to the west and south, one can see the offspring of this philosophy, like stars dancing around the moon. Some sing hymns to the Creator in Greek, others in the local language. But I am attempting the impossible in trying to recount everything that godly soul achieved. So I must bring this account to an end and turn to another, gathering its benefit in turn, and begging to share in the blessing of these great men.

At the same time there lived a man named Publius. He was striking in appearance, and his soul matched his appearance; indeed, it showed itself far more wonderful than his body. He came from the class of city councillors, and his city was the one where the famous Xerxes, campaigning against Greece and eager to cross the river Euphrates with his army, gathered a multitude of ships, yoked them together, and so bridged the river. He named the place Zeugma, "the Yoking," and from this deed gave the city its name.
Setting out from there, and sprung from such a family, he took possession of a high spot no more than thirty stades from the city.

There he built a small hut, and sold everything he had inherited from his father: his house, I mean, and his lands, his livestock, his clothing, his silver and bronze vessels, and anything else he happened to own besides. He distributed all this to those in need, as the divine law commands, and so freed himself from every earthly care. In place of them all he took on a single care, the service of the One who had called him. This he kept turning over in his soul, considering night and day how he might increase it. For this reason his labour grew continually and became more intense every day. Yet it was sweet and full of delight, and kept all weariness far away. No one ever saw him take rest for even a small part of the day. Prayer followed psalmody, and psalmody followed prayer, and the reading of the divine oracles followed both. Then came the care of visiting strangers, and then some other necessary task. Travelling through life in this way, he was set before those who wished to imitate him as a model of virtue. Like some sweet-voiced bird, he gathered many of his own people into these saving nets. At first he would not allow anyone to live with him. Instead he built small huts near one another and told each of those who came to him to live by himself. He visited them often and searched the huts, in case they had stored anything beyond their needs. They say that he even carried scales about with him and checked the weight of the loaves precisely. If he ever found more than the fixed amount, he was displeased, and called those who had done it gluttons.

For he commanded them not to eat or drink until they were full, but to take only as much as sufficed to keep the body alive. If he ever saw flour that had been sifted from the bran, he rebuked those who had done it for indulging in Sybaritic luxury. He would also arrive suddenly at each one's door at night. If he found someone awake and singing hymns to God, he would quietly withdraw again. But if he found someone in the grip of sleep, he struck the door with his hand and lashed the sleeper with his tongue for giving the body more care than it needed. Some like-minded men saw how much this cost him and proposed building a single dwelling for everyone. They said that those who were now scattered would live more strictly, and that he himself would be spared much of his care.

That wisest of men accepted their advice. He gathered everyone together, pulled down those little huts, and built a single dwelling for the assembled brethren. He urged them to live in common and to spur one another on: this one was to imitate that one's gentleness, that one was to temper his gentleness with this one's zeal, and another, while sharing his own vigilance, was to learn the lesson of fasting in return. "For in this way," he said, "by receiving from one another what we lack, we shall achieve the most perfect virtue. In the markets of a city one man sells bread and another vegetables, one deals in clothing and another makes shoes. By supplying one another's needs they live more pleasantly: the man who gives a cloak receives a shoe in return, and the man who buys vegetables pays for them with bread. In just this way we ought to exchange with one another the precious portions of virtue." So those who spoke the same language trained and contended together and sang hymns to God in Greek. Then a love of this way of life seized those who spoke the local language as well, and some of them came running and begged to join the flock and share in his holy teaching. He granted their request, remembering the Master's command to the holy apostles: "Go and make disciples of all nations." He built another dwelling beside the first and told them to live there. He also built a holy church, and he ordered both groups to gather in it at the beginning and end of each day. There they were to offer the evening and morning hymns to God together, divided into two choirs, each using its own language and sending up the song in turn. This form of community life has lasted to this day. Time is always eager to change such things, yet neither time nor those who succeeded to his charge have been persuaded to overturn any of the rules he laid down. And this is so even though not two or three, but more, have succeeded to the leadership. As soon as he had finished his contest, departed this life, and passed into that life free of grief, Theotecnus took over the leadership of the Greek-speaking community

and Aphthonius that of the Syriac-speaking community. Both became, as it were, living pillars and images of his virtue. They showed themselves to be true impressions of his way of life, and so allowed neither those who lived with them nor visitors from outside to feel his death. The divine Theotecnus, however, did not survive him long, and

handed the leadership over to Theodotus. Aphthonius, on the other hand, remained for a very long time, caring for the flock and guiding it according to the established rules. This Theodotus came from Armenia. When he saw that ascetic company, he at first took his place among those under obedience, submitting to the great Theotecnus as he steered. But when the latter departed, as I have said, and he himself took over the leadership, he flourished in so many good qualities that he almost eclipsed his predecessors in fame. Divine longing so wrought upon him, and wounded him with so many and such arrows, that night and day he shed tears of compunction. And he was so full of spiritual grace that when he prayed, all who were present fell silent and listened only to those holy words, counting the hearing of them as earnest prayer. For who was so hard as adamant that his soul was not charmed when those words were offered in such a way, its hardness and stubbornness softened, and itself brought over to the service of God? So he increased his wealth every day and filled the inviolable treasuries with such goods. After shepherding the flock for twenty-five years, he was gathered to his fathers, as divine Scripture says, nourished in a good old age. He handed the reins to Theotecnus, who was his nephew by birth and his brother in character. And that divine Aphthonius, after presiding over the community for more than forty years, received the presidency of the episcopate. He changed neither his ascetic cloak of skins nor his tunic made of goat hair, and he ate the same food he had eaten before he became bishop.

Even after he had taken on this charge, he cared no less for that flock. He spent most of his days there. Now he settled the quarrels of those at odds with one another, now he provided for those who were in any distress, and at other times he offered divine exhortation to the brethren. And he did each of these things while patching the rags of his fellow monks, or cleaning lentils, or washing wheat, or busy at some other such task. Having thus adorned his episcopal see and increased his virtue, he reached the divine harbour with its cargo. And what need is there to speak of Theotecnus and of Gregory, who came after him? The former gathered every form of philosophy in his youth and departed with the glory of his forebears. The latter, even today, in deep old age, labours with his body as though in his prime.

For he has continued to refuse the fruit of the vine entirely. He takes neither vinegar nor raisins, and no milk, whether fresh or curdled. This was the rule of life laid down by the great Publius. They take oil during the season of Pentecost, and then give it up again.

These are the things I have learned about the great Publius. Some I received by hearsay, while others I learned by seeing his disciples, coming to know the teacher through them, as one knows the trainer through his athletes. I thought it unjust and envious to betray so great a benefit by keeping silent. So I have added this story for those who do not know it, procuring its benefit for them and securing for myself the gain that comes from remembering them. For I have heard the Master say: "Everyone who acknowledges me before men, I too will acknowledge before my Father in heaven." And I know clearly that, since I have brought the memory of these men before people, I shall enjoy their remembrance of me before the God of all.

If anyone were knowingly to pass over Symeon the Elder and consign the memory of his philosophy to oblivion, he could rightly be charged with injustice and envy. He would be refusing to praise what deserves praise, and failing to set before those who wish to benefit a lovely example to imitate. But it is not fear of such a charge that moves me to tell of this man's way of life. It is the desire to praise him. He spent a very long time embracing the solitary life and living in a small cave. He enjoyed no human consolation, since he had chosen to live alone. Instead he conversed continually with the God of all, and he lived on edible herbs. This labour won him rich grace from above, so that he gave orders even to the strongest and fiercest beasts. This became plain not only to the pious but also to unbelieving Jews. Some of them were travelling on some business to one of the forts that lie beyond our inhabited world. A violent rain fell and a storm struck, and they lost their way, unable to see ahead. They wandered through the desert and found neither village, nor cave, nor traveller. Tossed about in the middle of dry land like sailors at sea, they came upon the cave of the divine Symeon as though it were a harbour. There they saw a squalid, dirty man wearing a short cloak of skins on his shoulders.

As soon as he saw them, he greeted them, for he was affable, and asked why they had come. They told him what had happened and begged him to show them the road that led to the fort. "Stay," he said, "and I will give you guides at once to show you the road you are looking for." They did as he said and rested. While they were sitting there, two lions arrived. They did not glare fiercely, but fawned on him as on a master and showed that they were his servants. With a nod he ordered them to escort the men and lead them back to the road they had left when they went astray. Let no one think this story a fable, since the common enemies of the truth bear witness to its truth. For the very men who received the kindness went on telling of it everywhere.

This was told to me by the great James, who said he was present when they recounted the miracle to the inspired Aaron. If anyone disbelieves Jews who bear witness to the miracles of Christians, how could he not rightly be called more unbelieving than the Jews? They are hostile, yet they are defeated and yield to the rays of the truth. But some who are thought well-disposed and partners in the faith do not believe even enemies who bear witness to the power of grace.

Through such miracles that holy man became famous and drew many of the neighbouring barbarians to himself. (That desert is inhabited by those who pride themselves on having Ishmael as their ancestor.) Because he loved stillness, he was forced to leave the cave. After a long journey he reached the mountain called Amanus. This mountain had long been full of the madness of polytheism, but he cultivated it with many miracles of every kind and planted there the piety that now flourishes on it. To tell everything, however, would be very laborious, and perhaps impossible for me.

So I shall recall one miracle and set it out as a sample of his apostolic and prophetic wonder-working. From it I leave my readers to infer the power of the grace he received. It was summer, at harvest time, and the sheaves were being carried to the threshing floors.

A certain man was not content with the fruits of his own honest labour, but coveted what belonged to others. He stole some of his neighbour's sheaves and tried to enlarge his own stack with them. But God at once pronounced sentence on the theft. A fiery whirlwind swept down and set his threshing floor ablaze. The wretched man went to the man of God, who was living not far from the village, and told him about the disaster, while trying to hide the theft. When he was ordered to tell the truth, he confessed the theft, for his suffering forced him to accuse himself. That divine man then told him to undo the punishment by undoing the wrong. "For when you repay those sheaves," he said, "that fire sent by God will be put out." Then one could see the man running and bringing the stolen ears to the man he had wronged, and the blaze being put out without water through the prayer and intercession of the divine elder. This filled not only the people round about with fear. It also drove the whole city (I mean Antioch, to which the district belonged) to rush to him, one telling of his need for deliverance from demonic frenzy, another of his need for relief from fever, another seeking a cure for some other affliction. And he poured out the streams of the grace that dwelt in him without stint. But once again, because he loved stillness, he longed to reach Mount Sinai. When they heard of this, many of the best men, who pursued the same philosophy, gathered around him, longing to share his journey. After travelling for many days, they reached the desert of Sodom. There they saw from far off a man's hands stretched up towards the sky from a pit. At first they thought it was a demon's deception. But after praying more earnestly and seeing the same thing, they hurried to the spot. They saw a small hole, such as foxes are accustomed to dig when they make burrows for themselves, but they saw no one there.
For the man with outstretched hands had heard the sound of their feet and hidden himself inside the burrow.

The old man stooped down, peered in, and earnestly begged him to show himself, if he was human by nature and not some deceiving demon taking on such a form. "For we too," he said, "pursue the ascetic life and love stillness, and we are wandering through this desert because we long to worship the God of all on Mount Sinai. There he appeared to his servant Moses and gave him the tablets of the law. It is not that we think the Divine is confined to a place. We hear him say, 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord,' and we hear that he holds the circle of the earth and those who dwell on it like locusts. But to those who love ardently, not only are the beloved thrice longed for, but the places that received their presence and company are dear as well." As the elder was saying these and similar things, the hidden man showed himself, coming out of the burrow. He was wild to look at. His hair was squalid, his face wrinkled, and every limb of his body withered. He was clothed in poor rags stitched together with palm shoots.

He greeted them, gave them the salutation of peace, and asked who they were, where they had come from, and where they were going. They answered his questions and asked him in turn where he had come from and why he had chosen this life. He said: "I too had the same zeal that is now carrying you on your way. I had taken as companion on this journey a friend of mine, a like-minded man who shared my aim, and we had bound each other by oath not to break off our companionship even in death.

"Now it happened that on the journey he met the end of his life here. Bound by my oath, I dug as well as I could and gave his body burial. Then I dug another grave for myself beside it, and here I await the end of my life and offer the Master my customary service. For food I have dates, which a brother of mine has been appointed by the One who cares for me to bring me." While he was saying this, a lion appeared in the distance. Those with the elder were seized with alarm. When the man sitting by the burrow noticed this, he stood up and signalled to the lion to go round to the other side.
The lion obeyed at once and came, bringing a cluster of dates. Then, when told, it went off again, lay down at a distance from the men, and went to sleep.

So he shared the dates among them all and joined with them in prayer and psalmody. At dawn, when the service was over, he embraced them and sent them away, astounded at so strange a sight. If anyone disbelieves what I have said, let him remember the way of life of the great Elijah and the ministry of the ravens, which brought him bread every morning and meat every evening.

It is easy for the Maker of all things to find all kinds of means to care for his own. So he kept Jonah safe in the belly of the sea monster for three days and nights, made the lions in the pit stand in awe of Daniel, and caused lifeless fire to act as if it had reason, giving light to those inside the furnace and burning up those outside. But it is superfluous for me to offer proofs of God's power. When the old man reached the mountain he longed for, they say that this wonderful elder knelt down in the very place where Moses was counted worthy to see God, and saw him as far as mortal nature could. He did not rise until he heard a divine voice declaring the Master's favour towards him. He remained bowed down like this for a whole week without taking even a little food. Then the voice that had come to him told him to take what had been set before him and eat it with good heart. He stretched out his hand and found three apples. When he had eaten his fill of them, as the Giver had instructed, he was filled with all his strength again and, as was natural, embraced his companions with joy. So he made his way back rejoicing and exulting, having heard a divine voice and once again enjoyed food given by God. On his return he built two schools of philosophy. One was on the ridge of the mountain we mentioned earlier, the other below it, at the very edge of the foothills. In each he gathered athletes of virtue, and he became trainer and coach to both. He taught them the assaults of the adversary and enemy, and promised them the favour of the One who presides over the contest. He urged them to take courage and filled them with high spirit. He told them to be humble towards their brethren, and charged them to show greatness of spirit against the enemy. Teaching such things, living in this way, working such miracles, and sending out radiance of every kind, he reached the end of his life of toil and departed to the life that knows neither age nor grief. He left behind undying fame and a memory that endures forever. My blessed, thrice-blessed mother received his blessing while he was alive, and often told me many stories about him. For my part, I beg to enjoy his present power and intercession, and I know that I shall obtain them. For he will surely grant my request, imitating the Master's love for mankind.
The much-celebrated Palladius lived at the same time as this man. He shared his way of life and was his companion and close acquaintance.

They visited one another, so it is said, and drew benefit from each other, sharpening one another and stirring each other to godly zeal. Palladius had shut himself up in a little hut near a very large and populous village called Immae. I think it unnecessary to describe the man's endurance, his fasting and keeping vigil, and his unceasing prayer, for in all this he pulled the same yoke as the divine Symeon. But I thought it worthwhile to tell of the miracle that is still celebrated today, which came about through his voice and his hand.

A festival was being held in that village. It drew merchants from every quarter and attracted a crowd beyond counting. At this festival a certain merchant sold off the goods he had brought, gathered up his gold, and meant to set off by night.

A murderer had seen the gold he had collected. He was seized by a kind of frenzy and madness, drove sleep from his eyes, and watched for the man's departure. After cockcrow the merchant set off without fear. The other went on ahead and took up a spot suited for an ambush. He sprang out suddenly, struck the blow, and dared to commit the murder. Then he added a further impiety to this abomination: he took the gold and threw the dead body down at the door of the great Palladius. When day came, word spread, and the whole festival was talking about what had happened. Everyone came running. They broke down the door and demanded that the divine Palladius answer for the murder, and one of those doing this was the very man who had committed it. Surrounded by so great a crowd, the godly man looked up to heaven. In his mind he rose beyond heaven, and he begged the Master to expose the falsehood of the accusation and bring the hidden truth to light.

After this prayer he took the dead man by the right hand and said, "Tell us, young man, who struck you this blow. Point out the one who did this abomination, and show that the innocent man is free of this wicked false charge." The dead man obeyed the word, and as Palladius held his right hand he sat up. He looked around at those present and pointed out the murderer with his finger. A great cry went up from them all, for they were astounded at the miracle and amazed at the false charge that had been brought. They stripped the murderer and found the knife, still red with blood, and the gold that had been the cause of the killing. The divine Palladius had long been admired, and from then on he was naturally admired all the more, for the miracle was enough to show how freely the man could speak before God.
The admirable Abraames also belonged to the same company. He lived at the place called Paratomos and sent the brilliant rays of his virtue out in every direction.

The miracles worked after his death bear witness to the brilliance of his life, for his tomb still pours out every kind of healing to this day. Those who draw these healings abundantly from it through faith are its witnesses. May I too obtain the help of these men, since I have sanctified my tongue by remembering them.

All human beings share one nature, and the life of philosophy is easy for those who desire it, whether they are Greeks or barbarians. This can readily be learned from many sources, but Aphraates alone is enough to show it clearly. He was born and raised among the Persians, the most lawless of peoples. He sprang from such parents and was educated in their customs, yet he reached such heights of virtue that he outshone even those born of devout parents who had received a devout upbringing from childhood. First he disregarded his lineage, which was distinguished and illustrious, and hastened to worship the Master, imitating his forefathers the Magi. Then, loathing the impiety of his own people, he chose a foreign land over his own. He came to Edessa, a very great and populous city that is especially distinguished for its piety. He found a small dwelling outside the walls, shut himself in, and devoted himself to the care of his own soul. Like an excellent farmer, he cut out the thorns of the passions by the roots, cleared the divine field of weeds, and offered the Master the ripe fruits of the seeds of the gospel.

From there he went to Antioch, which was being badly tossed about by the storm of heresy. He settled in a retreat for the ascetic life outside the city and learned a few little phrases of the Greek language. He drew as many people as possible to listen to the divine oracles, and in his half-barbarian speech he brought forth what his mind had conceived, receiving such streams from the grace of the divine Spirit. For which of those who pride themselves on their eloquence, who knit their brows, speak pompously and show off with the snares of syllogisms, ever got the better of that uneducated, barbarian voice? He met reasoning with reasoning, and the arguments of the philosophers with the divine oracles, crying out with the great Paul, "Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge." He went on always in the manner described in the apostle's words: "Casting down reasonings and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ." One could see people of every kind flocking to him: those in office and of high rank, those enrolled in some branch of service, and those who lived by the work of their hands. In short, there were civilians and soldiers, the educated and those with no schooling in letters, those who lived in poverty and those who abounded in wealth. Some received what he offered in silence, while others asked questions, made inquiries, and gave occasions for his teaching. Though he took on such heavy labor, he would never accept anyone to live with him. He preferred to do things for himself rather than be waited on by others. He held his conversations at the outer door, and he himself opened it to those who came in and saw them off when they left. He never accepted anything from anyone, neither bread, nor any other food, nor clothing. Only one of his acquaintances supplied him with bread, and when he had reached a great age he also took some vegetables after sunset. They say that Anthemius, who later became prefect and consul, brought him a tunic woven in Persia when he returned from his journey there as an appointed ambassador. He said, "Father, I know that to everyone his own country is sweet and the fruits that grow there are the most delightful, so I have brought you this tunic from your homeland. I beg you to accept it and to give me your blessing in return." Aphraates first told him to lay it on the bench. Then, after they had talked of other things, he said that he was distressed because his mind was torn two ways. When Anthemius asked the reason, he said, "I have always chosen to have one companion living with me, and I have made it a rule for myself to refuse absolutely to live with two. For sixteen years I have had someone living with me who has been very dear to me. Now a fellow countryman of mine has come, wanting to live with me and asking that I allow it. This is what is tearing my mind in two. I will not put up with having two at once. I welcome my countryman as my countryman, but to throw out the first, who has become so dear to me, I consider both painful and unjust." Anthemius replied, "You are right, Father. It would not be right to send away, as unsuitable, the one who has served you for so long, and to take in one who has not yet given any proof of his character, merely because he is from your homeland." To this the divine Aphraates said, "Then, my good friend, I will not take this tunic. I will not put up with having two, and by my verdict the one who has served me for so long is dearer, and by yours he is the better." Having outwitted Anthemius in this way and caused him to marvel at his shrewdness, he persuaded him not to say another word to him about that tunic.

I have related this because I wanted to show two things at once: that he received only from one person what was enough for his bodily needs, and that he was so full of wisdom that he brought the very man who was begging him to accept a gift to cast his own vote that he should not accept it. But I will leave such matters aside and tell of greater things.

After Julian, the enemy of God, had paid the penalty for his impiety in the land of the barbarians, the nurslings of true religion enjoyed a little calm while Jovian took up the helm of Roman rule. But when he too reached the end of his life after reigning only a very short time, and Valens received the rule of the East, squalls and tempests again stirred up our sea. A fierce surge arose, and huge waves struck the ship from every side.
The storm was made worse by the absence of the pilots, for the emperor, bold only against true religion, compelled them to live in exile.

Even after such lawlessness, he did not have his fill of impiety. He scattered every gathering of the faithful, eager to tear the flock apart like a wild beast. For this reason he drove them not only out of every church but also from the foot of the mountain, from the bank of the river, and from the military training ground. They kept moving from one of these places to another and became the sport of the soldiery. Meanwhile the Scythians and the other barbarians were freely plundering all of Thrace, from the Danube to the Propontis. Yet he would not even give an attentive ear, as the saying goes, to news of this, while he took up arms against his own people, his subjects, who were distinguished by their piety. God's people, lamenting the untimeliness of those evils, sang that song of David: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion." But the rest of the song no longer suited them. Aphraates, Flavian, and Diodore did not let the instruments of teaching be hung on the willows, nor would they allow anyone to say, "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" Instead, on the mountains and in the plains, in the city and in the suburbs, in houses and in marketplaces, they sang the Lord's song without ceasing. For they had learned from David that "The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it." They had also heard the same prophet say, "Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion." They had heard the divine Paul instruct that "men should pray in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing." And the Master himself, speaking with the Samaritan woman, foretold this still more clearly: "Truly I tell you, woman," he said, "the hour is coming, and now is, when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in every place, they will worship the Father." Instructed by these words, they went on bearing witness at home and in the marketplace, or, to use the apostle's words, "publicly and from house to house." Like excellent generals, they armed their own side and riddled their opponents with wounds.

That the great Flavian and the divine Diodore, who were at that time serving as under-shepherds and had been given the rank of the second seat, did what I have described is admirable and worthy of praise. Still, they did these things as appointed generals, bound by the laws that govern generals. The most wise Aphraates, however, leapt into these contests of his own free will. He had been raised in stillness and had chosen to live on his own, sitting out of range of the arrows, as the saying goes. Yet when he saw how fierce the war was, he did not cling to his own safety. He bade farewell to stillness for the time being and became the champion in the front line of the faithful, striking with his life, his word and his miracles, but never struck himself. One day the utterly senseless emperor saw him as he was going out to the military training ground, for that was where those devoted to the Trinity happened to be gathering at the time. Someone pointed him out to the emperor, who was looking down from the palace, as he walked along the riverbank. The emperor asked where he was hurrying to. When the man answered that he was going off to offer prayers for the world and for the empire, the emperor replied, "Why is it that you, who profess the monastic life, have left your stillness and walk boldly through the marketplace?" Aphraates, who was accustomed to reason in parables in imitation of the Master, said, "Tell me, Emperor: if I were a maiden hidden away in some chamber, and I saw someone setting fire to my father's house, what would you advise me to do as I watched the flames being kindled and saw the house burning? To sit inside and ignore the house as it went up in flames? But then I too would be consumed by the blaze. If you say that I ought to run, fetch water, dash up and down, and put out the flames, do not blame me, Emperor, for doing exactly that. What you would have advised a maiden kept in her chamber is what I, who profess the monastic life, am compelled to do. If you blame me for leaving my stillness, blame yourself for throwing this fire into the house of God, and not me for struggling to put it out. You yourself have admitted that one ought, of course, to help when one's father's house is on fire. And that God is more truly a father than our fathers on earth is plain to everyone, even to those utterly uninstructed in divine things. So, Emperor, we are not acting contrary to our aim or to the choice we made at the beginning when we gather and pasture the nurslings of true religion and offer them the divine grass." When he had said this, the emperor, convinced by the justice of his defense, gave his approval.

But one of those who count neither among men nor among women, who have been deprived of the ability to become fathers in due time, and who for this reason are thought to be well-disposed to the emperor and derive their name from this, reviled the man of God from above and even threatened him with death. Before long, however, he paid the penalty for his insolence. The emperor wished to refresh his body with a bath, and the wretch went ahead to see whether the bathtub was properly mixed. His wits deserted him, and he jumped into the tub that received the unmixed hot water. Since no one else was inside, for he had gone in alone to see whether all was ready, he remained there, boiling and dissolving.
After some time had passed, the emperor sent in another man to call him. This man found no one in any of the rooms and reported this to the emperor.
Then more of them ran in and searched all the tubs. When at last they came to that one, they saw him lying there, dead.

There was an uproar and everyone lamented. Some drained off the hot water while others carried out the miserable body. Then fear fell upon the emperor and upon all who were arming themselves against true religion. Word of it echoed through the whole city: what a penalty that wretch had paid for his drunken insolence against Aphraates! Everyone kept praising the God of Aphraates. Although his opponents were pressing for it, this prevented the man of God from being banished. Thoroughly frightened, the emperor turned away those who were urging it and held the man in respect. He also learned of his virtue from another source.
There was a well-bred horse, very well trained to carry a rider, of which the emperor was extremely fond. An ailment befell it that greatly distressed the emperor: it could not pass its urine.

Those skilled in the art of treating such things were called in to cure it. When their skill too was defeated, the emperor was distressed, and the man entrusted with the care of the horses was in despair. Being devout and strong in faith, he went at midday with the horse to the dwelling of the great Aphraates. He told him of the ailment, made his faith known, and begged him to relieve the illness by prayer. Aphraates did not delay but at once prayed to God. He had water drawn from the well, made the sign of the saving cross over it, and ordered it to be given to the horse. The horse drank, which it had not been doing. Then he filled some oil with blessing by calling on God and anointed the horse's belly. At the touch of his hand the ailment was relieved at once, and immediately the horse passed water naturally. Overjoyed, the man took the horse and ran back to the stables.

Late in the afternoon (for it was at that time that the emperor was accustomed to visit the stables) he came and asked how the horse was. The groom told him it was well and brought it out. Seeing it in good health, prancing, neighing and proudly lifting its neck, the emperor asked the reason for its recovery. The groom put off telling him many times, for he was afraid to reveal the healer, knowing that the one asking was hostile to him. At last he was compelled to tell the truth, and he explained how the cure had been done. The emperor was astounded and acknowledged that the man was worthy of admiration.

Yet he was not freed from his earlier madness, but went on raging against the Only-begotten, until he was consumed by a barbarian fire and was not even granted a burial equal to that of slaves or beggars. The divine Aphraates displayed his virtue in that storm, and when calm returned he went on doing the same. He also worked countless other miracles, of which I will mention one or two.
A woman of noble family, who bore the yoke of marriage with a licentious husband, came to that blessed man, wailing over her misfortune.
She said that her husband was attached to a concubine and had been bewitched by some sorcery, so that he hated her, who was joined to him by the law of marriage.

The woman said this while standing in front of the outer door, for that was how he was accustomed to converse with women: he never admitted a single one inside his door. Taking pity on the woman in her distress, he weakened the power of the sorcery by prayer. He sanctified a small flask of oil that she had brought by calling on God, and he told her to anoint herself with it. When the woman had carried out these instructions, she turned her husband's love toward herself and persuaded him to prefer the lawful bed to the unlawful one. They also say that once, when locusts suddenly descended on the land and, like fire, devoured everything — crops, plants, marshes, groves and meadows — a devout man came to him and begged for help. He had only one field, from which he fed himself, his wife, his children and his household, and on which he was also required to pay the imperial tax. Again imitating the Master's love for humanity, Aphraates told him to bring a jar of water. When the man asking for the prayer brought the jar, Aphraates laid his hand on it and begged God to fill the water with divine power. When he had finished the prayer, he instructed the man to sprinkle the water along the boundaries of his land. The man who took it did as he was told, and the water became an unassailable and inviolable fence for those fields. The locusts, crawling and flying about like armies, came as far as those boundaries and then turned back again, afraid of the blessing laid upon them, as though choked by a bridle and prevented from going any further. But why should I tell everything accomplished by that blessed soul? These are enough to show the splendor of the grace that dwelt in him. I too was an eyewitness of it and reaped the blessing of that holy right hand. I was still a boy then and went with my mother when she visited the man. He opened the door slightly, as was his custom, and granted her conversation and a blessing. But he admitted me inside and gave me a share of the riches of his prayer. May I enjoy this even now, for I believe that he lives, that he dances in the chorus with the angels, and that he speaks to God with greater freedom than before. For then that freedom was measured out according to the mortality of the body, so that greater freedom would not become an occasion for pride. But now that he has laid down the burden of the passions, he speaks freely to the president of the games as a victorious athlete. For this reason I beg to receive his intercession as well.
We hear of the Galatians in Europe, the western ones, and we know of those in Asia, their descendants, who settled along the Black Sea.

From this people sprang Peter, blessed three times and many times over. They say he was brought up by his parents for seven years from birth, and spent all the rest of his life in the contests of philosophy. He is said to have died at the age of ninety-nine. Who could admire as he deserves a man who struggled for ninety-two years, and walked on in victory through every day and night? What tongue could suffice to tell the achievements he toiled for as a youth and a boy, as a grown man, as an older man and as an old man? Who could measure his sweat? Who could count the bouts he fought over so long a time? What words could reach the seeds he sowed or the sheaves he gathered? Who has a mind lofty enough to see clearly the wealth amassed by his noble trading? I know the ocean of his achievements, and for that reason I am afraid to venture onto the open sea of telling them, lest my account be swamped. So I will walk along the shore, and admire and relate what lies at the edge of the sea by the land. The deep I will leave to the One who, as the divine Scripture says, searches the depths and knows hidden things.
He first contended in Galatia.

From there he went to Palestine to see it for himself, so that, after beholding the places that had received the saving passion, he might worship in them the God who saved us. Not that he thought God was contained in a place, for he knew that his nature is uncircumscribed; rather, he wanted to feast his eyes as well on the sight of what he longed for, so that it would not be only the soul's eye, without bodily sight, that enjoyed the spiritual delight through faith.

For those who are lovingly devoted to someone are somehow so made that they take delight not only in seeing the person but also look with every pleasure on his house, his clothes and his sandals. It is with this love for the Bridegroom that the bride in the Song of Songs cries out: "Like an apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. In his shade I longed to sit, and sat, and his fruit was sweet in my throat." So this man of God did nothing strange when he conceived the same love for the Bridegroom and used the bride's words: "I am wounded with love." Longing to behold, as it were, a shadow of the Bridegroom, he sought out the places that had poured forth the springs of salvation for all mankind. When he had enjoyed what he longed for, he came down to Antioch. Seeing the city's love of God, he chose this foreign place over his homeland, counting as his fellow citizens not those of the same race and kin but those of the same mind, who shared his faith and drew the same yoke of piety. Having grown fond of living there, he did not pitch a tent, build a hut or put up a small house, but spent all his time in someone else's tomb. It had an upper room, with a kind of railing in front, and a ladder fitted to it allowed those who wished to climb up. Shut up in this, he spent the greater part of his time, drinking cold water and eating only bread, and not even these every day: he would go one day without food and on the next partake of these same things. Once a man came to him in a frenzy, raving and filled with the working of an evil demon; Peter cleansed him by prayer and freed him from that diabolical madness.

The man would not go away, but begged to repay the cure with his service, so Peter made him his companion. I know this man myself, I remember the miracle, I saw the fee he paid for his cure, and I heard a conversation they had about me. Daniel—for that was his name—said, "I too will share in his fine service." But that inspired man would not agree to this, taking into account my parents' affection for me. Many times he sat me on his knees and fed me grapes and bread. My mother, having experienced his spiritual grace, told me to gather that blessing once every week. She had come to know him for the following reason. A disease had struck one of her eyes and proved stronger than medical skill: there was nothing written down by the ancients or discovered by later practitioners that was not applied to the ailment. When it had defeated everything and shown that none of it was any use, one of her acquaintances came and told her about the man of God, describing a miracle he had worked. She said that the wife of the man who at that time held the helm of the East—this was Pergamius—had fallen into this same affliction, and that he had healed her by prayer and the sign of the cross. My mother heard this and ran at once to the man of God. She was wearing earrings, necklaces and other gold ornaments, and a many-colored dress woven of silk threads. For she had not yet tasted the more perfect virtue; she was in the bloom of her years and still clung to the finery of youth. When that inspired soul saw all this, he first healed her weakness for finery, using words like these: "Tell me, my child"—I will use his own words and not alter the address of that holy tongue—"if a painter well practiced in his art were to paint a portrait as the rules of the art dictate and display it to those who wished to see it, and then someone else came along who did not properly understand that art but who wanted to sketch whatever took his fancy, and finding fault with that skillful painting, added longer lines to the eyebrows and eyelashes, made the face whiter and daubed red color on the cheeks, do you not think the first painter would rightly be indignant, since his art had been grossly insulted and had received additions it did not need from an ignorant hand? Then believe," he said, "that the Creator of all things, the Molder and Painter of our nature, is indignant too, because you accuse that ineffable wisdom of ignorance. For you women would not pour on red and white and black color unless you thought you needed this addition; and in supposing that the body needs these things, you condemn the Maker for weakness. You ought to know that his power matches his will. For, as David says, the Lord has done whatever he willed; and since he provides what is good for all, he does not give what is harmful. So do not spoil God's image, do not try to add what the Wise One did not give, and do not contrive this counterfeit beauty, which corrupts even chaste women by laying a snare for those who look at them." When that most excellent woman heard this, she was at once inside Peter's net, for he too fished like his namesake. Clasping his feet and pleading, she begged that her eye be healed. He said that he was a man, with the same nature as hers, that he bore a great load of sins, and that for this reason he lacked boldness before God. But when my mother wept and implored him, and declared she would not leave unless she obtained healing, he said that God is the healer of such things and always grants the requests of those who believe. "So he will grant it now too," he said, "bestowing the favor not on me, but because he sees your faith.

If, then, you have this faith pure and sincere and free of all doubt, bid farewell to doctors and drugs, and receive this God-given remedy." With these words he laid his hand on her eye, traced the sign of the saving cross, and drove the disease away. She went back home, washed off the ointment, threw away all her artificial finery, and lived by the rules laid down by her physician, neither putting on colorful clothes nor adorning herself with gold. And this when she was quite young: she was in her twenty-third year and had not yet become a mother. It was seven years later that she went into labor with me, her first and only childbirth. So much did she profit from the great Peter's teaching: she received a double cure, for in seeking healing for her body she gained health of soul as well.
Such was the effect of his words, and such the power of his prayers.

On another occasion she brought him a servant, a cook, who was troubled by an evil demon, and begged that he might receive help from him. The man of God prayed and ordered the demon to state the reason for its power over God's handiwork. Like a murderer or a burglar standing before a judge's tribunal and ordered to tell what he has done, the demon recounted everything, forced by fear to tell the truth, contrary to its custom. It said that in Heliopolis the servant's master had fallen ill, and the mistress was sitting at her sick husband's side. The maidservants of the house where they were staying were telling stories about the life of the monks practicing philosophy in Antioch, and of how much power they have over demons. Then, being girls who enjoyed a game, they pretended to be possessed and raving, while this very servant put on a goat-hair cloak and exorcised them in the manner of a monk. "While this was going on," it said, "I was standing by the door, and since I could not bear the boastful talk about the monks, I wanted to learn by experience what power they boldly claimed to have. That is why I left the girls and slipped into this man, wishing to find out how I would be driven out by the monks.

And now," it said, "I have found out, and I need no further test: I will come out at once at your command." With these words it fled, and the servant enjoyed his freedom. Another time, the one who was my mother's mother and my own nurse brought him a farmhand who was possessed, and begged the adversary of evil to help him. Again he asked where the demon came from and from whom it had received its power over God's handiwork. When the man stood in silence, giving no answer, Peter knelt and prayed, entreating God to show the wicked spirit the power of his own servants. Then he stood up again, and again the demon held out in silence, and this went on until the ninth hour. When he had offered a more fervent and earnest prayer to the Master, he stood up and said to the wicked spirit: "It is not Peter who commands you, but Peter's God. So answer, compelled by his power." The avenging spirit, shameless though it was, was abashed by the saint's gentleness, and crying out in a very loud voice, it said that it used to dwell on Mount Amanus: "I saw this man on the road drawing water from a spring and drinking it, and I wanted to make him my dwelling." "Well, come out," said the man of God, "for he who was crucified for the world commands you to." The demon heard and fled, and the farmhand, freed from his madness, was given back to my nurse.

Though I have countless other such stories to tell of that blessed soul, I will pass over most of them, fearing the weakness of the many: for they judge by themselves, and so disbelieve the miracles of men of God.
After telling one or two more, I will move on to another contestant.
In earlier times there was a licentious general.

Now an unmarried girl of marriageable age, who lived under his authority, left her mother and her family and took refuge in a women's house that held a band of athletes. For women too contend just as men do, and go down into the stadium of virtue. When the general learned of her flight, he flogged her mother and hung her up, and did not release her from her bonds until she had shown him the lodging of the devout women. Giving rein to his madness, he carried the girl off from there and brought her back to his own house, and the wretch hoped to satisfy his lust. But he who afflicted Pharaoh with great and grievous plagues on account of Sarah, Abraham's wife, and kept that chaste woman untouched, and who struck the Sodomites with blindness when they tried to assault the bodiless ones as if they were strangers—he struck this man's sight with blindness too and enabled the prey to escape from the middle of the nets. He went into the bedroom, while she, who was being kept inside, went straight out and was gone, and reached the lodging she longed for so dearly. So the fool, learning that he would not prevail over a woman who had chosen the divine Suitor, was forced to keep quiet, and no longer sought the girl who had been caught and had escaped by divine power.

Some time later she fell victim to a grievous affliction: it was a cancer, and as her breast swelled the pain grew with it. But at the height of the pain she would call for the great Peter, and she said that as soon as that holy voice fell on her ears, all the pain was lulled to sleep and she felt not the slightest distress from it. For this reason she sent for him quite often and enjoyed relief, for she said that the whole time he was present the pains left her completely. Having contended in this way, she was sent on by him from this life with praises fit for a victor. Another time, when my mother had come close to the gates of death after giving birth to me, he came at the earnest request of my nurse and snatched her from the hands of death. She was lying there, they say, with the doctors having given up hope and her household lamenting and waiting for the end, her eyes closed, gripped by a raging fever, recognizing none of her familiar circle. But when the man who had been granted both the name and the grace of the apostle came and said, "Peace be with you, little child"—for this was how he addressed her—they say she at once opened her eyelids, gazed intently at him, and asked for the fruit of his blessing.

When the company of women raised a cry—for dejection and joy were mingled together and produced that shout—the man of God urged them all to join him in prayer, for, he said, this was how Tabitha too had obtained her recovery: the widows wept, and the great Peter offered their tears to God.
They prayed as he bade them, and received what he had foretold.

For as the prayer came to an end, the illness also came to an end: sweat suddenly poured out all over her, that fever was quenched, and signs of health appeared. Such are the wonders the Master works in our own times too through his servants.

The garments that touched his body had power too, just as with the most divine Paul. I have not set this down by way of exaggeration: the truth bears me out. He cut his own belt in two—it was broad and long, plaited from thick linen—and with one half girded his own waist and with the other mine. My mother often laid it on me when I was sick, and often on my father, and drove the illness away; and she herself used this remedy to regain her health. Many of our acquaintances, learning of this, kept borrowing the belt to help the sick, and everywhere it made known the working of his grace.
In the end someone took it and deprived those who had lent it, proving ungrateful to his benefactors; that is how we were stripped of that gift.

Having shone in this way and lit up the city of Antiochus with his rays, he passed beyond the contests, and awaits the crown laid up for the victors. As for me, I beg to enjoy now too the blessing I enjoyed while he was alive, and with that I will bring this account to an end.

Rhosus is a city of Cilicia, on the right as one sails into the Cilician gulf. To the southeast of it there is a high mountain, thickly wooded and shady, whose thickets also harbor wild beasts. Here the great and widely renowned Theodosius found a glen sloping down toward the sea, built a small hut, and embraced the gospel way of life alone. He came from the city of Antiochus and was distinguished by the splendor of his family; yet he left behind his house, his kin and everything else, and bought, in the words of the Gospel, the pearl of great price. As for his fasting, sleeping on the ground and garment of hair, it is superfluous to speak of them to those who see his followers and disciples, and observe this way of life in them. Yet he practiced these things to an exceptional degree, since he was setting himself up as an example to the newcomers. In addition to these he bore a load of iron on his neck, his waist and both his hands.
He also wore his hair unkempt. It reached down to his very feet and even beyond them, so he tied it up at his waist.

He prayed and sang hymns without ceasing, and so lulled to sleep desire, anger, pride and the other wild beasts of the soul. Always adding labour to labour, he also took up manual work. At times he wove what are called fans, and baskets; at other times he laid out small fields in the glen, sowed seed, and gathered from them enough food to live on. As time went on and his fame spread everywhere, many people came hurrying from many places, eager to share his dwelling, his labours and his way of life. He welcomed them and guided them into this life. One could see some weaving sails, others haircloth coverings, others plaiting fans or baskets, and others who had taken up farming. Since the place lay beside the sea, he later built a boat as well and used it to carry goods, shipping out the work of his companions and bringing in what they needed. He remembered the words of the Apostle: “Working night and day, so as not to be a burden to any of you,” and, “These hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me.” So he worked himself, and urged those who shared his dwelling to add the sweat of bodily toil to the labours of the soul.

“For it is absurd,” he said, “that people living in the world should toil and labour to feed children and wives, and besides this pay taxes and have tribute demanded of them, offer their first fruits to God, and relieve the need of beggars as far as they can, while we do not provide our necessities by our own labour, though we live on cheap and scanty food and wear cheap clothing, but sit with our hands folded, enjoying the fruit of other people's hands.” With these and similar words he urged them to work. He celebrated the divine services customary everywhere at their proper times and gave the time in between to work. He took particular care over the care of strangers, entrusting this charge to men adorned with gentleness and humility of mind who had love for their neighbour. He himself oversaw everything, inquiring closely whether each task was carried out according to the established rules. He became so widely renowned that sailors more than a thousand stades away would call on the God of Theodosius in their dangers and calm the storms of the sea by invoking the name of Theodosius. Even bold and savage enemies, who had plundered most of the East and carried off its people as slaves, showed him reverence. For who among the inhabitants of our world has not heard of the evils done at that time by the people once called the Solymi and now named the Isaurians? Yet though they spared neither city nor village, but plundered and burned all they could capture, they revered that philosophy. They asked only for bread, promised to pray, and left that ascetic dwelling unharmed—and they did this not once but twice. The leaders of the churches were nevertheless afraid that the devil might inspire the barbarians with a love of money and so arrange for that great luminary to be taken captive, since it was likely that very large ransoms would be sent to them for him from every quarter by all who honour divine things. So they appealed to him and persuaded him to move to Antioch. For the barbarians had already taken two leaders of churches captive. They did treat them with every attention, but only after receiving fourteen thousand gold pieces for the two of them did they let them go wherever they wished. When he arrived at Antioch, he lived in a dwelling beside the river, and drew to himself all who knew how to gather such a harvest.
Carried along by the current of my narrative, I have left out a miracle performed by this inspired man.

To many it may well seem incredible, but it still remains today as a witness to my account, showing what grace and confidence before God this wonderful man had obtained. A steep rock rises above the monastery that he built, and formerly it was utterly waterless and dry. On this rock he made a water channel running from the summit down to the monastery, as though he had the flow of water under his control.

Full of trust in God, confident, as was natural, that he had the Master's favour, and possessing unwavering faith, he rose in the night and went up to the top of the channel before his companions got up for their usual prayers. He besought God in prayer, trusting in him who does the will of those who fear him, and struck the rock with the staff on which he leaned. The rock split and water gushed out like a river. Passing through the channel into the monastery and supplying every need abundantly, it flows out into the nearby sea. Down to this day the Mosaic grace of the great Theodosius can be seen at work. This alone is enough to show the man's confidence before God. After living a short time in Antioch, he passed over to the choir of angels. His holy body was carried through the middle of the city, adorned with that iron of his as with golden crowns, while everyone led the procession, even those entrusted with high offices. There was strife and contention over the bier, as all pressed to carry it, eager to receive the blessing that came from it.

Carried in this way, he was laid in the shrine of the holy martyrs, coming to share the tent and the roof of Julian, the victorious champion of piety. The same tomb received him as received the inspired and blessed Aphrahat. The leadership of the flock passed to the wonderful Helladius, who persevered for sixty years in those labours and then received from God the presidency of the church of Cilicia. He did not abandon his former philosophy, but daily added the sweat of the episcopate to those labours. The blessed Romulus too, who had been his disciple, was appointed leader of a very large flock, and he and his company have continued in the same way of life to this day. Next to the monastery lies a village called Marato in Syriac. I, making this the end of this account, pray that I too may share in the blessing that comes from it.

The great Theodosius, then, set out from the territory of Antioch, contended in the mountains of Rhosus, and on returning to the city of Antiochus there met the end of his life. The godly Romanus, on the other hand, was born and brought up in Rhosus, but undertook the contests of virtue at Antioch. He lodged outside the city walls at the foot of the mountain, and spent his whole life in someone else's little dwelling, and a small one at that. He continued into old age without using fire or accepting the light of a lamp. His food was bread and salt, his drink spring water; his hair was like that of the great Theodosius, and so too were his clothing and his iron.

He excelled in simplicity of character, gentleness of manner and humility of mind, and for this reason he shone with the radiance of divine grace.
