For, it says, “On whom shall I look, but on the one who is gentle and quiet and trembles at my words?” And again he said to his own disciples, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” And again, “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.” This was also the distinguishing mark of the achievements of Moses the lawgiver. For, it says, “Moses was the gentlest of all the people on the face of the earth.” The all-holy Spirit bore the same witness to the prophet David: “Remember,” it says, “David and all his gentleness.” And of the patriarch Jacob we have learned that he was a plain man, dwelling in a house. Gathering these virtues like a bee from those divine meadows, he made the honey of truth. Yet he did not enjoy the fruit of his labours alone. His sweetest streams poured out also to those outside. To those who came to him he spoke in a gentle and sweet voice, offering much counsel on brotherly love and much on concord and peace, and many he made lovers of divine things merely by being seen.

For who would not have been filled with admiration at the sight of an old man with a worn-out body, who chose to carry as much iron as possible, wore a garment of hair, and took only enough food to keep off death by starvation? Besides the greatness and number of his labours, the grace that blossomed in him also moved everyone to admire and honour him. Many times he drove away grievous diseases from many people, and to many barren women he granted children. Yet though he had received such power from the divine Spirit, he called himself a poor man and a beggar. So he spent his whole life filling with benefit all who came to him, both by his appearance and by his words. And when he departed from here and was transferred to the choir of angels, he left behind a memory not buried with his body but blooming and flourishing, remaining unquenched for ever and sufficient to benefit all who desire it. Having gathered the blessing from this source too, I shall narrate, as far as I can, the stories of the other athletes.

Not many know the wonderful Zeno, and those who do know him cannot admire him as he deserves. He left behind very great wealth in his homeland, which was Pontus. As he used to say, he enjoyed the streams of the great Basil, who lived nearby and watered Cappadocia, and he yielded fruits worthy of that watering. As soon as the emperor Valens was killed, he laid aside the military belt; he had been enrolled among the couriers who carry the emperor's letters at speed. From the palace he hurried to a tomb—the mountain near Antioch has many—and lived there alone, purifying his soul, cleansing its power of sight, contemplating the divine vision, setting ascents to God in his heart, longing to take wings like a dove and yearning to fly up to the divine rest. For this reason he had no bed, no lamp, no hearth, no pot, no oil flask, no chest, no book, nothing else at all. He wore old rags, and shoes that likewise needed tying on, for the leather of their soles had come apart. He obtained his necessary food from one acquaintance only: it was a single loaf, supplied every two days. He fetched water himself and carried it from far away. Once someone saw him carrying his load and begged to relieve him of the labour. At first he refused, explaining that he would not bear to drink water carried by another. But when he could not persuade the man, he handed over the jars—he was carrying two, one in each hand.

When they were inside the door of his dwelling, he poured out the water and sprinkled it about, and ran back again to the spring, confirming his words by his action. I too, when I first went up the mountain longing to visit him, saw him holding the jars in his hands. I then asked him where the dwelling of the wonderful Zeno was. He said he did not at all know of any monk called by that name. But I guessed that it was he and followed him, taking the modesty of his words as evidence. When I came inside the door, I saw a bed made of hay, and some other litter spread over the stones so that those who sat on it would come to no harm.

We held a long conversation about philosophy—I asked questions, and he unfolded the answers to what I sought. When it was time to go home, I begged him to give me the provision of his blessing. He refused, saying that it was proper for us to offer the prayer, calling himself a layman and us soldiers; for at that time I happened to be reading the sacred books to the people of God. When we pleaded our youth and our immature age—we had only just grown a little down on our cheeks—and swore that we would not come again if we were compelled to do this now, he at long last gave way to our entreaties and offered the prayer to God. But he made a long apology for the prayer, saying he had done it out of love and obedience; and we heard him as we drew near while he prayed. Who could worthily admire an old man—for he had already completed forty years in ascetic practice—who had such humility of mind at such a height of philosophy? What praise could one offer equal to its greatness? Possessing such wealth of virtue while living in the utmost poverty, he went with the crowd to the divine church every Lord's Day, listened to the divine words, gave ear to the teachers, received the mystic table, and returned to that extraordinary dwelling of his. He had no key and left no one on guard, for it was untouched by thieves and wholly safe from plunder, since it held nothing but that litter. He would borrow one book from his acquaintances and read it all through, and only after returning it would he take another. And though he had no locks and used no bars, he was guarded by the grace from above. This we learned clearly from experience itself. When a band of Isaurians seized the heights by night and then, after dawn, ran down as far as the foot of the mountain, they shot down without mercy many men and many women who were following the ascetic life. Then this godly man, seeing the slaughter of the others, darkened their sight by prayer, and though they passed by his door they could not see the entrance. As he told us, calling the truth to witness, he also clearly saw three young men driving off that whole [?].
What kind of life this godly man lived, and what grace he enjoyed from God, this is enough to show. But I must add the following as well.

It grieved and troubled him greatly that his property remained and had not been sold and distributed according to the law of the Gospel. The reason was that his brothers were not yet of age. Since the land and the money were held in common, he did not wish to go back to his homeland to divide them, and he was afraid to sell his share of the estate to someone else, in case the buyers took advantage of his brothers and so brought reproach on him.

Turning these thoughts over in his mind, he put off the sale for a long time. Later he sold everything to one of his acquaintances and distributed most of it, but meanwhile an illness overtook him and forced him to decide about what remained. So he sent for the bishop of the city—this was the great Alexander, the ornament of piety, the model of virtue, the exact image of philosophy—and said, “Come, my godly friend, and become the best steward of this money too. Distribute it according to God's purpose, as one who will give account to that Judge. The rest I handled myself and gave away as I thought best, and I wanted to manage what remains in the same way.

“But since I am called to depart from this life, I appoint you steward of it, since you are a high priest and live in a way worthy of the high priesthood.” So he handed over the money to him as to God's treasurer. He himself did not live long after this, but departed from the arena like an Olympic victor, receiving acclaim not only from men but also from angels. I, having begged him too to intercede with the Master on my behalf, shall now turn to another narrative.

Macedonius, surnamed the Barley-eater—this kind of food gave him that nickname—is known to everyone, Phoenicians, Syrians and Cilicians alike; and he is known also to their neighbours and those on their borders. Some of them have seen the man's miracles with their own eyes; others have heard of them as rumour sings and spreads them abroad.

Not everyone knows everything. Some have learned one thing and some another, and naturally each admires only what they know. But I know the story of that man, so holy to me, more exactly than most, because many things moved me to visit him and to admire him. So I will tell it, each part as well as I can. I have kept him in this place and set his account after many others, not because he came second to the others in virtue (he was a match for the highest and the first), but because he lived an exceptionally long time and came to the end of his life after those I have already recorded.

This man, then, had the mountain peaks for his wrestling-ground and his racecourse. He did not settle in one spot. He would live in one place for a time, then move on to another. He did this not because he disliked the places, but to escape the crowds that came together to see him and ran to him from every direction. He kept up this way of life for forty-five years, using neither a tent nor a hut, but making his station in a deep pit. For this reason some nicknamed him Gubba; translated from the Syriac language into Greek, the name means "pit." After this time, when he had grown old, he gave way to those who pleaded with him and put up a hut.
Later, at the urging of his friends, he even made use of small dwellings, though they were not his own but belonged to others.

He spent twenty-five years living in the hut and the small dwellings, so that the whole span of his contests came to seventy years. For food he ate neither bread nor pulses, but hulled barley, merely soaked in water. My own mother, who had come to know him, supplied him with this food for a very long time. Once, when she was ill, he came to see her, and learned that she would not agree to take food suited to her illness (for she too had by then embraced the ascetic life). He urged her to give way to the doctors and to regard such food as medicine, since it is taken not for pleasure but out of need. "For I too," he said, "as you know, have lived on barley alone for forty years, but yesterday, when I fell somewhat ill, I told my companion to ask for a little bread and bring it to me.

A thought came to me: if I died, I would be called to account for my death before the just Judge, as one who had fled the contests and run away from the labors of his service. For when death could be prevented by a little food, and I could stay on in this life, laboring and enduring hardship and gathering the wealth that comes from it, I had judged death by starvation preferable to the life of philosophy.

"So, filled with fear at this, and wanting to blunt the stings of the thought, I told him to ask for the bread, and when it was brought I ate some. And now I urge you too: no longer give me barley, but bread." From that truthful tongue, then, we have heard that he made barley his food for forty years. This is enough to prove the man's asceticism and love of toil. His old-fashioned simplicity of character I will show by other stories.

When the great Flavian was appointed to shepherd God's great flock, he learned of the man's virtue (for it was celebrated and on everyone's lips). He had him brought down from the mountaintop as though a charge had been laid against him. Then, when the sacred mystery was being celebrated, he brought him up to the altar and enrolled him among the priests. When the liturgy was over and someone told him what had happened (for he had been entirely unaware of it), he first railed at everyone and pelted them all with words. Then he took his staff (for because of his age he was used to walking leaning on it) and chased after the archbishop himself and all the others who were there. For he supposed that his ordination would deprive him of the mountaintop and the way of life he longed for. On that occasion some of his friends managed with difficulty to calm his indignation. But when the week had come full circle and the Lord's day had come round again, the great Flavian sent for him once more, inviting him to join them in the festival. He said to those who came, "Isn't what has already been done enough for you? Do you want to make me a presbyter again?" When they told him that it was impossible for the same ordination to be conferred twice, he did not give in or come, until time and his friends had taught him this many times over. Now we know that many will not think this story worth admiring. But I have included it because I consider it worth recording, as enough to prove both the simplicity of his mind and the purity of his soul. It is to such people that the Lord promised the kingdom of heaven: "Truly I tell you," he said, "unless you turn and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." Now that we have shown the character of his soul in brief, let us also show the boldness of speech that came from his virtue.

A certain general who enjoyed hunting went up the mountain to hunt, followed by dogs, soldiers, and everything needed for the chase. When he saw the man from a distance and learned from his companions who he was, he at once leapt down from his horse, approached and greeted him, and asked what he was doing living there. He asked in return, "And what have you come up here to do?" When the general said, "To hunt," he replied, "I too am hunting my God. I long to catch him and yearn to see him, and I will not give up this fine hunt." Hearing this, the general marveled, as one would, and went away. On another occasion, when the city had been driven to frenzy by some wicked demon and in its madness had attacked the imperial statues, the most eminent of the generals arrived, bringing a sentence of total destruction against the city. This man came down from the mountain and stopped both generals as they were passing through the marketplace. When they learned who he was, they leapt down from their horses, clasped his hands and knees, and greeted him. He charged them to tell the emperor: "You are a man, and you share the same nature as those who have insulted you. Though you ought to measure your anger by your nature, you have given way to boundless wrath. For the sake of your own images you hand over God's images to slaughter, and in exchange for bronze statues you send bodies to death. It is easy and simple for us to remold and reshape the bronze ones, but for you, even though you are emperor, it is impossible to bring slaughtered bodies back to life. And why do I say bodies? You cannot even remake a single hair." He said this in Syriac, and as the interpreter rendered it into Greek, they listened and shuddered, and promised to carry his words across to the emperor. I think everyone would agree that these words came from the grace of the divine Spirit. How else could such things have been spoken by a man without any education, brought up in the countryside, living on the mountain peaks, carrying perfect simplicity in his soul, and not even versed in the divine Scriptures? So, having shown both his spiritual wisdom and the boldness that befits a righteous man (for "the righteous is bold as a lion"), I will pass on to his miracles.

The wife of a wealthy man fell victim to a disorder of insatiable gluttony. Some called the disorder the work of a demon; others thought it a bodily illness. Whichever it was, it was like this: they said that she ate thirty birds a day without quenching her craving, but still longed for more. As his fortune was being spent on her in this way, her relatives took pity and begged that man of God for help. He came and prayed, laid his right hand on some water, marked it with the saving sign, told her to drink, and healed the disorder. He so thoroughly blunted her excessive appetite that from then on a small piece of a bird each day satisfied her need for food. That was the cure this disorder received. Another time, a girl still kept in her chamber was suddenly seized by the working of a wicked demon. Her father ran to the man of God, pleading and lamenting, and begging that his little daughter be healed. He prayed and ordered the demon to leave the girl at once. The demon said that it had not entered her willingly but had been forced by sorcerer's magic. It even gave the name of the man who had compelled it, and said that love was the reason for the sorcery. When he heard this, the father could not bear the onrush of his anger, nor did he wait for his child's cure. He went to the governor who ranks above the greater governors and presides over most of the provinces, brought a charge against the man, and recounted the affair. The accused, brought to court, denied it and called the charge a slander. The father called no other witness than the demon that had served the sorcery, and begged the judge to go to that man of God and receive the demon's testimony. When the judge said it was neither lawful nor right for an interrogation to take place in an ascetic's dwelling, the girl's father promised to bring the holy Macedonius to the court, and he ran off, persuaded him, and brought him. The judge sat outside the court building and became not a judge but a spectator. For the great Macedonius did the judge's work, using the power that dwelt in him: he commanded the demon to drop its usual lying and tell the whole tragic tale of the affair truthfully. Driven by the strongest compulsion, the demon pointed out both the man who had compelled it with his sorcerer's incantations and the maidservant through whom that potion had been given to the girl. When it pressed on to tell other things it had done under compulsion from other people—burning down one man's house, destroying another's livestock, doing some other harm to another—the man of God ordered it to be silent and to go at once far away from both the girl and the city. Like one obeying the Lord's law, it did as it was told and immediately fled. In this way that man of God freed the girl from her madness, snatched that wretched man from the charge, and prevented the judge's death sentence, saying it was not right for execution to follow on proofs brought about by him, but that the man should rather be granted salvation through repentance. These things are enough to show the abundance of divine power given to him. But I will tell of others all the same.

A woman of noble family and very great wealth (her name was Astrion) lost her mind. She recognized none of her household and would not consent to take food or drink. She went on raving for a very long time. Others called this the work of a demon, but the doctors called it a disease of the brain. When all their art had been exhausted and no help came from it, her husband (this was Avodianus, a man of high office and rank) ran to that holy man, told him of his wife's disorder, and begged him to heal her. The holy man agreed, went to the house, and offered earnest supplication to God. When he had finished his prayer, he had water brought, marked it with the saving sign, and told her to drink. The doctors forbade it, saying that the disorder would grow worse from drinking cold water, but her husband pushed the whole crowd of them aside and gave his wife the drink. As she drank, she came to herself at once and was in her right mind. Completely freed from the disorder, she recognized the holy man, begged to take his right hand, laid it on her eyes and put it to her lips. And from then on she remained of sound mind.

When he was still embracing the mountain life, a shepherd searching for stray sheep came to the place where the man of God was. It was the dead of night and snow was falling heavily, and he saw, as he said, a fire burning around him and two figures dressed in white feeding the fire with wood. For since he contributed his zeal, he enjoyed divine help.
He also shared in the gift of prophecy.

Once a general famed for his piety came to him (and who does not know the virtue of Lupicinus?) and said he was worried about some men who were bringing him supplies by sea from the imperial city. He said fifty days had passed since they set sail from the harbor, and he had received no news of them. Without hesitating, the man said, "One ship, my friend, has been lost, but the other will reach the harbor of Seleucia tomorrow." The general heard this spoken by that holy tongue, and learned the truth of the words by experience.

But to leave the rest aside, I will tell what concerns us ourselves. My mother lived with my father for thirteen years without becoming a mother of children, for she was barren, prevented by nature from bearing fruit. This did not trouble her much, since, having been instructed in divine things, she believed it to be for the best. But childlessness grieved my father greatly, and he went around everywhere begging God's servants to ask God for children for him. The others promised to pray and urged him to accept the divine will. But this man of God promised outright to make the request, and assured him that he would receive one son from the Creator of all things. When three years had passed and the promise had not been fulfilled, my father ran to him again, demanding what had been promised. He told him to send his wife to him. When my mother came, the holy man said that he would ask and she would receive the child, but that it was fitting for the child to be given back in return to the one who gave it. My mother pleaded to receive only the salvation of her soul and deliverance from Gehenna, and he said, "In addition to that, the generous Giver will give you the son as well. For to those who ask sincerely he grants their requests twice over." My mother returned from there carrying the blessing of the promise. In the fourth year after the promise she conceived and became heavy with child, and she went to the man of God to show him the sheaves grown from the seeds of his blessing. But in the fifth month of the pregnancy there arose a danger of miscarriage.

She sent again to her new Elisha (for her condition kept her from running to him herself), reminded him that she had not wished to become a mother of children, and brought his promises before him. When he saw the messenger from afar, he recognized him and knew why he had come, for during the night the Lord had revealed to him both the danger and the deliverance.

So he took his staff and came, leaning on it. Once inside the house, he gave the greeting of peace, as was his custom, and said, "Take heart and do not be afraid. The Giver will not take back the gift unless you break the agreement that was made.
You promised to give back in return what would be given, and to consecrate it to the service of God." "That is how I too want to give birth," said my mother, "and it is what I pray for.

For I consider an unfinished birth preferable to the child's being brought up in any other way." "Then drink this water," said the man of God, "and you will feel God's help." So she drank, as he had told her, and the danger of miscarriage fled. Such are the miracles of our Elisha. I myself often enjoyed his blessing and his teaching.

For he often admonished me, saying, "You were born with much toil, my child. I spent many nights begging God for this alone: that your parents might become what, after your birth, they came to be called. So live a life worthy of that toil.

You were dedicated by promises before the birth pangs. Things dedicated to God are revered by all and not to be touched by the many. So it is fitting for you, too, not to admit the base impulses of the soul, but to do, say, and think only those things that serve God, the lawgiver of virtue." The man of God never ceased admonishing me in this way. I remember his words and have learned of the divine gift. But though I do not show his admonition in my deeds, I pray that through his intercession I may obtain God's help and live the rest of my life according to his counsels. What kind of man he was, and by what labors he drew down divine grace, this is enough to teach. Yet even in this life the end of his labors received fitting honor. Everyone—citizens, foreigners, and those entrusted with governing the great offices—carried that sacred bier on their shoulders to the shrine of the victorious martyrs, and laid that holy body, beloved of God, beside those holy men Aphrahat and Theodosius. His fame has remained unquenched, and no length of time will be able to blot it out. As for us, having brought our account to an end, we have reaped the fragrance of the telling.

I know that many other lights of piety shone out near the city of Antiochus: the great Severus, Peter the Egyptian, Eutychius, Cyril, Moses, Malchus, and very many others who traveled the same road. But if we tried to write the lives of them all, all the time in the world would not be enough. Besides, reading about too many grows tiresome for most people.
From what has been written, then, let everyone infer the rest of his life, which has been left out; let all speak well of him, let them emulate him, and let them reap the benefit.
I shall now cross over to the meadows of Cyrrhus and show, as far as I can, the beauty of a few of the fragrant and lovely flowers that grow in them.

In the times before ours there lived a certain Maesymas. He was Syrian in speech and raised in the countryside, and he displayed every form of virtue. Because he shone in the life he led, he was entrusted with the care of a certain village. As he performed the sacred rites and shepherded God's sheep, he said and did what the divine law prescribed. They say that for a very long time he changed neither his tunic nor his cloak. Instead, he sewed other rags over the tears that appeared in them, and in this way he tended to their old age. He cared for strangers and the poor so eagerly that he threw his doors open to everyone who passed by. He is said to have had two jars, one of grain and one of oil. From these he always supplied everyone in need, and yet he always kept them full, because the blessing given to the widow of Zarephath had been extended to these jars as well. For the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon him. Just as he made that jar and that flask overflow, providing sheaves from the seeds of hospitality, so he also gave this admirable man a supply that matched his eagerness. He also received from the God of the universe great grace for working miracles. I shall mention one or two of these and pass over the rest, since I am eager to come to the others.

A woman distinguished both by birth and by faith had a son who fell ill. He was quite young, and she brought him to many physicians. When their art had been defeated, and the physicians had given up and declared plainly that the child would die, the woman did not throw away her better hopes. Instead, she imitated the famous Shunammite woman and had the covered carriage harnessed to the mules.
She placed herself and the child in it and came to that man of God. Wailing and showing all the anguish of nature, she begged him to help.

He took the child in his arms, went up to the step of the altar, and lay face down, entreating the Physician of souls and bodies. When his request was granted, he gave the son back to his mother in good health. I heard this from the woman herself, who saw the miracle and received her child back safe.

They also say that the owner of that village once came there. This was Letoius, who held first place in the council of Antioch but was held fast in the darkness of impiety. He exacted the produce from the farmers more harshly than he should have. The man of God urged and counselled him to be humane, and set out to him arguments for mercy and compassion. Letoius remained implacable, but he learned by experience the harm that disobedience brings. When it was time for him to leave and the carriage was ready, he sat down and ordered the driver to urge on the mules. The mules pulled with all their strength, straining and struggling to drag the pole forward, but the wheels seemed to be bound with iron and lead. A crowd of peasants tried to move the wheels with levers, but they achieved nothing. Then one of Letoius' better-disposed attendants pointed out the cause: the old priest, he said, had cursed him, and he ought to win back his favour. So Letoius leaped down from the carriage and supplicated the man he had despised. Rolling at his feet and embracing his filthy rags, he begged him to relax his anger. The holy man accepted his supplication and offered it to the Master. He loosed the invisible bonds on the wheels and made the vehicle move as usual.
They tell many other such stories about that holy man. From these one can also learn that living in towns and villages does very little harm to those who choose the life of philosophy.

For he, and those of his time who devoted themselves to the service of God, showed that it is possible to reach the very summit of virtue even while living among many people. Helped by their prayers, may I climb at least a little way up the foothills of that summit.

Acepsimas lived at the same time, and his fame spread widely throughout the East. He shut himself up in a small cell and spent sixty years there, neither seen nor speaking. Turned inward and contemplating God, he received all his consolation from that source, in keeping with the prophecy that says, "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart." He stretched out his hand through a small hole to receive the food that was brought to him. The hole was not dug straight through, so that it would not lie open to those who wanted to look in. It was cut slantwise and made to wind. His food was lentils soaked in water. Once a week he went out at night and drew enough water from a nearby spring. One night a shepherd grazing his flock some distance away saw him moving in the dark and took him for a wolf, since he walked stooped over, weighed down by a great deal of iron. The shepherd swung his sling to hurl a stone. But his hand stayed motionless for a long time and could not release the stone until the man of God had drawn his water and gone back. Then the shepherd realized his mistake. After dawn he came to that school of virtue, told what had happened and asked forgiveness. He received pardon for his offence, not by hearing a spoken word but by learning the saint's goodwill from the movements of his hand. Another man, driven by malicious curiosity and longing to know what Acepsimas did all the time, dared to climb the plane tree that grew beside the enclosure wall. But he immediately reaped the fruits of his daring. Half of his body was crippled, from the top of his head to his feet, and he came as a suppliant, confessing his sin. The saint foretold that he would be healed when the plane tree was cut down. So that no one else would do the same thing and suffer the same fate, he ordered the tree to be cut down at once. Release from the punishment followed the cutting. Such was the endurance this inspired man practised, and such was the grace he received from the Judge of the contest.
When he was preparing for his departure from this world, he foretold that he would reach the end of his life after fifty days, and he received everyone who wished to see him.

When the bishop of the church also came, he pressed him to take up the yoke of the priesthood. "Father," he said, "I know both the height of your philosophy and the depth of my own poverty. But I have been entrusted with the stewardship of the high priesthood, and I perform ordinations by virtue of that office, not by virtue of philosophy. So accept the gift of the priesthood. My right hand will serve, and the grace of the all-holy Spirit will supply it." To this, it is said, he replied: "Since I shall depart from here in a few days, I will not struggle against this at all. If I were going to live a long time, I would have fled altogether from this heavy and fearful burden of the priesthood, dreading the account I would have to give for what was entrusted to me. But since I shall soon go away and leave the things of this world behind, I will obediently accept what is commanded." At once, with no one needing to lead him, he bent his knees and awaited the grace, while the bishop laid his hand on him and served the Spirit.

He lived only a few days after his ordination and then exchanged one life for another, receiving a life free of age and grief in place of one full of cares. Everyone wanted to seize his body, and each group meant to carry it off to its own village. But someone made known the saint's oaths and so ended the dispute. He said the saint had made him swear to bury the body in that very place.

So careful were the citizens of heaven to stay humble even after death. While they lived, they never let themselves think highly of themselves, and when they died they did not seek honour from men. They transferred all their love to the Bridegroom, like chaste wives who are eager to be loved and praised by their husbands alone and who despise praise from others.

For this reason the Bridegroom made them famous even against their will and gave them glory among men in abundance. For whenever someone who pursues divine things asks for heavenly things, he adds a great many other things as well, giving many times more than was asked. This is indeed what he said when he gave his laws: "Ask for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all the rest will be added to you." And again: "Whoever leaves father and mother and brothers and wife and children for my sake and for the sake of my gospel will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the age to come will inherit eternal life." This he said, and this he did.
May it be granted to us, taught by these words and supported by their prayers, to press on toward the goal, for the prize of the upward call in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

With these I shall also mention Maron, for he too adorned the divine choir of the saints. He embraced the life in the open air and took possession of a certain hilltop that the impious had honoured in former times. He consecrated to God the precinct of the demons that stood there and lived in it. He pitched a small tent there, though he seldom used it. He not only practised the customary labours but also devised others, amassing the wealth of philosophy. And the Judge of the contest measured out grace to match his labours.
The generous Giver bestowed the gift of healing on him so richly that his fame spread everywhere. It drew everyone from everywhere, and their experience taught them that the report was true.

One could see fevers quenched by the dew of his blessing, shivering fits stopped, demons put to flight, and all kinds of diseases cured by a single remedy. The sons of physicians apply a remedy suited to each ailment, but the prayer of the saints is a common antidote to every ailment. He healed not only illnesses of the body but also gave fitting treatment to souls. He cured one man's greed and another's anger. To one he offered teaching on self-control, to another he gave lessons in justice. He corrected one man's licentiousness and roused another from sluggishness. By practising this kind of farming he raised many plants of philosophy, and it was he who planted for God the garden that now flourishes in the region of Cyrrhus. The great James is the fruit of his planting, and one could fittingly apply to him the prophetic saying, "The righteous will flourish like the palm tree; he will grow like a cedar in Lebanon." So are all the others, whom, God willing, I shall mention one by one.

As he tended this divine farming in this way, healing souls and bodies alike, he suffered a brief illness, so that we might learn both the weakness of nature and the courage of his will, and he departed this life. Then a fierce war broke out among his neighbours over his body.

The whole population of a large neighbouring village came out in force, scattered the others, and carried off that treasure so dearly longed for. They built a very large shrine and reap its benefit to this day, honouring that victor with a public festival. We too, though far away, reap his blessing, for his memory is enough for us in place of his tomb.
Nor would it be right to leave out the memory of the admirable Abraham on the pretext that, after his solitary life, he lent lustre to a bishop's throne.

Surely he deserves to be remembered all the more for this very reason. When he was forced to change his station, he did not change his way of life. He brought his ascetic hardship with him, and he completed the course of his life surrounded at once by the labours of a monk and the cares of a bishop. He too was a fruit of the region of Cyrrhus, for he was born and raised there, and there he gathered the wealth of ascetic virtue. Those who knew him say that he subdued his body with so much vigil, standing and fasting that for a very long time he remained unable to move and could hardly walk at all. When divine providence freed him from that infirmity, he wished to face dangers in return for the divine grace. He went to Lebanon, having learned that a very large village there was held in the darkness of impiety. He hid his monk's identity behind the mask of a merchant. He and his companions carried sacks, as if they had come to buy nuts, since that was the village's chief crop. He rented a house, paid the owners a little money in advance, and kept quiet for three or four days. Then, little by little, he began the divine liturgy, singing in a moderate voice. When the villagers heard the psalm-singing, the herald cried out and summoned everyone. Men and women gathered, walled up the doors, and from above, from the roof, they heaped up a great quantity of earth and poured it down on them.

They saw that the men were being choked and buried, yet were unwilling to do or say anything and only offered prayer to God. Then, at the suggestion of some others, they stopped their madness. They opened the doors, pulled them out of the earth, and ordered them to leave at once. But at that very moment tax collectors arrived and began forcing the villagers to pay their dues, binding some and maltreating others. That man of God remembered none of what had been done to him. He imitated the Master, who cared for those who nailed him to the cross, and begged the collectors to make their collection gently. When they demanded guarantors, he willingly accepted the obligation and promised to pay a hundred gold pieces in a few days.

Those who had done those terrible things were amazed at the man's kindness. They asked forgiveness for what they had dared to do and urged him to become their patron. The village had no owner; they themselves were both its farmers and its masters. So he went to the city, which was Emesa, found some acquaintances there, and borrowed the hundred gold pieces. Then he returned to the village and kept his promise on the appointed day. When they saw his zeal, they pressed their request on him even more zealously. He promised to do it if they would undertake to build a church. They begged him to begin at once and led the blessed man around, showing him the most suitable places. One praised this site, another that. He chose the best one and laid the foundations, and in a short time he had put the roof on. When the building was finished, he urged them to accept a priest. They said they would choose no one else and begged to have him as their father and shepherd, so he received the grace of the priesthood. He spent three years with them and guided them well toward divine things. Then he arranged for one of his companions to be appointed in his place and went back to his monastic dwelling. So as not to make the story long by recounting all his deeds, I will say only that, having shone in these labours, he was given the see of Carrhae. This city was drunk with impiety and had given itself over to the Bacchic frenzy of demons. But it was thought worthy of his farming and received the fire of his teaching. It was freed from its former thorns, and now it waves with the crops of the Spirit and offers to God sheaves of ripe grain.

But the man of God did not carry out this divine farming without toil. He laboured countless labours and imitated the art of those entrusted with healing bodies. Some cases he soothed with encouragement, others he treated with harsher, astringent remedies, and sometimes he even cut and cauterized. In this way he brought about health.

The brilliance of his life also supported his teaching and his other forms of care. Enlightened by it, people obeyed what he said and gladly accepted what he did. For during the whole time of his episcopate he had no need of bread or of water. A bed was useless to him, and he had no need of fire. Every night he completed forty antiphonal hymns, with twice that number of prayers between them. For the rest of the night he sat on a chair, allowing his eyelids a little rest.

Moses the lawgiver said that man shall not live by bread alone, and the Master recalled this saying when he rejected the devil's challenge. But that it is possible to live without water we have been taught nowhere in divine Scripture. Even the great Elijah first met his need from the brook. Then, when he came to the widow of Zarephath, he ordered water to be brought to him first, and only after that did he ask for bread. Yet during the time of his episcopate this admirable man took no bread, no pulses, and no vegetables that had been cooked over a fire. Nor did he take water, which experts in such matters considered the first of the four elements because of how necessary it is. Instead he made lettuce, endive, celery and the like into both his food and his drink, and so made the arts of bakers and cooks superfluous. In the fruit season he met his need with fruit, and he ate these things only after the evening service. While he wasted his body with such labours, he lavished insatiable care on others. For visiting strangers a bed was always ready, and they were served fine, choice loaves, fragrant wine, fish, vegetables, and everything else that goes with these. At midday he sat with the diners himself, offering each a share of what was set out, handing everyone cups and urging them to drink. In this he imitated his namesake, the patriarch I mean, who waited on his guests but did not eat with them. He spent whole days hearing the lawsuits of people in dispute. Some he persuaded to be reconciled with one another. Those who would not be persuaded by gentle teaching he compelled to do what was just. No one who was in the wrong ever went away having defeated justice by his audacity. For he always added the weight of justice to the side of the injured party and so made him invincible and stronger than the one who wanted to do wrong. He was like an excellent physician who always checks the excess of the humours and restores balance among the elements of the body.

The emperor too longed to see him, for rumour has wings and readily reports everything, good and bad. He summoned him, embraced him when he came, and valued that rustic goat-hair cloak more highly than his own purple. The choir of empresses also clasped his hands and knees and made supplication to a man who could not even understand the Greek language. So worthy of reverence, from emperors and from all people, is philosophy, and its lovers and devotees win even greater glory when they die. This can be learned from many examples, not least from the story of this inspired man. When he died and the emperor learned of it, he wanted to lay him to rest in one of the holy shrines. But when he learned that it was right for the shepherd's body to be returned to his flocks, he led the funeral procession himself. The choir of empresses followed, along with all the officials and their subjects, soldiers and private citizens alike. The city of Antiochus received him with the same zeal, and so did the cities after it, until he reached that great river. On the bank of the Euphrates citizens and strangers ran together, and all the country people and neighbours hurried to enjoy his blessing. Many rod-bearers walked beside the bier. By threatening to strike them, they scared off those who were trying to strip the body of its clothing and wanted to take rags from it. One could hear some singing psalms and others lamenting. One woman, wailing, called him her patron, another her provider, another her shepherd and teacher. One man, weeping, called him father, another helper and protector. With such praises and laments they committed that holy and sacred body to the tomb. As for me, I marvelled that when he changed his station he did not change his way of life. He did not choose an easy regime in the episcopate but increased his ascetic labours. So I have included him in this history of the monks and have not separated him from the company he loved, since I long for the blessing that comes from him.

To the saints already described I shall add the great Eusebius, who died not long ago. He lived a great many years, endured toil equal to the length of his life, gathered virtue equal to his toil, and carried away from it a reward many times greater. For the President of the Games outdoes the contests in the generosity of his rewards. At first this man entrusted his care to others and let himself be led wherever they led him, for they too were godly men, both athletes and trainers in virtue. After spending some time with them, and acquiring the science of the philosophic life well and thoroughly, he embraced the solitary life. He took possession of a ridge of a mountain, above which lies a very large village called Asikha. He used only a low wall, without even joining the stones with mud, and spent the rest of his life enduring hardship in the open air, covered with a garment of skins and living on chickpeas and beans soaked in water. Sometimes he also took a few dried figs, trying in this way to prop up the weakness of his body. Even when he had reached a great old age, so that he had lost most of his teeth, he changed neither his food nor his dwelling. Frozen in winter and scorched in summer, he bore steadfastly the opposite extremes of the weather, his face shrivelled and wrinkled and every limb of his body dried up like salted fish. He so wasted his body with his many labours that his belt would not even stay on his waist but slipped downward, for there was nothing to stop it: his buttocks and hips had been consumed, and gave the belt an easy passage downward. So he sewed the belt to his tunic, and by this device kept it in place. Conversation with the crowds wore him out completely, for since he was continually contemplating divine things in his mind, he did not wish to draw his thoughts away from them. Yet even though his love was so ardent, he allowed a few of his acquaintances to unseal his door and come inside; and after giving them teaching from the divine oracles, he would tell them as they left to put the mud back on the door.
Later, judging it better to avoid even meeting with these few, he walled up the entrance completely, fitting a very large stone into that doorway.
Through an opening he spoke with a few of his familiar friends, but without being seen, for that was how it had been contrived; and through it he also received that meagre food of his.

Then, having given up conversation with everyone, he granted me alone the privilege of that sweet voice, so dear to God; and when I wanted to leave, he would keep me for a very long time, talking about heavenly things. But when many people came to him asking for the gift of his blessing, he was greatly vexed by the commotion; and without taking his old age into account or reckoning with the weakness that afflicted him, he climbed over his wall, which was not easy to scale even for men in the prime of their strength. He went to the nearby community of ascetics, and there, using once again a small enclosure by the corner of the wall, he continued his contest with his usual labours. The man who presided over that flock, a man full of every virtue, told me that he passed the seven weeks of the holy fast on fifteen dried figs. He fought this contest when he had lived more than ninety years and was worn down by an indescribable weakness; but his zeal was stronger than his weakness, and his longing for God made everything seem easy and light. Drenched in such sweat as this, he too reached the finishing post of the race, beholding the President of the Games and longing for the crowns. And I ask to obtain that intercession which I enjoyed while he was still alive.
For I believe that he lives, and has a purer freedom of speech before God.

I would think I was wronging virtue if I did not make known the life of the admirable Salamanes to those who need it, but allowed it to be buried in oblivion; so I shall give a summary account of it. There is a village on the western side of the river Euphrates, lying on the very bank, called Kapersana. This man came from there. Embracing the life of stillness, he found a small cell in the village on the opposite bank and shut himself in, leaving neither door nor window. Once a year he would dig through at ground level and receive his food for the whole year, never speaking to anyone. In this way he lived not a short time but a very long one indeed. The bishop of the city to which the village belonged, learning of the man's virtue, came wishing to confer on him the gift of the priesthood. He broke through part of the cell, went in, laid his hand on him and completed the prayer; he said a great deal to him and told him of the grace that had come upon him. But hearing not a word in reply, he went away, ordering the opening to be built up again. Another time, the people of the village he had come from crossed the river at night, broke into his dwelling, took him—he neither resisting nor giving any orders—and carried him bodily to their own village; and building a similar cell by dawn, they shut him in at once. He kept his stillness just as before, saying nothing to anyone. A few days later the people of the village opposite came by night, broke into the dwelling and took him back to themselves, while he neither objected nor insisted on staying, nor again went off eagerly. So completely had he made himself dead to this life, and he truly uttered that saying of the apostle: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Such was this man too. These things are enough to show the whole purpose of his life. And now that I have reaped the blessing from this account, I shall pass on to the story of the others.

There is a village in our region called Omeros. Near it the inspired Maris built a tiny dwelling and lived shut up in it for thirty-seven years. It took in a great deal of damp from the adjoining mountain, and trickles of water would well up in it. How much harm comes to the body from such conditions both townspeople and country folk know; even rustics are well aware of the ailments that arise from them. Yet not even this persuaded that holy head to change his cell; he persevered until he had finished his race. His earlier life too he had passed in the labours of virtue, and so he kept his purity of both body and soul.

He himself told me this plainly, informing me that his body had remained undefiled, just as it was when it came forth from his mother's womb. And this although he had taken part in many festivals of the martyrs when he was young, and had charmed the congregations with the beauty of his voice; for he spent a very long time as a singer of psalms, and was also radiant with bodily beauty. Yet neither the beauty of his body, nor the brilliance of his voice, nor mixing with the crowds, spoiled the beauty of his soul. Living like those who are enclosed, he took care of his own soul, and he increased his virtue through the labours of his enclosure. I often enjoyed his company, for he would tell me to unseal the door; and when I came in he would embrace me and speak at length about the philosophic life.

He too shone with simplicity, and utterly loathed devious characters; and he loved poverty more than the greatest wealth. At ninety years of age he wore clothes made of goat's hair, and a little bread and salt met his need for food. Having long desired to see the spiritual and mystical sacrifice offered, he asked that the offering of the divine gift be made there. I gladly agreed, and had the sacred vessels brought—for the place was not far away—and using the hands of the deacons as an altar, I offered the mystical, divine and saving sacrifice.
He was filled with every spiritual delight; he thought he was seeing heaven itself, and said he had never enjoyed such gladness.

Since he loved me so very warmly, I thought I would be doing him wrong if I did not praise him after his death too; and that I would be doing others wrong if I did not [?] this excellent [?]. Having entreated to obtain help from him, [?]

Since we have recounted the contests of the athletes of virtue already mentioned, describing in summary their labours in training, their sweat in the contests, and their most brilliant and illustrious victories, come, let us also write the way of life of those who are still alive, who are contending magnificently and striving to surpass their predecessors by their sweat, and let us leave to those who come after a profitable memorial. For just as the way of life of the saints who were distinguished long ago brought the greatest benefit to those who came later, so the accounts of these men will become models for those after us. I shall begin with the great James, for he is first among the others both in time and in toil, and those who emulate him perform wonderful and extraordinary deeds. It has somehow come about that this name stands first both among the departed and among those still living. For when I recounted the way of life of those others too, I began with that divine James who scattered that Persian army by prayer: when the city walls had fallen, he did not allow the city to be taken, and forced the enemy to flee by sending gnats and mosquitoes to make war on them. So let the man who shares his honour and his character head the company of contestants still living—not because he shares his name, but because he emulated his virtue and himself became a model of the philosophic life for others. For he was a companion of the celebrated Maron and shared in his divine teaching, and by his greater labours he has outshone his teacher.

The other man had a precinct of the ancient error as his enclosure, and he put up a tent of hair skins and used it to escape the onslaught of rain and snow. But James said goodbye to all of these, to tent, hut and enclosure alike. He has the sky for his roof, and he takes every hostile assault the weather brings. Now he is drenched by torrential rain, now frozen by frost and snow; at other times he is scorched and burned by the sun's rays. He endures it all, as though he were struggling in someone else's body, and he strives to conquer the nature of the body by his zeal. Though he is clothed in this mortal body that can suffer, he lives as though in one beyond suffering. He practises the bodiless life in the body, and cries out with the inspired Paul: "Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God for the destruction of strongholds. We destroy arguments and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ." He trained for these superhuman contests with lesser labours. First he shut himself up in a small cell, freed himself from the noise outside, and fastened his mind on the remembrance of God. In this way he practised perfect virtue.

When he had trained himself excellently and made his soul accustomed to good labours, he ventured on greater contests. He took possession of this mountain, which lies thirty stades from our town, and made it famous and venerable, though it had long been obscure and completely barren. Now it is believed to have received so great a blessing that its soil is being used up, as people who come from every direction carry it off for their benefit. Living there, he is watched by all who come. As I said, he has no cave, no tent, no hut, no wall, no fence around him. He is seen praying and resting, standing and sitting, in health and when gripped by some illness, so that he always struggles in front of spectators and must hold off the needs of nature. For even other people, brought up with little freedom, find it hard to [?] when strangers are present, still less one who has trained in the highest philosophy.

I say this not because I learned it from someone else but because I saw it myself. Fourteen years ago a severe illness fell on him and affected him as one would expect of a man with a mortal nature. It was the height of summer, and the sun's rays blazed more fiercely, for the winds had dropped and the air was still. His illness was a flood of bile running downward, gnawing at his bowels, pressing on them and forcing its way out. It was then that I saw the man's great endurance. Crowds from a great many villages had gathered to carry off his victorious body, and he sat there, assailed from two sides. Nature compelled him to go and relieve himself, while shame before the crowd standing there forced him to stay in place. Knowing this, I urged those who had come to go away, often pleading and often threatening. In the end I even bound them with the sanctions of the priesthood, and late in the evening, with great difficulty, I sent them away.
But even when they had left, the godly man did not give in to nature. He went on enduring until deep night fell and forced everyone to go home.

I came back to him the next day. When I saw that the heat had grown fiercer, and that the fever upon him was being fed and increased by the fire from outside, I pretended to have a headache and said that I could not bear the force of the sun. I begged him to let me rig up a little shade beside him. When he gave permission, we stuck three reeds in the ground, laid two goat-hair cloaks over them, and so contrived a shade. He told me to go inside, but I said, "It would be shameful, father, for me, young and healthy as I am, to enjoy this comfort while you, gripped by a raging fever and in need of such relief, sit outside under the full force of the sun. So if you want me to enjoy the shade, share this little tent with me. I want to stay with you, but the sun prevents me." When he heard this he gave way, choosing to look after me. Once we were sharing the shade, I started on another tack and said I needed to lie down, because my hip could not bear sitting without pain. Again he urged me to lie down, but I answered that I could not bear to recline while I saw him sitting. "So if you want me to enjoy this rest as well, father," I said, "let us lie down together, for then I will not be ashamed of lying down alone." By such arguments I outwitted his endurance and brought him the relief of lying down. And as he lay stretched on the ground, I talked pleasantly to him to turn his mind to more cheerful things.

I put my hand inside his garment to rub his back gently, and then I saw the heavy load of iron that bound both his waist and his neck. Other chains ran from the ring around his neck, two in front and two behind, crossing down to the lower ring and forming the shape of the letter X, and so they joined the two rings to each other front and back. His arms, too, had similar fetters inside, around the elbows. When I saw this load, weighing many talents, I begged him to help his suffering body, which could not bear both the burdens he had chosen and the sickness he had not. "For now, father," I said, "the fever is doing the work of the iron. When it abates, we will put the load of iron back on your body." He gave way on this too, charmed by many such persuasions. That time, after being ill a few days, he easily recovered.
Some time later, however, he fell into a more serious illness.

Many people gathered from many places to carry off his body. When the people of the town heard of it, they all came running, soldiers and civilians alike, some taking up military gear and others using whatever weapons came to hand. They massed together and fought, shooting arrows, not to hit anyone, only to frighten them. In this way they drove off the people from the surrounding area. They laid the champion of the pentathlon on a bed, though he was completely unaware of what was happening; he did not even notice the country people pulling out his hair. Then they set off for the city, and when they reached the shrine of the prophets, they set the bed down in the monastery next to it. Someone came to Beroea, where I happened to be, to report what had happened and bring news of his death. So I set out at once, spent the whole night on the road, and after dawn I reached the godly man. He was not speaking and could not recognize any of those present. But when I spoke to him and told him that the great Acacius sent his greetings, he immediately opened his eyes, asked how I was, and wanted to know when I had come. When I had answered, he closed his eyes again. After three days he asked where he was. When he learned, he was greatly upset and asked to be carried back to the mountain at once.

Wanting to serve him in every way, I immediately ordered the bed to be carried and taken to the place he longed for. It was then that I saw how free that venerable head was from vainglory. The next day I brought him some barley water, which I had cooled, for he would not touch anything hot, having entirely renounced the use of fire.

When he would not take it, I said, "Father, show some consideration for all of us, for we regard your health as the salvation of us all. You are set before us not only as a model to profit from, but you also help us by your prayers and win God's favour for us."
"And if the unfamiliar food troubles you, father," I said, "endure this too, for this also is a form of philosophy.

When you were well and wanted food, you conquered the desire by endurance. In the same way, now that you have no appetite at all, show endurance by taking it." As I said this, the man of God Polychronius was with me, and he joined in my argument. Though it was early morning, he offered to take food first himself, he who often nourished his body only once in seven days. Defeated by the argument, James swallowed one cup of the barley water with his eyes shut, as we usually do with bitter drinks. We also persuaded him to bathe his feet in water, since they had lost the ability to walk from weakness. I think it worthwhile to lay bare this philosophy of his as well. A bowl lay near him, and one of his attendants tried to cover it with a mat so that it would not be visible to those who came to him.

He said, "Why are you covering the bowl?" The attendant said, "So that it will not be lying there for those who come to see you." "Away with that, my son," he said. "Do not hide from men what is known to the God of all. I want to live for him alone, and I have no concern for human glory. What good would it be if these people credited me with greater asceticism, but God with less? It is not they who give the reward for our labours; it is God who supplies it." Who would not greatly admire both the words and the mind that produced them, a mind so far above human glory? I have learned of something similar that happened on another occasion.

It was evening, late evening, and time for his meal. He took the earthenware dish beside him and was eating soaked lentils, for this was his food. Someone came from the town who had been entrusted with collecting a military levy. James saw him from a distance but did not put the lentils down; he went on eating as usual. Supposing it to be an apparition of a demon, he pelted it with words and tried to drive it away as an enemy, and to show that he was not afraid, he kept putting lentils into his mouth meanwhile. The man under this barrage of abuse begged him, saying he was a human being, and that he had come at that hour because he was bound by an oath to leave the city before evening. James said, "Take heart and do not be afraid. Say a prayer and go. But first share my table and take part of my meal." And as he said this, he filled his right hand and gave him some of the lentils. In this way he drove the passion of vainglory from his mind along with the others. As for his endurance, it is superfluous even to speak of it, since sight bears witness. Often, when snow fell for three days and as many nights, he was so buried as he lay face down beseeching God that not even a scrap of the rags he wore could be seen. Often the neighbours use shovels and mattocks to scrape away the snow around him, and so pull him out and raise him as he lies there.
From these labours he has reaped the gifts of divine grace, which all who wish may share.

Through his blessing many fevers have been quenched and are still being quenched, many agues have abated and gone away completely, and many demons have been forced to flee. Water blessed by his right hand becomes a medicine that wards off evil. Who does not know of the dead child raised to life through his prayer? The child's parents live in the suburbs of the city. They had become the parents of many children, but had sent them all to the grave before their time. So when this last child was born, the father ran to the man of God and begged that the child might be granted a long life, promising to dedicate him to God if he lived. The child lived for four years and then came to the end of his life. The father was away, but he arrived suddenly and saw the child already being carried out for burial. He snatched him from the bier and said, "I must fulfil my promise and give him to the man of God, even dead." He took him away, as he had said, and laid him before those holy feet, telling him what he had also told his family. The godly man laid the child before him, bent his knees, and lay face down, entreating the Lord of life and death. Late in the evening the child cried out and called his father. Then that inspired man, perceiving that the Lord had accepted his supplication and granted life, rose up. He worshipped the one who does the will of those who fear him and hears their prayer, finished his supplication, and gave the child back to his father. I saw this child myself, heard the father tell of the miracle, and have passed on this apostolic story to many, knowing that it will bring great benefit to those who hear it.
I too have often enjoyed his help. I will mention one or two instances, since I think it very ungrateful to pass over in silence and not make known the kinds of kindness I have received.

The loathsome Marcion sowed many thorns of impiety in the territory of the city of Cyrrhus. In trying to pull them up by the roots I left no stone unturned, as the saying goes, and used every means I could.

But those who benefited from my care, to use the words of the prophet, "slandered me instead of loving me, and repaid me evil for good and hatred for my love." They resorted to sorcery and magic tricks, and with evil demons as their helpers they tried to wage war on me unseen.

One night an accursed demon came, shouting in the Syriac language: "Why, So-and-so, are you making war on Marcion? Why ever have you taken up this fight against him? What harm has he ever done you? End the war, stop this hostility, or you will learn by experience how good it is to keep quiet. You can be sure that I would have struck you down long ago if I had not seen the choir of martyrs with James guarding you." I heard this, and said to one of my companions who was sleeping nearby, "Do you hear what is being said, So-and-so?" He said, "I heard it all. I wanted to get up and look out to find out who was speaking, but I kept quiet for your sake, thinking you were asleep." So we both got up and looked out, but we neither saw anyone moving nor heard anyone speaking. The others who lived with us had also heard those words. Then I understood that by the choir of martyrs he meant the little flask of oil of the martyrs, which held a blessing collected from many martyrs and hung beside my bed; and under my head lay the old cloak of the great James, which had become stronger for me than any wall of adamant. On another occasion, when I was about to approach the largest of their villages and then many obstacles kept arising to prevent my setting out, I sent to my Isaiah, begging to receive divine aid. He replied, "Take heart, for all those obstacles have been dissolved like cobwebs. God showed me this during the night, not by sketching it in a dream but by showing it to me while I was awake. When I had begun the psalmody," he said, "I saw, in the region where those villages lie, a fiery serpent crawling from west to east and moving through the middle of the air. After I had finished three prayers, I saw it again, bent round into a circle, with its tail joined to its head. When I had completed eight more prayers, I saw it cut in two and dissolve into smoke." That is what he foresaw, and we saw the outcome agree with the prediction.

At dawn, led by the serpent who is the author of evil, those who were then of Marcion's faction, but have since joined the apostolic phalanx, came rushing at us from the west, brandishing naked swords.

Around the third hour of the day they drew together and looked to their own defence, just as the serpent had covered its head with its tail. At the eighth hour they scattered and gave us room to enter the village. And immediately we found a serpent made of bronze, which they worshipped.

For they were eager to honour the accursed serpent, which had openly made war on the Creator and Maker of all things, as being his enemy. But since my account has turned to the telling of divine revelations, let me relate what I heard from that truthful tongue.

He did not tell me this out of vanity, for that godly soul was far removed from this passion too. Some need compelled him to say what he would rather have kept hidden. I had been begging him to entreat the God of all to make my field clean of tares and to free it entirely from the seeds of heresy, because the error of the loathsome Marcion, which had held sway there for a very long time, grieved me deeply. When I pressed him, he said: "You need neither me nor any other ambassador to him. You have the great John, the voice of the Word, the forerunner of the Master, who is always offering this supplication on your behalf." I said that I trusted in John's prayers and in those of the other holy apostles and prophets, whose relics had recently been brought to us. He answered, "Take heart, for you have John the Baptist." But even then I could not keep quiet. I pressed him all the more with questions, eager to learn why he had mentioned John rather than the others. He said, "I wanted to embrace his beloved relics." I told him, "I will not bring them unless you promise to tell me what you have seen." He promised. The next day I brought what he longed for, and after ordering everyone to withdraw, he told the story to me alone. "When you received these guardians of the city on their arrival from Phoenicia and Palestine with the dancing of David," he said, "a thought came to me: were these truly the relics of the great John, and not of another martyr with the same name? A day later I rose at night to sing the hymns, and I saw someone dressed in white, who said, 'Brother James, tell me, why did you not come out to meet us when we arrived?' I asked who they might be, and he answered, 'We are the ones who came from Phoenicia and Palestine the day before. Everyone received us eagerly, the shepherd and the people, the townsfolk and the country folk, but you alone did not share in the honor.'" He was hinting at the doubt that had arisen. James said that he answered: "Even when you and all the others are absent, I worship God." "Again the next day, at the same hour," he went on, "the same figure appeared and said, 'Look, brother James, at the one standing over there, whose garment is like snow in color and before whom lies a furnace of fire.' I turned my eyes that way and supposed it was John the Baptist, since he wore that robe and stretched out his hand as if baptizing. Then the figure said, 'It is the one you supposed.'" On another occasion James told me: "When you went at night to the first village to discipline its people as rebels, you urged me to offer God a more earnest prayer, and I stayed awake entreating the Master. Then I heard a voice say: 'Fear nothing, James. The great John the Baptist is entreating the God of all through the whole night. There would have been much bloodshed if the devil's audacity had not been quenched by his intercession.'" After telling me this, he asked me to keep it to myself and to share it with no one else. But for the sake of the good it could do, I have not only passed the story on to many people but am also committing it to writing. He said that he had also seen the patriarch Joseph, with grey hair and beard, giving off in his old age the radiance of youthful beauty. Though Joseph stood at the height of virtue, he called himself the last of the saints. "When I called him the first of those who share the tomb with him," James says, "he called himself the last." He also told me about the many kinds of attacks the wicked demons had made on him. "As soon as I began this way of life," he said, "someone appeared to me naked, in the form of an Ethiopian, with fire shooting from his eyes. At the sight I was filled with fear and turned to prayer, and I could not bring myself to take food, because he appeared at mealtime. Seven, eight, ten days went by and I still went without food. At last I despised the wicked assault, sat down, and took my food. He could not bear this boldness of mine and threatened to beat me with a rod. But I said to him, 'If the Master of all has permitted you, strike, and I will gladly receive the blow as if he himself were striking me. But if you have not been permitted, you will not strike me, though you rage ten thousand times.' When he heard this, he ran off for the moment, but he went on raging in secret. Twice a week water was brought up to me from below. He would meet the man carrying it, take on my appearance, take the water, tell the man to go away, and pour it out. He did this not just twice but three times, and so he brought the torment of thirst upon me. In great distress I asked the man who usually brought it: 'Why have you brought no water in fifteen days?' He said he had brought it three or four times and that I had received it. 'And where,' I said, 'did I receive it from you as you carried it?' When he pointed out the place, I said, 'Even if you see me coming there ten thousand times, do not hand over the jar until you reach this spot.' Having foiled this plot too, he tried yet another. He shouted at night: 'I will fill you with such a stench and bring such disgrace on you that no human being will come from anywhere to see you.' I answered: 'I will be grateful to you. Without meaning to, you will do a kindness to your enemy, for you will let me delight all the more in remembering God. With more leisure to enjoy, I will make the contemplation of the divine beauty my constant occupation.' A few days later, at midday, while I was performing the usual service, I saw two women coming down from the mountain.

"I was annoyed at this unusual sight and was about to throw stones at them when I remembered that fiend's threat and took this to be the disgrace he had meant. So I called out first that even if they sat on my shoulders, I would not throw stones or chase them away but would use prayer alone. As I said this, they vanished, and the apparition ended with my words." Then he went on: "One night I was praying when there came the rattle of a carriage, the shout of a driver, and the neighing of horses. The strangeness of it alarmed me.

"I reflected that no governor was visiting the city at that time, that the road was not fit for carriages, and that the hour was not suitable for them. While I was thinking this over, I heard the noise of an approaching crowd. Some attendants with rods were going ahead, shouting and whistling, driving most people out of the way and clearing a path for the one in charge. When it seemed to have come very close, I said: 'Who are you? Where do you come from? What do you want, that you have come at this hour? How long will you play your games, you wretch, and despise the patience of God?' I said this facing east and offering my supplication to God. He pushed me but could not knock me down, for divine grace held firm, and at once everything vanished." He also told me about the time of those accursed brigands who set out from Isauria and burned and plundered most of the East. He was very much afraid then. It was not slaughter that he feared, for he was not so attached to his body. He feared being enslaved and taken captive, and having to look on impiety and lawlessness. The devil perceived this fear, since he had often heard James admit it to his acquaintances, and at night he imitated the wailing of women. "I thought I heard that the enemy had come and were setting fire to the villages," James said. "At once I parted the hair on my head in two and brought the locks on the right and on the left over my shoulders onto my chest. I made my neck ready for the stroke of the sword, so that a quick blow would spare me that dreadful sight.

"So I spent that whole night, expecting their attack the entire time. When day came and some people arrived, I asked what they had heard about the Isaurians. They said they had learned nothing of them in recent days. And so," he says, "I recognized that this apparition too came from the devil.

"Another time," he said, "he took the form of a vigorous youth, radiant with beauty and adorned with golden hair, and came up to me smiling and playful. Armed with anger, I drove him off with abuse. But he stayed, gazing at me like a courtesan, his smile and his voice brimming with allure. My anger grew sharper, and I said, 'How are you able to roam the whole world and lay such snares for everyone?' He said that he was not alone. A multitude of demons was scattered over the whole world, he said, playing such games and at the same time in deadly earnest.

"For by what looks like play they are striving to destroy the whole race of men. 'But you, be gone,' I said, 'at the command of Christ, who sent the whole legion through the swine into the deep.'" The demon heard and fled at the same moment. He could not bear the power of the Master's name, nor could he look upon the splendor of the servant's philosophy. I know many more stories besides these, but I do not wish to write them down, for fear that their sheer number might give the weaker a pretext for unbelief. To those who see the godly man, nothing of this kind seems incredible when they hear it, since the virtue they see confirms what is said.
