But this written account will also pass to those who come later, and for most people the ears are less trusting than the eyes. So I will measure my narrative to the weakness of my hearers. Others have built a very large shrine for him in the neighboring village, not many stades away, and I too prepared a tomb for him in the shrine of the triumphant apostles. When the godly man learned of this, he often and earnestly begged me to commit his body for burial on that mountain. I told him many times that it is not fitting for one who has disregarded the present life to make provision for burial. But when I saw that this was what he truly wanted, I gave my consent and agreed, and I had the coffin cut and carried up. When I saw the stone being damaged by the frost, I allowed a small building to be put up over the coffin. At his direction we finished the building and put on the roof. Then he said: "I will not allow this to be called the tomb of James. I want it to become a shrine of the triumphant martyrs, and I want to lie in another tomb like a resident alien, granted the privilege of dwelling beside them." He did not merely say this; he did it. He gathered many prophets, many apostles, and as many martyrs as he could from every quarter and laid them in a single coffin. He wanted to dwell among the people of the saints, and he longed to rise with them and be found worthy of the vision of God. This is enough to prove how modest his mind is. Though he had amassed such wealth, he lived as if in utter poverty and wished only to dwell as a neighbor among the company of the rich.

What toils this man I so revere has endured, how great his contests have been, how much grace he has enjoyed from God, how many victories he has won, and what crowns adorn him: what I have said is enough to show this.

But some accuse him of a difficult temper and take offense at his love of solitude and quiet. I will say a few words about this and then bring my narrative to an end. As I said, he lies open to everyone's view. He is not fenced in by a wall, nor sheltered by any hut or tent.

No enclosure holds anyone back, so everyone who comes wants to talk with him the moment he arrives. Other lovers of this philosophy have walls and doors and enjoy quiet. The one shut inside opens when he wishes and puts visitors off as long as he likes, and he fills himself with divine contemplation as much as he desires. Here there is none of this. That is why he is especially annoyed with those who disturb him at the time of prayer. If they leave at once when he tells them to, he goes back to his prayer. But if they persist in troubling him and he cannot persuade them after asking once and twice, then he grows annoyed, rebukes them, and sends them away. I have spoken with him about this. I told him that some people were upset at being driven away without receiving a blessing. I said it would be fitting for those who come for this purpose, after a journey of many days, not to go home aggrieved but full of joy, regaling those who did not know of it with stories of his philosophy. He answered: "I have taken to this mountain not for anyone else's sake but for my own. I am covered with a great many wounds of sin and need much treatment. That is why I beseech our Master to hold out to me the remedies against wickedness.

"How then could it be anything but absurd, and utterly senseless, to break off the thread of my supplication and hold a conversation with men in the middle of it? Suppose I were the servant of a man of my own kind. If, at the time of serving my master, I failed to bring food or drink at the proper moment and chatted with one of my fellow servants instead, how many blows would I not justly receive? Or suppose I went before a magistrate to tell him of the injustice I was suffering from someone, and broke off my speech in the middle to say other things to some of the bystanders. Don't you think the judge would be annoyed, deny me his help, add a flogging besides, and drive me from the bar of the court? A servant behaves fittingly toward his master, and a petitioner toward a judge. How then could it be right for me, when I approach God, the eternal Master, the most just Judge and the King of all, not even to approach him as they do, but to turn to my fellow servants in the middle of my prayer and hold a long conversation?" This is what I heard, and I passed it on to those who had taken offense. To me he seems to have spoken well and rightly. For besides what he said, it is the mark of lovers to disregard everything else and be wholly devoted to the one they love and cherish, dreaming of him by night and picturing him by day. That, it seems to me, is why he is annoyed: when he has entered the contemplation he longs for, he is prevented from taking his fill of the beloved beauty. I have written this down in the form of a narrative, taking great care to be brief, so as not to weary my readers with length.
If he lives on after this account, he will surely add countless other achievements to the earlier ones, and others will write of those too. For my own part, I long greatly to depart from here.

May the president of the games, who presides over the athletes of piety, grant him too an end worthy of his contests. May he make the rest of his race match what has gone before, so that he reaches the turning post victorious. And may he support our weakness through this man's prayers, so that we may be strengthened, may wrestle back from our many defeats, and may leave this life in victory.
There is a village in our region called Tillima. Long ago it received the seeds of Marcion's impiety, but now it enjoys the tillage of the gospel.

To the south of it there is a hill, neither very rugged nor very steep. On it the admirable Thalassius built a dwelling for the ascetic life. He was a man adorned with many good qualities, and in simplicity of character, gentleness and humility of mind he surpassed the people of his time.

I say this not on the strength of hearsay alone but from my own experience, for I knew the man and often enjoyed his sweet company. Limnaeus, who is now praised by everyone, joined his company. He came to that training ground when he was still quite young and was well schooled there in this highest philosophy. First of all, knowing how easily the tongue slips, he laid down a law for his own while he was still a boy that it should keep silent, and for a very long time he went on without speaking a word to anyone.

When he had received enough of the inspired old man's teaching and had made himself an impression of his virtue, he went to the great Maron, whom we have mentioned before. He came there at the same time as the inspired James.

After reaping much benefit there too, he set his heart on the life in the open air and took up his place on another summit, which overlooks a village called Targala. He has remained there to this day. He has no hut, no tent and no shelter, only a bare wall around him, built of stones not even joined with mud. It has a small door that is kept sealed with mud at all times. He never opens it when others come, and allows it to be opened only when I arrive. For this reason very many people gather from all around when they hear I am coming, eager to share my entry.
To those who visit him at other times he speaks through a small window and gives them his blessing, and through it he grants healing to very many.

By invoking the Saviour's name he stops diseases, drives out demons and imitates the wonder-working of the apostles. He makes healing well up not only for those who come to him; he has often applied it to his own body as well. Some time ago he was attacked by colic. The pain and agony it causes are known exactly to those who have suffered it, and are known also to those who have watched it. Sufferers roll about like madmen, twisting this way and that, stretching out their legs and drawing them in again. Sometimes they sit down, get up and walk about, trying to find some way to relief. For this reason they also haunt the baths and go into them often, finding a little comfort there.

But why should I go on at length, listing what everyone knows well? Wrestling with such an illness and struck by so many and such great pains, he did not have the help of medicine, would not put up with a bed, and accepted no comfort from drugs or food. Instead, sitting on a plank lying on the ground, he received his cure by prayer and the sign of the cross, and lulled his pains to sleep with the charm of the divine name. Another time, walking at night, he stepped on a sleeping viper. It seized his foot and sank its teeth in. He tried to defend his foot, bending down and putting his hand to it, but this only transferred the beast's mouth to his hand. Then he used his left hand to help the other, and drew the beast's fury upon that one too. When it had had its fill of rage—for it had bitten him more than ten times—it went away and returned to its own hole, while he was racked on every side by bitter pains. But even then he would not put up with the art of medicine; he applied to his wounds only the remedies of faith: the sign of the cross, prayer and calling on God. It was for this reason, I think, that the God of all allowed that beast to rage against his holy body: to display to everyone the endurance of that inspired soul in all its nakedness. We see this same dispensation of his in the case of the noble Job too. He allowed him to be swamped by many waves of every kind because he wished to show everyone the helmsman's skill. For how else would we have known either Job's courage or this man's endurance, if the adversary of godliness had not been given room to shoot all kinds of arrows at them? This is enough to show the man's endurance; let us demonstrate his love for others from another source. He gathered together many people who had lost their sight and been forced to beg, built dwellings for them on either side, to the east and to the west, and urged them to live in them and sing hymns to God, instructing those who came to him to supply them with the food they needed. He himself, shut in between them, stirred up both groups to sing, and one can hear them continually singing hymns to the Lord. Such was the love he went on showing to his fellow human beings. He and the great James have spent the same length of time in their contests in the open air: they have now completed their thirty-eighth year.
John too emulated this way of life, a man who shone, among his other qualities, with mildness and gentleness.
He took up his place on a rugged ridge, exposed to harsh winters and facing north, and has so far spent twenty-five years there, enduring the assaults of the weather from every side.

All the rest—so that I need not go through each item—his food, his clothing and his burdens of iron, are similar to those already described. He is so far above all human things that he takes no comfort from any of them. I will give a clear proof of this at once. One of the devout had planted an almond tree right beside his resting place. In time it grew into a tree and gave him shade and [?] his eyes, and so he ordered it to be cut down, so that he would not enjoy even a single comfort from it.

Moses too embraced this life, contending on a high peak that overlooks the village of Rhama; so did Antiochus, an old man, who built his enclosure in a very desolate place; and Antoninus, who in an aged body contends like the young. They have the same clothing, the same food, the same standing and prayer, the same labours all night and all day. Neither length of time nor old age nor natural weakness puts their endurance to the test; rather, they keep their love of toil in full bloom within them. And God, who presides over the contests of virtue, has very many other contestants in our parts, in mountains and plains, so many that it is not easy even to count them, let alone to write the life of each. So, having set out enough benefit from these for those who wish to profit, I shall turn to another kind of narrative, asking to share in their blessing.

Those who were thought worthy to see Zebinas still sing his praises to this day. They say that he reached a ripe old age and kept up the same labours until his very death, changing nothing of the practices of his youth, though oppressed by the heaviest old age. He surpassed, they said, everyone of his time in perseverance in prayer. He spent whole days and nights in it, and not only did he never grow weary of it, but his longing for it grew ever warmer.

Even when he spoke a few words with those who came to him, he would not bring his mind down from heaven; he would leave them at once and, as one who had not been separated even for a moment from the God of all, offer up his supplication again.

When old age no longer allowed him to bear continual standing without distress, he took a staff as a support for it, and leaning on it he sang hymns to the Lord and prayed. Adorned among his other good qualities with hospitality, he would invite many of those who came to him to stay for the evening. But they, dreading his all-night standing, would plead some business or other and slip away from the labours.

The great Maron himself admired him greatly. He urged all who visited him to hurry to the old man and reap his blessing, naming him father and teacher and calling him the model of every virtue. He even asked to share his tomb, but those who seized his holy body and carried it off to the place mentioned earlier did not allow it. The inspired Zebinas died first and received the customary rites in the village next to him—it is called Kitta—and they built a very large shrine over the tomb, for it pours out healing of every kind for those who approach with faith.
He now also has martyrs sharing his roof, who contended among the Persians and are honoured by us with annual festivals.

The great Polychronius enjoyed his teaching, and the most inspired James said that it was he who first gave him a hair shirt. I never saw Zebinas myself, for the end of his life came before my arrival, but in this excellent Polychronius I see the philosophy of the inspired Zebinas. Wax does not take the impression of a signet ring as faithfully as this man bears the features of that one. I know this clearly from comparing the stories told about the one with the things done by the other.

Like him, he is set ablaze with divine longing and is above all earthly things. Though bound to the body, he has a winged soul. He passes through the air and the heavens beyond, rises higher than the heavens, and continually beholds in his mind the vision of God.

He never allows his mind to be dragged down from there; even while talking with those who come to him, he roams in the realms above. I learned of his all-night vigils and standing in this way. Seeing him struggling with old age and illness at once and enjoying not a single attendant, I persuaded him after many entreaties to take two companions and enjoy the comfort they could give him. Since he asked for men shining with virtue, who were living apart by themselves in another monastery, I persuaded those admirable men to prefer serving a man of God to everything else. After spending a short time with him, they tried to run away, unable to bear the all-night standing.

When they begged the inspired man to measure his labour by the weakness of his body, he said to them, "Not only do I not force you to share my standing all the time, I urge you to lie down often." But they said, "How could we lie down, men who are healthy and in the middle of life, while one grown old in labours is standing and disregarding the weakness of his body?" That is how I learned of the night labours of that head I revere. In time these men gained such virtue that they took up the same philosophy as this great man. Moses—for that is the name he has kept to the present—gives him every service as to a father and master and takes the impression of the virtue that flashes out from that holy soul. Damian—that was the other's name—took up his place in a town not far away (its name is Niara), found a small hut beside the threshing floors, and lives there, following the same way of life, so that those who know both men well, when they see him, think they are seeing the soul of the great Polychronius in another body. There is the same simplicity, gentleness and humility, the same mildness of speech and sweetness of company, the same watchfulness of soul and contemplation of God, the same standing, labour, vigils and food, and the same poverty according to the divine law. Apart from a small basket holding soaked lentils, his dwelling contains nothing. Such was the benefit he gained from the company of the great Polychronius. But I shall leave the disciple and return to the teacher, for the stream has its water from the spring.

Having driven out ambition from his soul along with the other passions and trampled on the tyranny of vainglory, he has always been eager to hide his labours. He would not put up with wearing iron, fearing he might draw some harm from it if his soul caught the inflammation of conceit. Instead he had someone bring him a very heavy oak root, supposedly because he needed it for some other purpose, and he would put it on his shoulders at night and pray with it lying on him, and in the daytime too when he had leisure. When anyone came and knocked at the door, he would hide it somewhere. Someone who had seen it showed it to me, and wanting to know how heavy the burden was, I barely lifted it with both hands. When he saw me, he told me to put it down. I in turn begged to take it, so as to steal away the means of his labour. But when I saw him distressed, I gave way to his longing for victory. From these labours God-given grace blossoms in him, and many miracles are worked through his prayers.

For when that severe drought was wearing people down and driving them to supplication, a crowd of priests came to him. With them was a man from the territory of Antioch who had been appointed to shepherd many villages.

He begged the senior men present to persuade the holy man to lay his right hand on a small flask. They told him he would not allow it. Afterwards, when there was prayer and that inspired head was praying, the man stood behind him and held out the flask in both hands. It overflowed, so that two or three of those present stretched out their hands and received them filled with oil. Yet though he sends out the rays of divine grace, is laden with achievements of every kind and gathers the riches of philosophy day by day, he is so humble in mind that he embraces both feet of everyone who comes to him and touches his forehead to the ground, whether the visitor is a soldier, a craftsman or a farmer. I shall tell a story that can show both his simplicity and his humility.
A devout man who had been appointed governor of this province came to Cyrrhus and wished to enjoy with me the sight of these great athletes.
So we went round the others and came also to this man, whose virtue we are now describing.

When I told him that the man who had come with me was the governor, a guardian of justice and a lover of the godly, the inspired man at once stretched out both hands, took hold of both his feet and said, "I want to make a request of you." The governor was greatly embarrassed, begged him to get up and promised to do whatever he asked, for he supposed he was going to plead on behalf of one of his subjects. The inspired man said: "Well then, since you have promised and confirmed your promise with an oath, earnestly offer prayers to God for me." The governor, striking his forehead, begged him to release him from the oath, since he was not worthy to offer prayers to the Lord even for himself. What words could praise as he deserves one who, at such a height of philosophy, has such humility of mind? The diseases of every kind that have fallen on him have not put his love of labour to the test; besieged by various illnesses, he endures the same labours.

After using many arguments many times, we barely managed to build him this little house, contriving a little warmth for a body completely chilled. Many people often offered him gold while they were living and left it to him when they died, but he never accepted anything from anyone; he told them to be stewards of what they were offering. The great James sent him a blanket that someone had brought to James, but he sent this back too, seeing that it was too thick and well made. For he always used very poor and cheap clothes.
He considered poverty so much more desirable than any kingdom that he did not always have even the food he needed.
I know this because I often came, asked for a blessing, and found nothing but two dried figs.

This man's honeyed sweetness is longed for by those who see him and loved by those who hear of him. I know of no one, not even among the most fond of mockery, who has ever found fault with him. All sing his praises and speak well of him, and those who visit him do not want to leave.

To this company belongs also the admirable Asclepius, who lives ten stades away and has emulated the same way of life. He has the same food and clothing, the same humility of character, the same hospitality and love of the brethren, the same mildness and gentleness, the same converse with God and the most extreme poverty; and besides these, the same abundance of virtue, the same riches of philosophy, and everything else we have described in speaking of that holy head. They say that even when he was counted among the brethren living in the village, he embraced the ascetic and orderly life and drew no stain from mixing with the crowd.

Having excelled in both lives, the life in society and the life in the desert, he will rightly be deemed worthy of a double crown. Many others too have emulated his virtue, and not only our own city but also the neighbouring cities and villages are full of this kind of philosophy. One of them is the most inspired James, who is shut up in a small hut near a village called Nimouza. Though he is at the very end of his life—for he is more than ninety years old—he is shut in alone and gives his replies through a short tunnel dug in a spiral. He is not seen, he uses no fire, and he enjoys no lamplight. But twice he opened the door and bade me come in, honouring me in this way and showing the affection he has for me.

Those who are still living have no need of words from me, for they can, if they wish, become eyewitnesses of these men's philosophy. For those yet to come, who will not have the chance to see them, this is enough for their benefit, since it shows the character of these men's philosophy. So here I conclude my account of them too, and, asking for their blessing in return, I shall pass on to another narrative.

The famous Simeon, the great wonder of the world, is known to all the subjects of the Roman Empire. The Persians, the Medes and the Ethiopians have also come to know him, and his fame has even run as far as the nomadic Scythians, teaching them of his love of labour and his philosophy. Yet although I have, so to speak, all people as witnesses of his contests, which are beyond words, I fear that my account may seem to those yet to come a mere fable, wholly stripped of truth.

For what took place is beyond human nature. People like to measure what they are told by the standard of nature, and if something is said that lies beyond its limits, those uninitiated in divine things think the account false. But land and sea are full of the devout, who have been educated in divine things and taught the grace of the all-holy Spirit. They will not disbelieve what I am about to say; they will believe it entirely. So I will tell the story eagerly and with confidence. I shall begin from the point at which he was found worthy of the call from above.
There is a village lying on the border between our country and Cilicia; they call it Sisa.

Starting out from this village, he was first taught by his parents to tend sheep, so that in this respect too he might resemble those great men Jacob the patriarch, Joseph the chaste, Moses the lawgiver, David the king and prophet, Micah the prophet, and the inspired men like them. Once, when there had been a heavy snowfall and the sheep had been forced to stay inside, he took advantage of the respite and went with his parents to the holy church. I heard this from his own sacred tongue. He said that he heard the voice of the Gospel calling blessed those who weep and mourn, calling wretched those who laugh, and calling enviable those who possess a pure soul, along with everything else joined to these sayings. Then he asked one of those present what a person must do to obtain each of these. The man suggested to him the monastic life and pointed him to that highest philosophy.

So, having received the seeds of the divine word and hidden them well in the deep furrows of his soul, he said, he ran to the nearby shrine of the holy martyrs. There he pressed his knees and his forehead to the ground and begged the One who wills all people to be saved to guide him onto the perfect road of piety. After he had spent a long time in this way, a sweet sleep came upon him, and he saw a dream like this. "I seemed," he said, "to be digging foundations. Then I heard someone standing by say that I must dig the trench deeper still. So I added depth as he ordered and tried again to take a rest, but once more he told me to dig and not to stop the work. Three and four times he urged this on me, and at last he said the depth was sufficient, and told me to build from then on without toil, since the toil had ended and the building would go easily." Events bear witness to this prediction, for what has happened is beyond nature.

Rising from there, he went to the dwelling of some ascetics who lived nearby. After spending two years with them, he fell in love with a more perfect virtue and went to Teleda, the village we have mentioned before, near which those great and godly men Ammianus and Eusebius set up their ascetic wrestling-school. But the inspired Simeon did not go to that one; he went to another that had sprung from it. For Eusebonas and Abibion, after profiting fully from the teaching of the great Eusebius, built this school of philosophy. Of one mind and one way of life throughout their lives, showing as it were one soul in two bodies, they gained many who shared their love of that life. When they departed this life with glory, the admirable Heliodorus took over the leadership of the community. He lived sixty-five years, sixty-two of which he spent shut up inside; for after being brought up by his parents for three years, he entered this flock, and never saw anything of what goes on in the world. He used to say that he did not even know what pigs or roosters or other such creatures looked like. I too often enjoyed the sight of him, marveled at the simplicity of his ways, and greatly admired the purity of his soul. It was to him that this all-round champion of piety came, and he spent ten years in the contest. He had eighty fellow contestants, and he surpassed them all: while the others took food every two days, he remained without food the whole week. Those in charge were displeased and constantly resisted him, calling the practice a breach of discipline, but they could not persuade him by what they said, nor could they rein in his zeal.

I heard both from the man himself and from the present head of the same flock that once he took a rope made of palm fiber, which is very rough even to the touch of the hands, and girded his waist with it, not putting it on over his clothing but binding it right against his skin. He tied it so tight that the whole area it encircled became one ring of sores.

After he had continued in this way for more than ten days and the wound, growing worse, was letting fall drops of blood, someone saw it and asked him what was the cause of the blood. When he said that nothing was troubling him, his fellow contestant forced his hand in, discovered the cause, and reported it to the superior. At once, with rebukes and entreaties and denunciations of the cruelty of the thing, he barely managed to undo the binding. But even so he could not persuade him to apply any treatment to the wound. Seeing him doing other things of the same kind, they told him to leave that wrestling-school, so that he would not become a cause of harm to those of weaker bodily constitution who might try to imitate feats beyond their strength. So he went out, made his way to the more deserted parts of the mountain, found a dry cistern that was not very deep, let himself down into it, and offered hymns of praise to God.

After five days had passed, the leaders of that wrestling-school repented and sent out two men, instructing them to look for him and bring him back. These men went around the mountain and asked some people pasturing flocks there whether they had seen anyone of such a complexion and wearing such a habit. When the shepherds pointed out the cistern, they immediately called down many times; then they quickly fetched a rope and with great effort drew him up.

For the way up is not as easy as the way down. After spending a short time with them, he went to the village of Telanissus, which lies below the summit on which he now stands. There he found a small hut and spent three years shut up in it.
Always striving to increase his wealth of virtue, he desired to remain without food for forty days, like those men of God Moses and Elijah.

He persuaded the admirable Bassus, who at that time traveled around many villages as supervisor of the village priests, to leave nothing inside and to seal the door with mud. Bassus pointed out how hard the thing was and urged him not to think that a violent death was a virtue, since that is a crime, indeed the greatest and foremost. "Well then, Father," he said, "set aside ten loaves and a jar of water for me, and if I see that my body needs food, I will take some of them." It was done as he asked: the provisions were set aside, and the door received its mud.

At the end of the days that admirable man of God Bassus came, removed the mud, and went in through the door. He found the full number of loaves, and found the jar of water full as well, but Simeon himself lying stretched out without breath, able neither to speak nor to move.

So he asked for a sponge, moistened and rinsed his mouth with it, and gave him the symbols of the divine mysteries. Strengthened by these, Simeon raised himself up and took a little food, lettuce, chicory and the like, chewing it bit by bit and passing it down to his stomach. The great Bassus, filled with admiration, returned to his own flock and told of this great wonder. For he had more than two hundred disciples, and he permitted them neither to own a beast of burden nor a mill, nor to accept gold when it was offered, nor for anyone to go outside the gate, either to buy something necessary or to see an acquaintance; they were to live inside and receive the food sent by divine grace. His disciples keep this rule to this very day, and though they have grown more numerous, they have not transgressed the commandments given them. But I shall pass on to the great Simeon.

From that time to this day (and twenty-eight years have passed) he has remained without food for the forty days. Time and practice have taken away most of the hardship. At first he used to stand during the early days and sing hymns to God; then, when his body, through lack of food, no longer had the strength to stand, he would sit and perform the divine office; and in the last days he would even lie down. For as his strength was gradually used up and extinguished, he was forced to lie there half dead.
But once he took his stand on the pillar, he would not bear to come down, and he devised another way of standing.

He fastened a beam to the pillar and bound himself to the beam with ropes, and in this way spent the forty days. After that, enjoying a greater measure of grace from above, he no longer needed even this support, but stands for the forty days, taking no food, strengthened by his zeal and by divine grace.

So, as I said, after spending three years in that hut, he went to this famous summit. He had a stone enclosure built around it, and had a chain made of iron twenty cubits long. One end of it he fixed to a huge rock, and the other he fastened to his right foot, so that even if he wished he could not go beyond those bounds. He lived inside, constantly picturing heaven and straining to contemplate what lies above the heavens; for the iron fetter did not hinder the flight of his mind.

But the admirable Meletius, who at that time had been appointed to oversee the territory of the city of Antioch, a man shining with wisdom and understanding and adorned with keen intelligence, told him the iron was superfluous, since the will was enough to place rational bonds on the body. He yielded and accepted the advice obediently, and ordering a smith to be called, told him to remove the fetter. Now a piece of leather had been fitted around his leg so that his body would not be injured by the iron, and since this too had to be torn off (for it had been sewn on), they said they saw more than twenty huge bugs nesting in it; and the admirable Meletius said he had seen this himself. I have recorded it to show from this too the man's great endurance. Though he could easily have squeezed the leather with his hand and killed them all, he patiently endured their painful bites, welcoming in small things training for greater contests.

As his fame spread everywhere, everyone came running, not only those living nearby but also those who were many days' journey away. Some brought those whose bodies were paralyzed; others asked health for the sick; others begged to become fathers, and implored to receive through him what they had not received from nature. Receiving it and obtaining their requests, they went home rejoicing, and by proclaiming the benefits they had received, they sent out many times their number to ask for the same. So, with everyone arriving from every side and every road like a river, one can see a sea of people gathered in that place, receiving rivers from every direction. For it is not only the inhabitants of our part of the world who stream there, but also Ishmaelites, Persians, the Armenians subject to them, Iberians, Himyarites, and peoples farther inland than these. Many also came who live at the far ends of the West: Spaniards, Britons, and the Gauls who live between them. As for Italy, it is superfluous even to speak of it. They say the man became so celebrated in great Rome that at the entrances of all the workshops people set up small images of him, providing for themselves some protection and safety by this means.

Since those who came were beyond counting, and all of them tried to touch him and to reap some blessing from those garments of skin, he first thought the excess of honor out of place, and then found the troublesomeness of the thing hard to bear; so he devised standing on the pillar.

First he had a pillar cut six cubits high, then twelve, after that twenty-two, and now thirty-six; for he longs to fly up to heaven and to be released from this earthly sojourn. I for my part believe that this standing did not come about without divine providence. For this reason I urge those who like to find fault to curb their tongues and not let them run on at random, but to consider how often the Master has contrived such things for the benefit of the more careless. For he commanded Isaiah to walk naked and barefoot; Jeremiah to put a loincloth around his waist and in that way deliver his prophecy to the disobedient, and at another time, later, to put wooden and then iron collars around his neck; Hosea to take a prostitute as wife, and again to love a wicked woman and an adulteress; Ezekiel to lie on his right side for forty days and on his left for a hundred and fifty, and again to dig through a wall and go out as a fugitive, depicting captivity in his own person, and at another time to sharpen a sword to a keen edge, shave his head with it, divide the hair into four parts, and assign some to this and some to that—not to list everything.

The Ruler of all ordered each of these things to be done, gathering by the strangeness of the spectacle those who would not be persuaded by words or bear to listen to prophecy, and preparing them to hear the oracles. For who would not have been astonished to see a man of God walking naked? Who would not have longed to learn the reason for what was happening? Who would not have asked, "Why on earth does the prophet put up with living with a prostitute?" Just as the God of all ordered each of those things to be done, providing for the benefit of those who live in ease, so too he has brought about this new and strange spectacle, drawing everyone by its novelty to come and look, and making the exhortation offered to those who come persuasive. For the novelty of the spectacle becomes a trustworthy pledge of the teaching, and the one who comes to look goes home instructed in divine things. And just as those whose lot is to reign over men change the images on their coins from time to time, stamping them now with likenesses of lions, now of stars and angels, at other times trying by an unusual design to make the gold more valuable, so the King of all, setting these new and varied ways of life on piety like so many designs, moves to praise the tongues not only of the nurslings of the faith but also of those sick with unbelief.

That this is so, it is not words that bear witness but the loud voice of the facts. For the standing on the pillar has enlightened the Ishmaelites, many tens of thousands of whom were enslaved to the darkness of impiety. Like a lamp set on a lampstand, this most brilliant light has sent out its rays everywhere like the sun. One can see, as I said, Iberians, Armenians and Persians arriving and receiving divine baptism. The Ishmaelites come in bands, two hundred at a time, or three hundred, and sometimes even a thousand. With loud cries they renounce their ancestral delusion, smashing before that great luminary the idols they used to worship, and renouncing the orgies of Aphrodite (for they had accepted the worship of this demon from of old); then they partake of the divine mysteries, receiving laws from that sacred tongue, bidding farewell to their ancestral customs, and renouncing the eating of wild asses and camels. I was an eyewitness of these things myself, and I heard them renouncing their ancestral impiety and assenting to the teaching of the Gospel. Once I even faced very great danger.

For he told them to come up and receive the priestly blessing from me, saying that they would gain the greatest profit from it. But they rushed at me in rather barbarous fashion: some pulled me from the front, some from behind, others from the sides, while those farther back climbed over the others and stretched out their hands, some tugging at my beard, others grabbing at my clothes. I would have been suffocated by their over-ardent approach if he had not shouted and scattered them all.
Such is the benefit that has poured forth from the pillar mocked by the scoffers, and such is the ray of the knowledge of God that it has sent down into the minds of the barbarians.

I know of another such incident among these people. One tribe was begging the man of God to send a prayer and blessing to their chieftain, but another tribe that was present objected, saying the blessing ought not to be sent to him but to their own leader, since the one was utterly unjust and the other a stranger to injustice. After a long dispute and a barbarous quarrel, in the end they went at each other. I spoke at length, urging them to keep calm, since the man of God was well able to share his blessing with both the one and the other.

But these said that the one ought not to receive it, and those tried to deprive the other of it. He threatened them from above and called them dogs, and with difficulty quenched the quarrel. I have told this to show the faith in their minds.

For they would not have raged against one another like this if they had not believed that the blessing of the inspired man had the very greatest power.

I also saw on another occasion a famous miracle take place. Someone came in (he too was a chieftain of the Saracens) and begged that sacred head to help a man who had become paralyzed in his limbs on the road. He said he had suffered this affliction near Callinicum, which is a very large fortress. When the man had been brought into the midst, Simeon told him to renounce the impiety of his forefathers. When he gladly accepted, obeyed, and did what he had been told, Simeon asked whether he believed in the Father, and the only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit. When he confessed that he believed, Simeon said, "Believing in these names, rise up." When he rose, Simeon ordered him to carry the chieftain on his shoulders all the way to his tent. The chieftain had a very large body. The man picked him up and went off at once, and those present moved their tongues in hymns to God. Simeon gave this order in imitation of the Master, who told the paralytic to carry his bed. But let no one call the imitation presumption. For it is his own saying: "Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these." And we have seen the fulfillment of this promise too. For while the Lord's shadow nowhere worked a miracle, the shadow of the great Peter undid death, drove out diseases, and put demons to flight. But it was the Master who worked these miracles too through his servants; and so now likewise, using his name, the godly Simeon works countless miracles. For it happened that another miracle was worked by him that was in no way inferior to the previous one.

One of those who had believed in the saving name of Christ the Master, an Ishmaelite of some distinction, made a vow to God with Simeon as witness, and a promise. The promise was that he would abstain from then on, to the end of his life, from all animal food.
Some time later, somehow or other, he disregarded this promise, killed a bird, and dared to eat it.

But God wished to bring him to repentance by a rebuke, and to honor his own servant who had been witness of the broken promise; so the bird's flesh was changed into the nature of stone, so that even if he wanted to, he could no longer eat it.

For how could he eat from a body that had turned to stone, which he had taken hold of to eat? Struck with amazement at this extraordinary sight, the barbarian hurried to the holy man with great speed, bringing his hidden sin to light, proclaiming his transgression to everyone, and asking forgiveness from God for his fault, calling on the saint for help, so that by his all-powerful prayers he might drag him free from the bonds of sin. Many became eyewitnesses of the miracle, having felt the part near the breast, which was made of bone and stone.

I was not only an eyewitness of his miracles but also heard his predictions of things to come. For he foretold, two years in advance, the drought that came, that great failure of the year's crops, and the famine that followed, together with the plague, saying that he had seen a rod brought down upon mankind, signifying the scourges it would bring. At another time he foretold the onset of what is called the caterpillar, and that it would do no great harm, since divine loving-kindness would accompany the punishment. Thirty days later an immense multitude arrived, so great that it cut off the sunlight and made a makeshift shade; we all saw this clearly. But it ravaged only the fodder of the animals, doing no harm at all to human food. And when I was being attacked by someone, he revealed to me fifteen days beforehand the downfall of my enemy, and I learned by experience the truth of the prediction. I know a great many other such things, but I shall pass them over to avoid making the account too long. These are enough to show the spiritual insight of his mind.
His fame was great even at the court of the king of the Persians.

For, as the envoys who went to him reported, the king made careful inquiry about the man's way of life and the nature of his miracles. They say that the king's wife also asked for oil that had received his blessing, and accepted it as the greatest of gifts. All the king's courtiers, too, were struck by his fame. They had heard many slanders against him from the magi, yet they inquired into the facts carefully, and once they had learned them they called him a man of God. The rest of the crowd went up to the muleteers, the servants and the soldiers, offering them money and begging to receive a share of the blessed oil. The queen of the Ishmaelites was barren and longed for children. First she sent some of her most eminent nobles to beg that she might become a mother. When her request was granted and she had what she longed for, she took the prince she had borne and hurried to the godly old man. Since women were not allowed to approach him, she sent the baby to him and begged that it might receive his blessing. "This sheaf is yours," she said.

"For I brought the seed of prayer with tears, but you made the seed into a sheaf by drawing down the rain of divine grace through your prayer." But how long shall I keep striving to measure the depth of the Atlantic Ocean? For just as its depths cannot be measured by men, so the things he does day by day are beyond all telling. For my part, I admire his endurance above all of these. For night and day he stands in full view of everyone.

He has taken away the doors and pulled down no small part of the enclosure wall, and so he is set before everyone as a new and astonishing sight. Now he stands for a long time; now he bows down again and again, offering worship to God. Many of the bystanders even count these prostrations. Once one of my companions counted twelve hundred and forty-four, and then grew weary and gave up counting. Each time he bows down, he brings his forehead close to his toes. Since his stomach takes food only once a week, and only a little, it lets his back bend easily.

They say that from his standing a chronic ulcer has formed on one of his feet, and that a great deal of pus constantly runs from it. Yet none of these sufferings has broken his discipline. He bears them nobly, both those he has chosen and those he has not, and overcomes both kinds by the strength of his resolve. Once he was compelled to show this ulcer to someone, and I shall tell why. A man came from Rabaena, a worthy man honored with the diaconate of Christ. Reaching the top of the pillar, he said, "Tell me, by the Truth itself, which has turned the human race to God: are you a man, or a bodiless being?" Those present were annoyed at the question, but Symeon ordered them all to keep silent and said to the man, "Why have you asked me this?" The man replied, "Because I hear everyone repeating that you neither eat nor sleep, yet both belong to human beings; for no one with a human nature could live without food and sleep." Then Symeon had a ladder set against the pillar and told the man to climb up. He told him first to examine his hands, then to put his hand inside his leather garment and look not only at his feet but also at the terrible ulcer. When the man had seen it and marveled at how severe the ulcer was, and had learned from him that he did take food, he came down from there, came to me, and told me everything. At the public festivals he displays yet another kind of endurance. From sunset until the sun appears again on the eastern horizon, he stands all night long with his hands stretched up to heaven, neither beguiled by sleep nor overcome by fatigue.
Yet amid such labors, with so great a weight of achievements and so many miracles, he is so humble in mind that he regards himself as the least of all men in worth.

Besides his humility, he is also very approachable, gentle and gracious, and he answers everyone who speaks with him, whether craftsman, beggar or peasant. He has also received from the bountiful Lord the gift of teaching. Twice each day he gives exhortations and floods the ears of his hearers, speaking with great grace and offering the teachings of the divine Spirit. He urges them to look up to heaven and take wing, to break free of the earth, to picture the kingdom they await, to fear the threat of Gehenna, to despise earthly things and to wait for the things to come. One may also see him acting as judge and handing down right and just verdicts.
He does these and similar things after the ninth hour. For he spends the whole night, and the day until the ninth hour, in prayer.
After the ninth hour he first gives divine teaching to those present. Then he receives each person's request, performs some healings, and settles the quarrels of those in dispute.

Around sunset he begins his converse with God once more. But though he is occupied with all this and does all these things, he does not neglect the care of the holy churches. Now he fights against pagan impiety, now he crushes the insolence of the Jews, and at other times he scatters the bands of heretics. Sometimes he writes to the emperor about these matters; sometimes he rouses the magistrates to zeal for God; and at other times he urges the very shepherds of the churches to take greater care of their flocks.

In recounting these things I have tried to show the rain from a single drop, and to give the readers of this work a taste of the honey's sweetness on the tip of my finger. The things that everyone sings of are many times more than these. But I did not undertake to write down everything, only to show in a few examples the character of each man's way of life. Others will no doubt write far more than this, and if he lives on, they may perhaps add still greater miracles. For my part, I long for him, aided by his own prayers, to persevere in these good labors, for he is the common ornament of the world and the glory of true religion. And I beg God that my own life too may be ordered and guided toward the way of life the Gospel teaches.

The common destroyer of mankind has discovered many roads of wickedness, striving to hand over the whole of human nature to utter ruin; and the nurslings of piety, for their part, have devised many different ladders for the ascent to heaven. Some contend in companies (and such communities are countless, beyond number); they enjoy the incorruptible crowns and attain the ascent they long for. Others embrace the solitary life, making it their practice to converse with God alone and taking no share in any human consolation, and in this way they enjoy the herald's proclamation of victory. Others again spend their lives in tents, and others in huts, singing hymns to God.

Others embrace a life in caves and grottoes. But many, some of whom we have already mentioned, chose to have neither cave nor grotto, neither tent nor hut. Instead they gave their bodies over to the open air and endure its opposite extremes, now frozen by unrelenting frost, now scorched by the fire of the sun's rays. Among these, too, the way of life varies. Some stand continually; others divide the day between sitting and standing. Some shut themselves within enclosure walls and avoid the company of the many, while others use no such covering and are exposed to the view of all who wish to look. I have been obliged to go through each of these here because I wish to write the life of the wonderful Baradatus. For he too devised new practices of endurance. First he shut himself in a little hut for a long time and enjoyed divine consolation alone. From there he went up to the ridge above it, built out of wood a small chest that was not even the size of his body, and lived in it, forced to stoop continually, for it was not as high as his body was long.

It was not fitted together with boards, though, but was open like a lattice, and it resembled those windows that have wider openings to let in the light. Because of this he was neither spared the onslaught of the rains nor freed from the blaze of the sun, but received both, just like those others who live in the open air; he surpassed them only in the hardship of confinement.

After continuing in this way for a long time, he later came out, yielding to the exhortations of the inspired Theodotus, who received the presidency of the high priesthood of Antioch. He now stands continually, stretching out his hands to heaven and singing hymns to the God of all, his whole body covered with a leather tunic. Only around his nose and mouth has he left a small opening for breath, so that he can breathe in the common air, since human nature cannot live otherwise. And he endures all this toil although he has not been given a robust body, but is afflicted by a great many ailments. His zeal, however, boiling over and set ablaze by divine love, forces to toil a body that cannot toil.
His mind is also adorned with understanding: he both asks and answers questions excellently, and at times he reasons better and more powerfully than those who have read the labyrinths of Aristotle.

Yet though he stands at the very summit of virtue, he does not let his thoughts climb up with him, but bids them creep below, around the very foothills of the mountain. For he knows how much harm a mind swollen with conceit brings upon itself. Such, in sum, is this man's philosophy; may it keep growing until it reaches the goal of the race.
For the glory of these victors is the common joy of the pious. As for me, supported by his prayers, may I not be far from him who delights in contemplation.

Nor shall I pass over the story of Thalelaeus in silence, for the sight is full of wonder. I have not only heard of it from others' accounts, but have also been an eyewitness of this extraordinary marvel. Twenty stades from Gabala (a small and most charming city) he occupied a hill on which stood a sacred precinct dedicated to demons and honored with many sacrifices by the impious of former times, and there he put up a small hut.
They used to serve those accursed beings, so they said, trying to soothe their great savagery with sacrifices.

For the demons did harm to many, both passers-by and neighbors, and not only to people but also to asses and mules, oxen and sheep, not because they were at war with the dumb animals, but because through them they were plotting against human beings. So when they saw this man arrive, they tried to terrify him, but could not, since faith fenced him round and grace fought on his behalf. Filled therefore with rage and madness, they turned against the trees planted there. There happened to be many flourishing fig and olive trees around that hill, and of these, they say, more than five hundred were suddenly torn up by the roots. This I heard from the neighboring country people, who, though formerly held in the darkness of impiety, received the light of the knowledge of God through his teaching and wonder-working. When even after doing this the accursed demons failed to frighten the athlete of philosophy, they brought other devices against him in turn. At night they howled and displayed torches, trying to scare him and to throw his mind into confusion.

But since he laughed at all their attacks, they finally left him and fled. He then made two wheels two cubits in diameter and joined the two wheels together with boards that were not fitted against one another but set apart. Then he sat inside, fastened those separated boards with pegs and nails, and hung the wheel up in the open air: he fixed three other tall poles in the ground, joined their tops with other pieces of wood, tied that double wheel in the middle of them, and suspended it. The inside of it is two cubits high and one cubit wide. Sitting in it, or rather hanging in it, he has spent ten years so far. Since he has a very large body, he cannot even straighten his neck when seated, but always sits bent over, with his face pressed against his knees. When I came to him, I found him gathering the benefit of the divine Gospels.

I questioned him, eager to learn the reason for that novel way of life, and he answered in Greek, for he was a Cilician by birth: "Since I am subject to many sins and believe in the punishments that have been threatened, I devised this form of life, contriving moderate punishments for the body, so that I may steal away some of the weight of the punishments I expect. For those are harsher not only in quantity but also in their very quality, since they are involuntary. What happens against one's will is extremely painful, but what is voluntary, even if laborious, is less grievous, for the toil is self-chosen and not forced.

So," he said, "if by these small afflictions I lessen what I expect, I shall gain a great profit from it." When I heard this I greatly admired his shrewdness, because he not only contended beyond the appointed arenas and devised further contests of his own, but also understood the reasons for them and taught them to others. The people who live round about said that many miracles take place through his prayer, and that not only people but also camels, asses and mules receive healing. As a result that whole people, long held fast by impiety, renounced the deceit of their ancestors and received the radiance of the divine light. With them as his helpers he both demolished the precinct of the demons and raised a very large shrine to the triumphant martyrs, setting the divine dead against the falsely named gods.
Through their intercessions may he too reach the end of his contests with the same victory, and may we, helped by them and by him, become ardent lovers of the contests of philosophy.
Amen.

Having written of the way of life of the best of men, I think it worthwhile to commemorate also women who have contended no less, if not more. For they are worthy of greater praise, since, though they received a weaker nature, they display the same zeal as men and free their sex from its ancestral shame. I shall now commemorate Marana and Cyra, who have surpassed all other women in the contests of endurance. Their homeland was Beroea; their family was a distinguished one in that city, and their upbringing befitted their family. But they disdained all this, enclosed a small plot just outside the city, went inside it, and walled up the door with mud and stones. When their maidservants were eager to share this life with them, they built a small dwelling outside the enclosure and told them to live in it. Through a small window they watch what the servants do, often rousing them to prayer and kindling them to divine love. They themselves have neither house nor hut, but embrace life in the open air. Instead of a door, a small window has been made for them, through which they receive their necessary food and talk with the women who come to them. The season of Pentecost has been fixed for these conversations; for the rest of the time they embrace a life of silence. Only Marana speaks with the visitors; no one has ever heard the other utter a word. They wear iron chains, and carry such a load that Cyra, who has the weaker body, is bent down to the ground and is quite unable to straighten herself up.

They wear very large mantles, which at the back trail on the ground and completely cover their feet, and in front hang down as far as the waist, completely concealing the face, neck, chest and hands. I have often seen them, having gone in through that door.

For out of respect for the dignity of the priesthood they told me to break through it. So I saw the weight of that iron, which even a strong man could not bear, and after much pleading I managed to have it removed for the time being; but after we left they put it back on their limbs again: the collar on the neck, the belt round the waist, and the pieces meant for the hands and feet. And they have lived in this way not for only five or ten or fifteen years, but for forty-two. Yet after contending for so long, they love the sweat of their labors as though they had only just begun the contest. For as they picture the beauty of the Bridegroom, they bear the toil of the race very easily and lightly, and press on to reach the end of the contests, where they see the Beloved standing and showing them the crown of victory.
That is why, though exposed to the onslaught of rain, snow and sun, they are neither distressed nor pained, but reap delight from what seems grievous.
Emulating the fast of the inspired Moses, they have three times gone without food for that same length of time;
for they took a little food only after forty days.

Three times, too, they emulated the abstinence of the divine Daniel, completing three weeks of days and only then giving food to the body. Once, longing to see the holy places of Christ's saving sufferings, they hastened to Aelia, taking no food on the way; only when they had reached that city and completed their worship did they eat, and then they returned home, again making the journey without food, and the stages of that road are no fewer than twenty. And when they wished to see the shrine of the triumphant Thecla in Isauria, so as to kindle the flame of their love for God from every quarter, they went there and came back without food. To such a degree did divine affection fill them with holy frenzy; so madly did divine love make them long for the Bridegroom. Having adorned the female sex by such a way of life and become models for other women as well, they will be crowned by the Master with the wreaths of victory.
As for me, having set out the benefit to be had from this and gathered its blessing, I shall go on to another story.
The wonderful Domnina, emulating the life of the inspired Maron, whom we also mentioned earlier, set up a small hut in the garden of her mother's house. The hut is made for her of millet stalks.

Spending her days in it, she drenches with constant tears not only her cheeks but also her garments of hair, for in such clothing she covers her body. About cockcrow she goes to the divine church, which is not far away, and together with the others, both women and men, offers hymns to the Master of all. She does this not only at the beginning of the day but also at its close, both believing herself and teaching others that the place dedicated to God is more venerable than any other place. For this reason she also thought it worthy of great care, persuading her mother and brothers to spend their property on it. Her food is lentils soaked in water. And she endures all this toil with a body wasted and half-dead. For very thin skin, like a membrane, covers her thin bones, her fat and flesh having been consumed by her labors.

She is exposed to all who wish to see her, men and women alike, yet she neither looks anyone in the face nor shows her own face to another, but is completely covered by her mantle and bent down to her knees. She speaks very softly and indistinctly, and always utters what she says with tears.

Often she took my right hand and placed it on her eyes, and when she let it go it was so soaked that the hand itself dripped with her tears. What words could worthily praise a woman who, possessing such wealth of philosophy, weeps, laments and groans like those who live in the direst poverty? It is the fervent love of God that gives birth to those tears, kindling the mind toward divine contemplation, piercing it with its rays, and urging it on toward departure from this life. Yet though she spends her days and nights in these things, she does not neglect the other forms of virtue either, but ministers as far as she can to the excellent contestants we have mentioned and to those we have passed over. She also ministers to those who come to her, telling them to lodge with the village pastor while she herself sends them everything they need.

For the property of her mother and brothers is at her disposal to spend, and it reaps a blessing through her. And whenever I come to that area (it is the southern part of our territory), she sends me loaves, fruit and soaked lentils.

But how long shall I strive to draw out an account of all her virtue, when I ought also to set before the public the lives of the other women who have imitated both her and those I mentioned before? For there are many others besides: some have embraced the solitary life, while others have loved life in community, so that two hundred and fifty, or more, or fewer, live together, content with the same food, choosing to sleep only on rush mats, devoting their hands to wool-work and consecrating their tongues to hymns.

Such schools of philosophy are countless, beyond number, not only in our region but throughout the whole East. Palestine is full of them, and Egypt, Asia, Pontus and all Europe. For ever since Christ the Master honored virginity by being born of a virgin, nature has put forth meadows of virginity and offers these fragrant and unfading flowers to the Creator, not dividing virtue into male and female, nor splitting philosophy into two kinds; for the difference lies in bodies, not in souls. For in Christ Jesus, as the divine Apostle says, there is no male and female; one faith has been given to men and women alike. For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in us all; and to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ's gift. And the President of the games has set before the victors one kingdom of heaven, appointing it as the common prize for the contests. So, as I said, there are many training-grounds of piety for both men and women, not only among us but also throughout Syria, in Palestine, in Cilicia and in Mesopotamia. And in Egypt, they say, some monasteries hold as many as five thousand men, who work and meanwhile sing hymns to the Master, and who not only provide their own necessary food from their labor but also help strangers who come to them and the poor.

But to tell of them all is impossible, not only for me but for any writer. And even if it were possible, I think it would be superfluous, an ambition with no profit in it. For those who wish to gain some benefit, what has already been said is enough to supply what they desire.

It is for this reason that we have recorded different ways of life, and have added stories of women to those of men: so that old men and young men and women may have models of philosophy, and that each, taking the impress of the life that suits him, may have the life set down in the story as a rule and measure for his own. Just as painters, looking at their model, copy the eyes, nose, mouth, cheeks, ears and forehead, and even the hair of the head and the beard, and besides these the way the person sits and stands, and even the expression of the eyes, whether cheerful or stern, so it is fitting that each reader of this work who chooses to imitate one of these lives should shape his own after the one he has chosen.

And just as carpenters, straightening boards with a cord, keep cutting away the excess until, laying the rule alongside, they see that the board has become straight, so whoever wishes to emulate one of these lives should set it beside himself as a rule, cut away the excess of vice, and fill up whatever is lacking in virtue. It was for this reason that we took on the labor of writing, offering an occasion of benefit to those who want it. And I ask those who will read it, enjoying the labors of others without labor of their own, to repay those labors with prayer.

I also implore those whose lives I have written not to disregard me as I live far from their spiritual choir, but to draw me up as I lie below, to lead me up to the height of virtue, and to join me to their own choir, so that I may not only praise the wealth of others but may myself have some grounds for praise, glorifying in deed and word and thought Christ the Savior of all, our God, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
